topics.name: Classification of Hydrocarbons
topics.summary: Hydrocarbons (compounds of only C and H) are classified by structure and bonding. Acyclic (open-chain) hydrocarbons include alkanes (C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub>, only C−C/C−H single bonds, saturated), alkenes (C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n</sub>, one or more C=C), and alkynes (C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n−2</sub>, one or more C≡C). Cyclic hydrocarbons include alicyclic compounds (rings of sp<sup>3</sup> carbons, e.g. cyclohexane) and aromatic hydrocarbons (benzene and its derivatives, with a cyclic, planar, conjugated, Huckel-aromatic ring). Degree of unsaturation (DoU), calculated as (2C+2−H)/2 for a C<sub>x</sub>H<sub>y</sub> hydrocarbon, counts the combined total of rings and π-bonds but does NOT by itself reveal which specific combination is present — the same DoU value can correspond to very different structures (e.g. one triple bond, two double bonds, or a ring plus a double bond), so classification ultimately requires knowing the actual connectivity, not the formula alone.
key_formulas: Alkanes: C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub> (DoU=0)
Alkenes / cycloalkanes: C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n</sub> (DoU=1)
Alkynes / alkadienes / cycloalkenes: C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n−2</sub> (DoU=2)
Benzene / arenes: C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n−6</sub> (DoU=4 for benzene itself)
General: DoU = (2C+2−H)/2
topics.worked_example: For C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>8</sub>: DoU = (2×5+2−8)/2 = 2. This could be an alkyne (e.g. pent-1-yne), a diene (e.g. penta-1,3-diene), or a cycloalkene (e.g. methylcyclobutene) — molecular formula alone cannot distinguish these; a chemical test (e.g. ammoniacal AgNO<sub>3</sub> for a terminal alkyne) or full structural information is needed.
common_mistakes: Assuming a compound is 'unsaturated' just because it decolourises bromine water is enough to identify WHICH class it belongs to, without further tests
Confusing DoU=2 automatically with 'must be an alkyne'; it could equally be a diene or a cycloalkene
Treating a ring as if it contributes zero to the degree of unsaturation, when a ring alone contributes exactly 1 DoU, the same as one π bond

topics.name: Nomenclature of Hydrocarbons
topics.summary: IUPAC nomenclature identifies the longest continuous carbon chain containing the principal characteristic feature (e.g. the double/triple bond for alkenes/alkynes), numbers it to give the LOWEST LOCANT to that feature (and, for alkanes, to the first point of difference among substituents), and names substituents as prefixes in strict ALPHABETICAL order (not the order they appear along the chain). Locants for multiple identical substituents use di-, tri-, tetra- (which are ignored in the alphabetization). For alkenes/alkynes, the locant of the multiple bond is the lower-numbered carbon of that bond. When there is a genuine tie in locant sets from either numbering direction, the LOWEST LOCANT RULE resolves it by comparing the complete locant sets term-by-term at the first point of difference, not simply by the substituent count.
key_formulas: Alkane suffix: −ane; Alkene: −ene; Alkyne: −yne
Numbering rule: choose the direction giving the LOWEST LOCANT SET to substituents/multiple bonds, compared at the first point of difference
Substituent citation order: strict ALPHABETICAL, regardless of chain-walking order or locant size
topics.worked_example: CH<sub>3</sub>−CH<sub>2</sub>−CH(C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>)−CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)−CH<sub>3</sub>: longest chain = 5 C (pentane); numbering from the right gives locants {2,3} (methyl at 2, ethyl at 3); numbering from the left gives {3,4} — {2,3} is lower, so that direction is used; substituents cited alphabetically (ethyl before methyl): 3-ethyl-2-methylpentane.
common_mistakes: Citing substituents in the order encountered while numbering, instead of strict alphabetical order in the final name
Numbering from the wrong end and getting a higher locant set purely by starting habit rather than checking both directions
Forgetting that for alkenes/alkynes, the locant is fixed by the position of the multiple bond first, before considering substituent locants

topics.name: Isomerism in Hydrocarbons
topics.summary: Constitutional (structural) isomers share the same molecular formula but differ in atom-to-atom connectivity (e.g. chain/skeletal isomers like n-pentane vs. isopentane, or positional isomers like but-1-yne vs. but-2-yne). Geometrical (cis/trans, a type of stereoisomerism) isomerism arises specifically at a C=C double bond (or in a ring) where rotation is restricted AND each double-bond carbon carries two DIFFERENT groups; if either carbon has two identical groups, no cis/trans distinction is possible. Isomerism strictly requires an IDENTICAL molecular formula — compounds with different formulas (even if 'similar' in some loose sense, like benzene vs. hexatriene) are never isomers of each other. Conformations (rotational forms about a single bond, like anti/gauche in butane) are NOT counted as isomers since they interconvert freely without any bond breaking.
key_formulas: Constitutional isomer test: same molecular formula, different connectivity
Geometrical isomer test: EACH double-bond carbon must bear two DIFFERENT substituents
Not isomers: different molecular formulas, or forms that interconvert by simple bond rotation alone
topics.worked_example: C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub> open-chain alkenes: but-1-ene, but-2-ene, 2-methylpropene are the 3 constitutional skeletons. But-1-ene (terminal =CH<sub>2</sub>, two identical H's on one carbon) and 2-methylpropene (two identical CH<sub>3</sub>'s on one carbon) show NO cis/trans isomerism. But-2-ene (CH<sub>3</sub>/H on each carbon, both different) DOES split into cis and trans — giving 4 total distinct isomers.
common_mistakes: Counting conformations (freely interconverting rotational forms) as separate isomers
Assuming any C=C automatically gives cis/trans isomers without checking BOTH double-bond carbons individually for two different substituents
Treating same-DoU compounds with different molecular formulas as isomers of one another

topics.name: Alkanes: Preparation
topics.summary: Key alkane syntheses: Wurtz reaction (2 RX + 2Na → R−R, dry ether) couples two alkyl halides, giving SYMMETRICAL, even-carbon alkanes cleanly from one halide, but a mixture of three products (statistical) if two DIFFERENT halides are used together (crossed/unsymmetrical Wurtz). Wurtz-Fittig couples an alkyl halide with an aryl halide, suffering the same crossed-coupling mixture problem. Decarboxylation of sodium carboxylate salts with soda lime (NaOH/CaO, Δ) removes the carboxyl carbon as Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>, giving an alkane ONE CARBON SHORTER than the acid. Kolbe electrolysis (2 RCOO<sup>−</sup> → R−R + 2CO<sub>2</sub> + 2e<sup>−</sup>) couples two carboxylate-derived radicals at the anode, also giving symmetric alkanes. Hydrolysis (protonolysis) of a Grignard reagent (RMgX + H<sub>2</sub>O → RH + Mg(OH)X) adds one H to the Grignard's own carbon skeleton, with no C−C coupling.
key_formulas: Wurtz: 2 R−X + 2Na → R−R + 2NaX
Decarboxylation: RCOONa + NaOH →(CaO,Δ) R−H + Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>
Kolbe: 2RCOO<sup>−</sup> → R−R + 2CO<sub>2</sub> + 2e<sup>−</sup> (anode)
Grignard protonolysis: RMgX + H<sub>2</sub>O → R−H + Mg(OH)X
topics.worked_example: To make butane via Wurtz: 2 CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br + 2Na → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>−CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> + 2NaBr (ethyl bromide self-couples to give a 4-carbon, even, symmetric alkane, NOT ethane).
common_mistakes: Expecting Wurtz coupling of a single alkyl halide to preserve its carbon count instead of doubling it
Assuming a crossed Wurtz or Wurtz-Fittig reaction cleanly gives only the desired cross-product, ignoring the two self-coupled side products
Miscounting the carbon-chain-shortening in decarboxylation (product has ONE fewer carbon than the acid, not the same number)

topics.name: Alkanes: Physical Properties and Conformations
topics.summary: Alkane boiling points rise with chain length (more surface area, stronger cumulative van der Waals/London dispersion forces) but FALL with increased branching at constant molecular formula, since branching makes the molecule more compact/spherical, reducing intermolecular contact area (e.g. n-pentane > isopentane > neopentane in boiling point, despite identical molar mass). Alkanes are essentially non-polar (very small electronegativity difference between C and H) and insoluble in water but soluble in non-polar organic solvents. Rotation about C−C single bonds is (nearly) free, giving rise to CONFORMATIONS — different 3D arrangements reached without breaking any bond. For ethane, the staggered conformation (60° dihedral) is lower energy (torsional strain minimised) than the eclipsed conformation (0° dihedral); for butane, anti (180°, substituents furthest apart) is lowest energy, followed by gauche (60°), with eclipsed forms as energy maxima.
key_formulas: Boiling point trend: straight chain > branched (for same molecular formula)
Ethane conformers: staggered (most stable) vs. eclipsed (least stable), energy difference ≈ 12.5 kJ/mol
Butane conformers, stability order: anti > gauche > eclipsed forms
topics.worked_example: Pentane isomers (all C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub>): n-pentane (36°C) > isopentane (28°C) > neopentane (9.5°C) — boiling point falls steadily as the molecule becomes more compact/branched, even though all three have identical molar mass.
common_mistakes: Assuming boiling point depends only on molar mass, ignoring the effect of molecular shape/branching on intermolecular contact area
Treating conformations as separate, isolable compounds like constitutional isomers
Forgetting that gauche (not just eclipsed) conformations are also higher in energy than anti, due to steric/steric-electronic strain between nearby substituents

topics.name: Alkanes: Free Radical Substitution
topics.summary: Alkanes undergo halogenation (X<sub>2</sub>, UV light or heat) via a radical CHAIN mechanism: initiation (X<sub>2</sub> → 2X•, homolysis), propagation (X• abstracts H to form R• + HX; R• abstracts X from X<sub>2</sub> to form RX + X•, regenerating the chain carrier), and termination (radical-radical combination). Selectivity among 1°/2°/3° hydrogens is governed by the relative STABILITY of the intermediate carbon radical (3° > 2° > 1°, via hyperconjugation/induction), which correlates with lower C−H bond dissociation energy (BDE) at more substituted positions. Chlorination is relatively UNSELECTIVE (small rate differences between 1°/2°/3°, e.g. roughly 1:3.8:5 per H), while bromination is HIGHLY selective (roughly 1:82:1600 per H), strongly favouring the most substituted product; this reflects bromination's later, more radical-like transition state (Hammond postulate) compared to chlorination's earlier, more reactant-like one. Benzylic and allylic C−H bonds are especially weak (resonance-stabilised radical), often reacting preferentially even over ordinary 3° positions; NBS is used specifically to achieve selective allylic/benzylic radical substitution over competing ionic addition, by maintaining a very low, steady-state Br<sub>2</sub> concentration.
key_formulas: Radical stability/reactivity order: 3° > 2° > 1° (and benzylic/allylic often exceed ordinary 3°)
Approximate relative rate per H at RT: Cl<sub>2</sub> 1°:2°:3° ≈ 1:3.8:5; Br<sub>2</sub> 1°:2°:3° ≈ 1:82:1600
Product ratio = Σ(H-count × relative rate) for each type, normalised
topics.worked_example: Isopentane (2-methylbutane) monobromination: 4 distinct H-environments exist (two different 1° environments, one 2°, one 3°); despite the 3° H being just 1 of 12 total H's, bromination's very high selectivity makes 2-bromo-2-methylbutane (from the 3° H) the dominant product.
common_mistakes: Using only the statistical H-count (ignoring relative rate per H) to predict the major halogenation product
Assuming chlorination and bromination give the same product ratio, when in fact chlorination is much less selective
Forgetting that benzylic/allylic positions can be MORE reactive than an ordinary 3° position due to resonance (not just hyperconjugative) radical stabilisation

topics.name: Alkanes: Combustion and Pyrolysis
topics.summary: Complete combustion of an alkane C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub> in excess O<sub>2</sub> gives CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O (C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub> + (3n+1)/2 O<sub>2</sub> → nCO<sub>2</sub> + (n+1)H<sub>2</sub>O); incomplete combustion (limited O<sub>2</sub>) instead gives CO or soot (C) alongside H<sub>2</sub>O. More hydrogen-rich (saturated) hydrocarbons require MORE O<sub>2</sub> per mole than less saturated ones with the same carbon count, since the extra hydrogens need additional O<sub>2</sub> to form H<sub>2</sub>O. Combustion analysis (moles CO<sub>2</sub> = moles C; moles H<sub>2</sub>O × 2 = moles H) is used to determine an unknown hydrocarbon's molecular formula. Pyrolysis (cracking) is the thermal decomposition of larger alkanes into smaller alkanes and alkenes (e.g. in petroleum refining) in the absence of air, distinct from combustion (which requires O<sub>2</sub> and is exothermic oxidation).
key_formulas: Complete combustion: C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub> + (3n+1)/2 O<sub>2</sub> → nCO<sub>2</sub> + (n+1)H<sub>2</sub>O
Combustion analysis: mol C = mol CO<sub>2</sub>; mol H = 2 × mol H<sub>2</sub>O
topics.worked_example: Propane: C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub> + 5O<sub>2</sub> → 3CO<sub>2</sub> + 4H<sub>2</sub>O. A sample giving 4 mol CO<sub>2</sub> and 5 mol H<sub>2</sub>O per mole burned implies x=4 (from CO<sub>2</sub>) and y=10 (from 5×2, H<sub>2</sub>O), i.e. C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>, consistent with the alkane general formula C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub> at n=4.
common_mistakes: Equating moles of H<sub>2</sub>O directly to moles of H atoms, forgetting the factor of 2 per H<sub>2</sub>O molecule
Assuming 'complete combustion' can still give CO, when complete (excess O<sub>2</sub>) combustion specifically gives only CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O
Confusing pyrolysis (thermal cracking, no O<sub>2</sub> required) with combustion (oxidation, requires O<sub>2</sub>)

topics.name: Alkenes: Structure and Nomenclature
topics.summary: The C=C double bond consists of one σ bond (sp<sup>2</sup>−sp<sup>2</sup> head-on overlap) and one π bond (unhybridised p-orbital sideways overlap), with all atoms directly attached to either double-bond carbon lying in one plane (trigonal planar geometry, ~120° bond angles). The π bond restricts free rotation about the C=C axis (unlike a C−C single bond), which is the structural basis for geometrical isomerism. IUPAC naming uses the −ene suffix, with the double bond given the lowest possible locant (lower-numbered carbon of the two) even ahead of substituent locants in the standard numbering priority. sp<sup>2</sup> carbons have 33% s-character, giving shorter, stronger C−H bonds than sp<sup>3</sup> carbons' C−H bonds (25% s-character).
key_formulas: C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n</sub> for a single open-chain alkene (DoU=1)
sp<sup>2</sup> hybridisation: 33% s-character; bond angle ≈120°; planar around C=C
π bond: sideways overlap of unhybridised p-orbitals, restricts rotation
topics.worked_example: Pent-2-ene: CH<sub>3</sub>−CH=CH−CH<sub>2</sub>−CH<sub>3</sub>; the double bond gets the lower locant (2) by numbering from the end nearer to it, regardless of where any substituents might otherwise prefer the numbering to start.
common_mistakes: Assuming free rotation is possible about a C=C bond, as it is about a C−C single bond
Miscounting s-character or bond-angle values for sp<sup>2</sup> vs. sp<sup>3</sup> carbons
Prioritising a substituent's locant over the double bond's own locant when numbering the chain

topics.name: Alkenes: Geometrical Isomerism
topics.summary: Cis/trans (geometrical) isomerism occurs at a C=C when EACH double-bond carbon bears two DIFFERENT substituents; if either carbon carries two identical groups, no such isomerism is possible. 'Cis' places the two reference groups (often the largest, or by CIP priority for E/Z) on the SAME side; 'trans' places them on OPPOSITE sides. Since the double bond restricts rotation, cis and trans forms are configurationally distinct, separately isolable compounds with different physical properties (e.g. differing dipole moments, melting/boiling points) — unlike conformations, which interconvert freely. Once a double bond is chemically converted to a single bond (e.g. by hydrogenation) or cleaved (e.g. by ozonolysis), the cis/trans distinction is destroyed, since free rotation is restored (or the molecule is fragmented) and the spatial information is lost.
key_formulas: Geometrical isomerism condition: EACH double-bond carbon must have two DIFFERENT attached groups
Cis: reference groups on same side; Trans: reference groups on opposite sides
topics.worked_example: But-2-ene, CH<sub>3</sub>−CH=CH−CH<sub>3</sub>: each carbon bears CH<sub>3</sub> and H (different), so cis- and trans-but-2-ene both exist as distinct, isolable compounds; cis-but-2-ene has a net dipole moment (bulky groups on the same side), while trans-but-2-ene's dipole moment is approximately zero (symmetric cancellation).
common_mistakes: Assuming ANY C=C shows geometrical isomerism without checking both carbons individually for two different substituents
Expecting cis/trans information to survive full hydrogenation or ozonolysis of the double bond
Confusing geometrical isomerism (restricted C=C rotation) with simple conformational differences (free C−C rotation)

topics.name: Alkenes: Preparation
topics.summary: Key alkene syntheses: acid-catalysed dehydration of an alcohol (conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> or H<sub>3</sub>PO<sub>4</sub>, heat; E1, via a carbocation, losing H<sub>2</sub>O), dehydrohalogenation of an alkyl halide (alcoholic KOH, E2/E1, losing HX), and partial hydrogenation of an alkyne (Lindlar's catalyst for the CIS alkene via syn addition, or Na/liquid NH<sub>3</sub> for the TRANS alkene via anti addition). Both elimination routes (dehydration and dehydrohalogenation) generally follow ZAITSEV'S RULE, favouring the MORE substituted (more stable, more thermodynamically favoured) alkene as the major product when more than one is possible. E2 eliminations proceed through an ANTI-PERIPLANAR transition state, making them stereospecific (a given starting stereochemistry predictably yields a given alkene geometry), unlike E1 (via a planar carbocation, not stereospecific).
key_formulas: Dehydration: R−CH(OH)−R' →(H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>,Δ) alkene + H<sub>2</sub>O (Zaitsev major product)
Dehydrohalogenation: R−CHX−R' →(alc. KOH) alkene + HX (Zaitsev major product)
Lindlar's catalyst: alkyne → CIS alkene (syn addition); Na/liq. NH<sub>3</sub>: alkyne → TRANS alkene (anti addition)
topics.worked_example: 2-Bromobutane + alcoholic KOH: E2 elimination can give but-1-ene (minor, less substituted) or but-2-ene (major, Zaitsev product, more substituted, more stable alkene).
common_mistakes: Predicting the LESS substituted (Hofmann-type) alkene as major, forgetting that standard E1/E2 with a simple base favours the Zaitsev (more substituted) product
Mixing up which catalyst (Lindlar's vs. Na/NH<sub>3</sub>) gives which stereochemistry (cis vs. trans)
Treating E1 as stereospecific in the same way E2 is, when only E2's concerted, anti-periplanar mechanism guarantees a defined geometric outcome

topics.name: Alkenes: Electrophilic Addition Mechanism
topics.summary: Electrophilic addition to an alkene proceeds via: (1) the alkene's electron-rich π bond attacks an electrophile (e.g. H<sup>+</sup> from HX), forming a carbocation intermediate at the carbon that gives the MORE STABLE cation (Markovnikov's rule: 3°>2°>1° cation stability via hyperconjugation/induction); (2) the resulting carbocation is captured by a nucleophile (e.g. X<sup>−</sup>) to give the final product. If a more stable carbocation is accessible via a 1,2-HYDRIDE or ALKYL SHIFT from the initially formed cation, REARRANGEMENT can occur, giving a product mixture reflecting capture of both the original and the rearranged cation. This is a genuinely different mechanism from radical addition (peroxide effect), which proceeds via a radical chain instead of an ionic carbocation pathway.
key_formulas: Carbocation stability: 3° > 2° > 1° (hyperconjugation + induction)
Markovnikov's rule: H adds to the carbon that gives the MORE STABLE carbocation
1,2-shift (hydride or alkyl): occurs when it generates a MORE stable carbocation than the initially formed one
topics.worked_example: 3-Methylbut-1-ene + HCl: H<sup>+</sup> adds to the terminal CH<sub>2</sub>, forming a 2° cation at C2, adjacent to the 3° C3−H; a 1,2-hydride shift converts this to a more stable 3° cation at C3, so BOTH 2-chloro-3-methylbutane (unrearranged) and 2-chloro-2-methylbutane (rearranged, major) can form.
common_mistakes: Predicting only the 'simple' Markovnikov product without checking whether a more stable carbocation is accessible via a hydride/alkyl shift
Confusing the ionic (carbocation) mechanism with the radical (peroxide-effect) mechanism
Forgetting that the mechanism requires TWO distinct steps (electrophile addition, then nucleophile capture), not a single concerted step

topics.name: Alkenes: Markovnikov's Rule and Peroxide Effect
topics.summary: Markovnikov's rule (no peroxide, ionic mechanism): H adds to the LESS substituted alkene carbon, placing the positive charge (and thus the incoming X) on the MORE substituted carbon, since this generates the more stable carbocation intermediate. The peroxide (Kharasch) effect is a documented EXCEPTION specific to HBr (not HCl or HI): in the presence of peroxides, a RADICAL chain mechanism operates instead — peroxide's weak O−O bond homolyses to initiate the chain, generating Br•, which adds FIRST to the LESS hindered (terminal) carbon (giving the more stable, more substituted radical), reversing the final regiochemistry to ANTI-Markovnikov. This effect does not extend to HCl/HI because their H−X bonds don't support a favourable radical chain the way H−Br's does. The same reversal-by-radical-mechanism logic extends to alkynes reacting with HBr/peroxide.
key_formulas: Markovnikov (no peroxide, ionic): H → less-substituted C; X → more-substituted C (via more stable carbocation)
Peroxide effect (HBr only, radical): Br• → less-hindered C first (giving more stable radical); H → more-substituted C (anti-Markovnikov overall)
Peroxide effect is specific to HBr; does NOT occur with HCl or HI
topics.worked_example: 2-Methylpropene + HBr: without peroxide, tert-butyl bromide forms (Br on the 3° carbon, via the 3° cation); WITH peroxide, isobutyl bromide forms instead (Br on the terminal carbon, via the 3° radical forming on the other carbon since Br• adds to the terminal position first).
common_mistakes: Applying the peroxide effect to HCl or HI, when it is specific to HBr
Forgetting that in the radical mechanism, Br (not H) adds FIRST, which is what reverses the final regiochemistry
Assuming peroxide always simply 'reverses Markovnikov's rule' without understanding that it's a genuinely different (radical, not ionic) mechanism operating

topics.name: Alkenes: Oxidation and Ozonolysis
topics.summary: Ozonolysis (O<sub>3</sub>, then a workup step) cleaves the C=C bond and converts EACH double-bond carbon into a carbonyl carbon, reflecting that carbon's own original substituents. REDUCTIVE workup (Zn/H<sub>2</sub>O or Zn/AcOH) stops at aldehydes/ketones; OXIDATIVE workup (H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>) further oxidises any resulting ALDEHYDE (a carbon that had an H) all the way to a carboxylic acid, while KETONE-generating carbons (no H) are unaffected by either workup. For an OPEN-CHAIN alkene, cleavage gives two SEPARATE fragment molecules; for a RING alkene, cleavage does NOT separate the molecule (both former double-bond carbons remain linked via the rest of the ring), giving a SINGLE ring-opened dicarbonyl product instead. Ozonolysis fragments directly encode the original alkene's substitution pattern (useful for structure elucidation, working in either direction), but the cleavage process destroys any cis/trans (geometric) information, since both isomers of a given constitutional alkene give identical fragments.
key_formulas: Reductive workup (Zn/H<sub>2</sub>O): C=C → two C=O (aldehyde if that carbon had an H, ketone if not)
Oxidative workup (H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>): aldehyde-generating carbons oxidised further to −COOH; ketone-generating carbons unaffected
Ring alkene: ONE ring-opened dicarbonyl product (not two separate fragments)
topics.worked_example: 1-Methylcyclohexene, ozonolysis (Zn/H<sub>2</sub>O): the ring opens (both former double-bond carbons stay connected via the other 4 ring carbons) to give a single product, 6-oxoheptanal (one ketone end, from the methyl-bearing carbon; one aldehyde end, from the H-bearing carbon).
common_mistakes: Expecting two separate fragments from a RING alkene's ozonolysis, instead of one ring-opened dicarbonyl compound
Forgetting that oxidative (H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>) workup changes ALDEHYDE fragments to carboxylic acids but leaves ketone fragments unchanged
Assuming ozonolysis products can reveal the original alkene's cis/trans geometry, when in fact that information is destroyed upon cleavage

topics.name: Alkenes: Hydrogenation and Polymerization
topics.summary: Catalytic hydrogenation (H<sub>2</sub>/Ni, Pt, or Pd) adds H<sub>2</sub> syn (same face) across a C=C, converting sp<sup>2</sup> carbons fully to sp<sup>3</sup> and destroying any cis/trans distinction that existed. Heat of hydrogenation (per mole of H<sub>2</sub> consumed) is LOWER for more stable (more substituted) alkenes, since a more stable starting alkene is already closer in energy to the saturated product. Benzene's measured heat of hydrogenation (−208 kJ/mol) is significantly LESS exothermic than 3× a simple alkene's heat of hydrogenation would predict (≈−360 kJ/mol for a hypothetical 'cyclohexatriene'), providing key experimental evidence for benzene's extra thermodynamic stability from aromatic delocalisation (resonance energy ≈152 kJ/mol). Addition (chain-growth) polymerisation of alkenes (e.g. propene → polypropylene) proceeds by repeatedly opening C=C π bonds to form long chains, without loss of any small molecule (unlike condensation polymerisation).
key_formulas: Hydrogenation: C=C + H<sub>2</sub> →(Ni/Pt/Pd) C−C (syn addition, both new C−H bonds on the same face)
More stable (more substituted) alkene → LOWER heat of hydrogenation per mole H<sub>2</sub>
Benzene resonance energy ≈ 3×(alkene ΔH<sub>hydrog</sub>) − (actual benzene ΔH<sub>hydrog</sub>) ≈ 152 kJ/mol
topics.worked_example: Propan-2-ol →(conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, Δ) propene (dehydration); propene monomers then undergo addition polymerisation to give polypropylene, −[CH<sub>2</sub>−CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)]<sub>n</sub>−, without any small-molecule byproduct.
common_mistakes: Expecting cis/trans stereochemistry to survive complete catalytic hydrogenation of a double bond
Assuming a MORE stable alkene releases MORE heat upon hydrogenation, when in fact it releases LESS (since it started closer in energy to the product)
Confusing addition polymerisation (alkenes, no byproduct) with condensation polymerisation (loses a small molecule like water at each step)

topics.name: Alkynes: Structure and Acidic Character
topics.summary: The C≡C triple bond consists of one σ bond and two mutually perpendicular π bonds (sp−sp σ overlap plus two p−p π overlaps), giving a LINEAR geometry (180° bond angle) at each triple-bond carbon. sp carbons have 50% s-character (vs. 33% for sp<sup>2</sup>, 25% for sp<sup>3</sup>), making sp C−H bonds the shortest/strongest (highest BDE) of the three, AND making a terminal alkyne's ≡C−H the most ACIDIC C−H in common hydrocarbons (pKa ≈25, vs. ≈44 for ethene, ≈50 for ethane) — because the resulting sp carbanion's lone pair is held unusually close to the nucleus (high effective electronegativity), strongly stabilising it. This acidity (NOT explained by BDE/radical-stability reasoning, which is a separate, unrelated criterion) allows terminal alkynes to be deprotonated by strong bases (NaNH<sub>2</sub>) or to form insoluble silver/copper acetylide precipitates with ammoniacal AgNO<sub>3</sub>/Cu<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>2</sub>, both standard diagnostic tests that INTERNAL alkynes (no terminal H) do NOT give.
key_formulas: s-character: sp<sup>3</sup> 25% < sp<sup>2</sup> 33% < sp 50%
Acidity (pKa): terminal alkyne ≡C−H (≈25) << alkene =C−H (≈44) < alkane C−H (≈50)
Terminal alkyne + NaNH<sub>2</sub> → sodium acetylide + NH<sub>3</sub> (acid-base, not radical)
topics.worked_example: But-1-yne (terminal) gives a precipitate with ammoniacal AgNO<sub>3</sub> and is deprotonated by NaNH<sub>2</sub>; but-2-yne (internal, both triple-bond carbons bear CH<sub>3</sub>, no terminal H) gives neither reaction — a standard chemical test distinguishing the two constitutional isomers.
common_mistakes: Using BDE/radical-stability reasoning (relevant to halogenation selectivity) to predict acidity, when acidity is governed by CARBANION stability, a different criterion entirely
Forgetting that INTERNAL alkynes give neither the AgNO<sub>3</sub> nor the NaNH<sub>2</sub> reaction, since they lack a terminal C−H
Misremembering the s-character trend or which hybridisation gives the strongest/shortest C−H bond

topics.name: Alkynes: Preparation
topics.summary: Key alkyne syntheses: dehydrohalogenation of a vicinal or geminal dihalide with EXCESS alcoholic KOH (two successive E2 eliminations are required, proceeding via an intermediate vinyl (haloalkene) halide before the second elimination forms the triple bond — using only one equivalent of base stops at the alkene stage). Calcium carbide + water (CaC<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O → Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub> + C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>2</sub>) is the classic industrial/laboratory route specifically to ethyne, historically important for oxy-acetylene welding gas supply. Chain-extension via acetylide alkylation first deprotonates a terminal alkyne with the strong, non-nucleophilic base NaNH<sub>2</sub> (an acid-base reaction, exploiting the terminal ≡C−H's unusual acidity), and the resulting acetylide anion then performs an S<sub>N</sub>2 attack on a PRIMARY alkyl halide only (secondary/tertiary halides instead favour E2 elimination with the strongly basic acetylide), adding one carbon and repositioning the triple bond internally along the newly extended chain.
key_formulas: Dihalide elimination: R−CHX−CH<sub>2</sub>X + 2 KOH(alc.) → R−C≡CH + 2KX + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (via a vinyl halide intermediate)
CaC<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O → Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub> + C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>2</sub>
Chain extension: R−C≡CH →(NaNH<sub>2</sub>) R−C≡C<sup>−</sup>Na<sup>+</sup> →(R'X) R−C≡C−R'
topics.worked_example: Pent-1-yne + NaNH<sub>2</sub>, then CH<sub>3</sub>Br: deprotonates the terminal ≡C−H, then the acetylide anion attacks CH<sub>3</sub>Br (S<sub>N</sub>2), giving hex-2-yne (chain extended by one carbon, triple bond now internal).
common_mistakes: Forgetting that acetylide alkylation only works cleanly with PRIMARY alkyl halides (secondary/tertiary favour E2 elimination instead, due to the acetylide's strong basicity)
Miscounting the number of KOH equivalents needed for full dihalide elimination to an alkyne (2 equivalents, not 1)
Confusing the carbide route's product (ethyne specifically, from CaC<sub>2</sub>) with a general alkyne synthesis applicable to any alkyne

topics.name: Alkynes: Addition Reactions
topics.summary: Alkynes undergo the same broad classes of addition reactions as alkenes (electrophilic addition of HX, X<sub>2</sub>; catalytic hydrogenation; acid-catalysed hydration), but can add TWO equivalents of a simple reagent (one across each π bond) since they start with two π bonds rather than one. HX addition follows Markovnikov's rule (ionic, no peroxide) or anti-Markovnikov (radical, WITH peroxide, extending the peroxide effect to alkynes); a second HX addition to the resulting haloalkene again follows the same regiochemical logic, ultimately giving a GEM-dihalide. Hydration (dil. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>/HgSO<sub>4</sub>) follows Markovnikov addition of water, giving an unstable enol that tautomerises to a ketone (or, for ethyne specifically, to acetaldehyde). Catalytic hydrogenation with Lindlar's catalyst stops cleanly at the CIS alkene (syn addition); Na/liquid NH<sub>3</sub> gives the TRANS alkene (anti addition) instead; excess H<sub>2</sub> over an unpoisoned Ni/Pt/Pd catalyst fully reduces the alkyne all the way to the alkane.
key_formulas: HX addition (Markovnikov, ionic): H → less-substituted C; can repeat for a 2nd equivalent → gem-dihalide
Hydration (Hg<sup>2+</sup>/H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>): alkyne + H<sub>2</sub>O → enol → ketone (Markovnikov, via keto-enol tautomerism)
Lindlar's catalyst → CIS alkene (syn addition); Na/liq. NH<sub>3</sub> → TRANS alkene (anti addition); excess H<sub>2</sub>/Ni → full alkane
topics.worked_example: But-2-yne + H<sub>2</sub>/Lindlar's catalyst → cis-but-2-ene (stops at the alkene stage, syn addition); but-2-yne + Na/liquid NH<sub>3</sub> → trans-but-2-ene (anti addition) instead.
common_mistakes: Forgetting that a second equivalent of HX can add to the intermediate haloalkene, ultimately giving a gem-dihalide rather than stopping after one addition
Mixing up which reagent (Lindlar's vs. Na/NH<sub>3</sub>) gives the cis vs. trans alkene
Assuming excess H<sub>2</sub> over ANY catalyst (including poisoned Lindlar's) fully reduces the alkyne to the alkane, when Lindlar's is specifically poisoned to stop at the alkene

topics.name: Aromatic Hydrocarbons: Structure and Aromaticity
topics.summary: Benzene is a planar, cyclic, fully conjugated ring of 6 sp<sup>2</sup> carbons, each contributing one electron to a continuous, delocalised π system spanning the whole ring (rather than three separate, localised double bonds as a naive Kekule structure might suggest). Huckel's rule (4n+2 π electrons, n=0,1,2,...) predicts aromatic stabilisation for a planar, fully conjugated, cyclic system; benzene (6 π electrons, n=1) satisfies this and shows substantial extra thermodynamic stability (resonance/delocalisation energy) beyond what a simple (hypothetical, non-aromatic) triene structure would have — demonstrated experimentally by benzene's measured heat of hydrogenation (−208 kJ/mol) being significantly LESS exothermic than 3× a typical isolated alkene's value would predict. Aromaticity requires ALL FOUR conditions simultaneously: cyclic, planar, fully conjugated (continuous overlap all the way around the ring), and satisfying the 4n+2 electron count.
key_formulas: Huckel's rule: aromatic if 4n+2 π electrons (n=0,1,2,3,...), and cyclic + planar + fully conjugated
Benzene: 6 π electrons (n=1), DoU=4 (1 ring + 3 π-equivalents)
Resonance/delocalisation energy ≈ 152 kJ/mol (from comparing actual vs. hypothetical hydrogenation enthalpy)
topics.worked_example: 1,3,5-Hexatriene (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>8</sub>, open-chain, 3 conjugated but LOCALISED double bonds) is NOT aromatic and not even an isomer of benzene (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub>, different molecular formula); only benzene's CYCLIC, fully delocalised structure satisfies Huckel's rule.
common_mistakes: Assuming any molecule with 'three alternating double bonds' is automatically aromatic, without checking the cyclic/planar/fully-conjugated requirements
Treating benzene and an open-chain triene as isomers, when they in fact have different molecular formulas
Forgetting that a charged species (e.g. a cation) can also be assessed by Huckel's rule by correctly counting its available π electrons, not just neutral molecules

topics.name: Aromatic Hydrocarbons: Preparation
topics.summary: Key benzene syntheses: cyclic trimerisation of ethyne (3 HC≡CH, passed through a red-hot iron/copper tube) directly builds the aromatic ring from three alkyne units. Catalytic reforming of alkanes (e.g. n-hexane, Pt/Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> catalyst, high temperature) proceeds via cyclisation (to cyclohexane, DoU 0→1) followed by dehydrogenation (losing 3 H<sub>2</sub>, DoU 1→4) to aromatise the ring — the industrially dominant route. Substituted arenes are made via Friedel-Crafts alkylation (RX/AlCl<sub>3</sub>) or acylation (RCOCl/AlCl<sub>3</sub>) on benzene, or via Wurtz-Fittig (aryl halide + alkyl halide + Na, suffering the same crossed-coupling mixture problem as ordinary Wurtz) or Fittig (2 aryl halides + Na, symmetric biaryl coupling) reactions.
key_formulas: Ethyne trimerisation: 3 HC≡CH →(red-hot Fe/Cu tube) C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub>
Catalytic reforming: n-hexane →(cyclisation) cyclohexane →(−3H<sub>2</sub>, dehydrogenation) benzene
Friedel-Crafts alkylation: ArH + RX →(AlCl<sub>3</sub>) Ar−R + HX (prone to POLY-alkylation, since the alkyl product is MORE activated than benzene)
Friedel-Crafts acylation: ArH + RCOCl →(AlCl<sub>3</sub>) Ar−COR + HCl (self-limiting, since the acyl product is DEACTIVATED)
topics.worked_example: n-Hexane (DoU=0) → cyclohexane (DoU=1, ring formed) → benzene (DoU=4, ring + 3 π-equivalents after losing 3 H<sub>2</sub> via dehydrogenation) — the standard industrial aromatisation sequence.
common_mistakes: Expecting Friedel-Crafts ALKYLATION to stop cleanly at monosubstitution, when the alkyl product is MORE reactive than benzene and readily over-alkylates
Attempting Friedel-Crafts reactions (alkylation or acylation) on an already strongly deactivated ring (e.g. benzoic acid, nitrobenzene), which is a known failure case
Confusing the roles of cyclisation (ring formation, DoU 0→1) and dehydrogenation (aromatisation, DoU 1→4) as a single step rather than two distinct stages

topics.name: Aromatic Hydrocarbons: Electrophilic Substitution Mechanism
topics.summary: Electrophilic aromatic substitution (EAS) proceeds via: (1) generation of a strong electrophile (e.g. NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> from HNO<sub>3</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>; an electrophilic Br species from Br<sub>2</sub>/FeBr<sub>3</sub>; SO<sub>3</sub> for sulfonation; a carbocation or acylium ion for Friedel-Crafts), (2) attack of the ring's π electrons on this electrophile, forming a resonance-stabilised ARENIUM (Wheland) intermediate with the positive charge delocalised over three ring positions, and (3) loss of H<sup>+</sup> from the substituted carbon to RESTORE aromaticity, giving net SUBSTITUTION (not addition). This contrasts with simple alkene + Br<sub>2</sub> addition, which needs no catalyst and gives a saturated addition product with no aromaticity to restore. A Lewis acid catalyst (FeBr<sub>3</sub>, AlCl<sub>3</sub>) is typically needed because benzene's aromatic stabilisation makes it markedly LESS reactive toward simple electrophiles than an ordinary alkene.
key_formulas: Nitration electrophile: HNO<sub>3</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> + H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> + 2HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup>
General EAS: ArH + E<sup>+</sup> → [arenium ion, resonance-stabilised] → ArE + H<sup>+</sup>
Friedel-Crafts acylation is self-limiting (acyl group is deactivating); alkylation is prone to over-substitution (alkyl group is activating)
topics.worked_example: Benzene + Br<sub>2</sub>/FeBr<sub>3</sub>: FeBr<sub>3</sub> polarises Br<sub>2</sub> into an electrophilic Br species; the ring attacks it, forming a resonance-stabilised arenium ion; loss of H<sup>+</sup> restores aromaticity, giving bromobenzene (substitution, not addition, unlike a simple alkene's reaction with Br<sub>2</sub>).
common_mistakes: Describing aromatic halogenation as an ADDITION reaction (like alkene + Br<sub>2</sub>), when it is in fact a SUBSTITUTION that restores aromaticity
Forgetting why a Lewis acid catalyst is needed for benzene (to overcome its aromatic stabilisation) when a simple alkene needs no such catalyst
Assuming Friedel-Crafts alkylation and acylation behave identically regarding over-substitution risk, when they in fact differ sharply (alkylation over-reacts; acylation self-limits)

topics.name: Aromatic Hydrocarbons: Directive Influence of Substituents
topics.summary: Substituents on benzene are classified as ACTIVATING/deactivating (do they speed up or slow down further EAS relative to benzene) and o,p-DIRECTING/meta-directing (where does the next substitution occur). Alkyl groups (e.g. −CH<sub>3</sub>) donate electron density by hyperconjugation/induction: activating, o,p-directing. Groups with a lone pair available for resonance donation into the ring (−OCH<sub>3</sub>, −NH<sub>2</sub>) are strongly activating, o,p-directing (resonance donation dominates over any inductive withdrawal). Halogens (−Cl, −Br) are a unique EXCEPTION: weakly o,p-directing (via resonance lone-pair donation) but NET DEACTIVATING overall (inductive withdrawal, from high electronegativity, dominates the rate). Carbonyl-containing and other strongly electron-withdrawing groups (−CHO, −COOH, −NO<sub>2</sub>, −CF<sub>3</sub>) are deactivating AND meta-directing: ortho/para attack would place positive charge (in the arenium resonance structures) directly on or next to the electron-poor substituent-bearing carbon, which is destabilising, so meta attack (avoiding this) is comparatively favoured. Steric hindrance can further modulate the ortho:para ratio within an o,p-directed reaction (often favouring para over the statistically-expected 2:1 ortho excess).
key_formulas: Activating, o,p-directing (resonance-donating or hyperconjugation): −NH<sub>2</sub>, −OH, −OCH<sub>3</sub>, −NHCOCH<sub>3</sub>, alkyl groups
Deactivating but o,p-directing (halogen exception, resonance-donates weakly but induction dominates): −F, −Cl, −Br, −I
Deactivating, meta-directing (inductive/resonance withdrawal): −NO<sub>2</sub>, −CN, −CHO, −COOH, −SO<sub>3</sub>H, −CF<sub>3</sub>
topics.worked_example: Chlorobenzene + HNO<sub>3</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>: −Cl directs o,p (via weak resonance lone-pair donation stabilising the arenium ion there) but net deactivates the ring overall (via stronger inductive withdrawal, making the reaction slower than with benzene itself) — giving predominantly ortho/para-chloronitrobenzene, but at a slower rate than benzene's own nitration.
common_mistakes: Assuming all o,p-directors are activating (missing the halogen exception, which is o,p-directing YET deactivating)
Assuming all deactivating groups are meta-directing (again missing the halogen exception)
Ignoring steric effects when predicting the exact ortho:para ratio within an o,p-directed reaction, especially for bulky substituents

questions.question: Hydrocarbons containing only C−C and C−H single bonds are classified as:
options: Alkanes
Aromatic hydrocarbons
Alkenes
Alkynes
questions.explanation: Compounds made up entirely of single (sigma) bonds between carbon atoms, and between carbon and hydrogen, are saturated hydrocarbons, called alkanes (general formula C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub>).
questions.hint: Think of the simplest, fully saturated hydrocarbon family.
distractor_logic: Alkynes contain a C≡C triple bond, which is also unsaturated.
Alkenes contain at least one C=C double bond, so they are unsaturated, not fully single-bonded.
Aromatic hydrocarbons contain a delocalised, partially double-bond-character ring system, not purely single bonds.

questions.question: Benzene and its derivatives, characterised by a cyclic, planar, conjugated ring, belong to which class of hydrocarbons?
options: Aromatic hydrocarbons
Alicyclic hydrocarbons
Acyclic (open-chain) hydrocarbons
Alkanes
questions.explanation: Benzene and its derivatives are aromatic hydrocarbons — cyclic, planar, fully conjugated systems obeying Hückel's (4n+2) rule, with special stability from electron delocalisation.
questions.hint: This class is named after the characteristic fragrant smell first noticed in early members.
distractor_logic: Alicyclic hydrocarbons are ring compounds that behave chemically like open-chain aliphatics (e.g. cyclohexane), lacking aromatic delocalisation.
Acyclic hydrocarbons have no ring at all, unlike benzene.
Alkanes are saturated open-chain or alicyclic compounds, not aromatic rings.

questions.question: The IUPAC name of CH<sub>3</sub>−CH<sub>2</sub>−CH<sub>2</sub>−CH<sub>3</sub> is:
options: Isobutane
Pentane
Propane
Butane
questions.explanation: A straight chain of four carbon atoms, fully saturated, is named butane using the root 'but-' (four carbons) with the suffix '-ane' for an alkane.
questions.hint: Count the carbon atoms in the chain.
distractor_logic: Pentane has five carbon atoms, one more than this structure.
Isobutane (2-methylpropane) is a branched-chain isomer, but the structure shown is the unbranched straight chain.
Propane has only three carbon atoms (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>), one fewer than this structure.

questions.question: In IUPAC nomenclature, which suffix is used to indicate the presence of a carbon−carbon triple bond?
options: -ene
-ane
-yne
-yl
questions.explanation: The suffix '-yne' replacing '-ane' of the parent alkane denotes one C≡C triple bond, e.g. ethyne, propyne.
questions.hint: This suffix rhymes with the family name 'alkyne'.
distractor_logic: '-ane' denotes a fully saturated chain with no multiple bonds.
'-ene' is the suffix for a carbon−carbon double bond (alkenes), not a triple bond.
'-yl' is used for substituent (alkyl) groups, not for the parent chain's bond type.

questions.question: n-Butane and isobutane (2-methylpropane) have the same molecular formula but different carbon skeletons. This is an example of:
options: Geometrical isomerism
Functional isomerism
Position isomerism
Chain isomerism
questions.explanation: When two compounds share a molecular formula but differ in the arrangement (branching) of the carbon skeleton, they are chain isomers — n-butane is a straight chain while isobutane is branched.
questions.hint: The difference here is in how the carbon chain itself is arranged, not where a substituent sits on an identical chain.
distractor_logic: Functional isomerism involves different functional groups (e.g. an alcohol vs. an ether); both butane isomers are alkanes with no functional group difference.
Geometrical isomerism arises from restricted rotation about a double bond or ring, which does not apply to butane isomers.
Position isomerism involves an identical carbon skeleton with a substituent or multiple bond at a different position, not a different skeleton.

questions.question: Cis−trans isomerism, arising from restricted rotation about a double bond, is a type of:
options: Tautomerism
Geometrical isomerism
Chain isomerism
Optical isomerism
questions.explanation: Cis and trans forms are geometrical (a class of stereo-) isomers: the atoms are connected in the same order, but their spatial arrangement about the rigid C=C differs.
questions.hint: This isomerism is about spatial arrangement around a rigid double bond, not connectivity.
distractor_logic: Tautomerism involves rapid interconversion between two structures differing in the position of a proton and a double bond, not a fixed cis/trans arrangement.
Chain isomerism involves different carbon skeletons, which is a structural (not spatial) difference.
Optical isomerism arises from a chiral centre producing non-superimposable mirror images, a different phenomenon from cis/trans geometry.

questions.question: In the Wurtz reaction, an alkyl halide is treated with sodium metal in the presence of:
options: Aqueous NaOH
Concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>
Dry ether
Alcoholic KOH
questions.explanation: The Wurtz reaction couples two alkyl halide molecules using sodium metal in dry ether (an inert, moisture-free solvent) to form a higher alkane: 2R−X + 2Na → R−R + 2NaX.
questions.hint: The solvent must be free of moisture, since sodium reacts violently with water.
distractor_logic: Aqueous NaOH would hydrolyse the alkyl halide and react destructively with sodium metal; it is not the Wurtz solvent.
Concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> is used in alcohol dehydration to alkenes, not in the Wurtz coupling.
Alcoholic KOH is used for dehydrohalogenation to form alkenes, the opposite of forming a saturated alkane by coupling.

questions.question: Kolbe's electrolytic method prepares alkanes by electrolysing an aqueous solution of:
options: A Grignard reagent
An alkyl halide
An alkene
Sodium or potassium salt of a carboxylic acid
questions.explanation: In Kolbe's electrolysis, the carboxylate anion loses an electron at the anode, decarboxylates, and the resulting alkyl radicals combine to give an alkane with double the carbon count of the acid's alkyl chain.
questions.hint: This method starts from a carboxylic acid salt, not a halide.
distractor_logic: An alkene is a product of elimination reactions, not a starting material for Kolbe's method.
An alkyl halide is the starting material for the Wurtz reaction, not Kolbe's electrolysis.
A Grignard reagent reacting with a protic source (like water or an alcohol) also gives an alkane, but that is a separate method, not electrolysis.

questions.question: The conformation of ethane in which the C−H bonds on adjacent carbons are maximally apart (dihedral angle 60°) is called the:
options: Anti conformation
Eclipsed conformation
Staggered conformation
Gauche conformation
questions.explanation: In the staggered conformation, the hydrogens on the front carbon are positioned exactly between those on the back carbon (60° apart), minimising torsional strain and making it the most stable conformation of ethane.
questions.hint: This is the lower-energy, more stable of the two extreme conformations of ethane.
distractor_logic: 'Gauche' is a term used for substituted systems like butane's 60° conformer, not the standard name for ethane's staggered form.
The eclipsed conformation has front and back hydrogens directly aligned (0° apart), which is higher in energy, the opposite of what is described.
'Anti' describes the 180° conformer of substituted ethanes like butane, a term not typically applied to plain ethane.

questions.question: Halogenation of alkanes in sunlight or UV light proceeds through which type of mechanism?
options: Electrophilic substitution
Electrophilic addition
Nucleophilic substitution
Free radical substitution
questions.explanation: Alkane halogenation is initiated by homolytic fission of the halogen molecule under light or heat, generating halogen free radicals that substitute a hydrogen atom in a chain mechanism (initiation, propagation, termination).
questions.hint: Alkanes have no pi bonds or polar sites, so ionic mechanisms are not favoured; the reaction needs light/heat to generate reactive species.
distractor_logic: Nucleophilic substitution is characteristic of polar substrates like alkyl halides reacting with a nucleophile, not the non-polar C−H bonds of alkanes.
Electrophilic addition applies to unsaturated substrates with a pi bond (like alkenes), which alkanes lack.
Electrophilic substitution is characteristic of aromatic rings with a delocalised pi system, not saturated alkanes.

questions.question: In the free radical halogenation chain mechanism, the step in which Cl<sub>2</sub> absorbs light energy and splits into two chlorine radicals is called:
options: Initiation
Chain transfer
Propagation
Termination
questions.explanation: Initiation is the first step, where the halogen molecule undergoes homolytic fission (Cl<sub>2</sub> → 2Cl•) to generate the radicals that start the chain.
questions.hint: This is the very first step that creates the reactive radical species.
distractor_logic: 'Chain transfer' is not one of the three standard steps (initiation, propagation, termination) of this mechanism.
Termination involves two radicals combining to end the chain, the opposite of generating the first radicals.
Propagation steps consume and regenerate radicals (e.g. Cl• abstracting H, then the resulting alkyl radical reacting with Cl<sub>2</sub>), occurring after initiation.

questions.question: Complete combustion of an alkane in excess oxygen produces carbon dioxide and:
options: Soot (carbon)
Hydrogen gas
Water
Carbon monoxide
questions.explanation: Complete combustion fully oxidises both carbon and hydrogen: C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub> + O<sub>2</sub> → CO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O, releasing heat and light.
questions.hint: Think of what a hydrocarbon's hydrogen atoms turn into when fully oxidised.
distractor_logic: Hydrogen gas is not released in combustion; the hydrogen atoms are oxidised to water, not liberated as H<sub>2</sub>.
Carbon monoxide forms only during incomplete combustion with limited oxygen, not complete combustion.
Soot (unburnt carbon) also forms under incomplete/limited-oxygen combustion, not complete combustion.

questions.question: The thermal decomposition of higher alkanes into smaller alkanes and alkenes in the absence of air is called:
options: Hydrogenation
Pyrolysis (cracking)
Wurtz reaction
Ozonolysis
questions.explanation: Pyrolysis (also called cracking) breaks C−C and C−H bonds of higher alkanes at high temperature without air, giving a mixture of lower alkanes and alkenes; this underlies industrial cracking of petroleum.
questions.hint: This is the industrial process by which petroleum fractions are broken down into smaller, more useful hydrocarbons.
distractor_logic: The Wurtz reaction builds a longer alkane by coupling two alkyl halides; it does not break down alkanes.
Hydrogenation adds H<sub>2</sub> across a multiple bond; it does not decompose alkanes thermally.
Ozonolysis is an oxidative cleavage of a C=C double bond using ozone, unrelated to thermal decomposition of alkanes.

questions.question: The two carbon atoms joined by a C=C double bond in an alkene are:
options: Not hybridised
sp<sup>3</sup> hybridised
sp hybridised
sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised
questions.explanation: Each doubly-bonded carbon in an alkene uses three sp<sup>2</sup> hybrid orbitals for sigma bonds (trigonal planar, 120° bond angles) and one unhybridised p orbital for the pi bond.
questions.hint: The geometry around each double-bond carbon is trigonal planar with 120° angles.
distractor_logic: sp<sup>3</sup> hybridisation gives tetrahedral geometry with no p orbital available for a pi bond, characteristic of alkanes.
sp hybridisation corresponds to linear geometry with 180° angles, found at triple-bond carbons in alkynes, not alkenes.
The carbons are definitely hybridised (sp<sup>2</sup>); an unhybridised carbon description does not apply here.

questions.question: The IUPAC suffix used to indicate one carbon−carbon double bond in the parent chain is:
options: -yne
-ane
-diene
-ene
questions.explanation: Replacing '-ane' with '-ene' in the parent alkane name signals exactly one C=C double bond, with a locant indicating its position, e.g. but-2-ene.
questions.hint: This suffix is one letter different from the alkyne suffix.
distractor_logic: '-ane' denotes full saturation, no multiple bonds at all.
'-yne' denotes a carbon−carbon triple bond, not a double bond.
'-diene' indicates two double bonds, not one.

questions.question: Geometrical (cis−trans) isomerism in alkenes arises because of:
options: Free rotation about the C−C single bond
The presence of a chiral carbon
Resonance delocalisation
Restricted rotation about the C=C double bond
questions.explanation: The pi bond of C=C prevents free rotation (rotation would require breaking the p-orbital overlap), locking substituents on each carbon into fixed relative positions — the basis of cis/trans forms.
questions.hint: Think about what a double bond restricts that a single bond does not.
distractor_logic: A chiral carbon gives rise to optical isomerism, a different phenomenon from cis/trans geometry.
Free rotation about a single bond is exactly what does NOT produce distinct, isolable geometrical isomers (conformers interconvert freely).
Resonance delocalisation (as in benzene) is unrelated to the fixed geometry that produces cis/trans forms.

questions.question: For a double-bonded carbon to be capable of showing geometrical isomerism, it must bear:
options: Two identical groups
No hydrogen atoms
Two different groups
Only one substituent
questions.explanation: Geometrical isomerism requires that each doubly-bonded carbon carry two different substituents; if either carbon bears two identical groups, swapping them gives the same molecule, so no distinct cis/trans forms exist.
questions.hint: If swapping the two groups on one carbon gave back an identical molecule, could there be a distinct 'other' isomer?
distractor_logic: Two identical groups on a double-bond carbon means swapping them changes nothing, so no separate cis/trans isomer can exist for that carbon.
The presence or absence of hydrogen is not the deciding factor; what matters is whether the two groups on each carbon differ.
Each double-bond carbon has exactly two substituents (not one), and both must differ for geometrical isomerism.

questions.question: Treating an alkyl halide with alcoholic KOH (dehydrohalogenation) produces:
options: An alcohol
An alkene
An alkyne
An alkane
questions.explanation: Alcoholic KOH acts as a base, eliminating HX from the alkyl halide (E2/E1 elimination) to form a carbon−carbon double bond, i.e. an alkene.
questions.hint: This is an elimination reaction, removing H and X from adjacent carbons.
distractor_logic: Aqueous (not alcoholic) KOH favours substitution to give an alcohol; the alcoholic medium favours elimination instead.
Forming an alkyne would require elimination of two equivalents of HX from a dihalide, not one equivalent from a monohalide.
Forming an alkane would require reduction/addition of hydrogen, not elimination of HX.

questions.question: Dehydration of an alcohol to an alkene is commonly carried out using:
options: Concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (or Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>) with heat
Alcoholic KOH
Sodium metal in dry ether
Dilute aqueous NaOH
questions.explanation: Heating an alcohol with concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (or passing its vapour over hot Al<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub>) removes a molecule of water, forming a C=C double bond.
questions.hint: This reagent is also a strong dehydrating agent used elsewhere in organic chemistry.
distractor_logic: Alcoholic KOH is used to eliminate HX from alkyl halides, not H<sub>2</sub>O from alcohols.
Sodium metal in dry ether is the Wurtz reaction reagent, used with alkyl halides, not alcohols.
Dilute aqueous NaOH would not dehydrate an alcohol; it is more associated with substitution/hydrolysis conditions.

questions.question: In the addition of HBr to an alkene, the reactive intermediate formed after the electrophile (H<sup>+</sup>) adds to the double bond is a:
options: Free radical
Carbene
Carbocation
Carbanion
questions.explanation: The alkene's pi electrons attack H<sup>+</sup>, forming a bond to one carbon and leaving a positive charge (an empty p orbital) on the other carbon — a carbocation, which is then attacked by Br<sup>−</sup>.
questions.hint: The pi electrons are used to bond to H<sup>+</sup>, leaving one carbon electron-deficient.
distractor_logic: A carbene is a neutral divalent carbon species, not the intermediate formed in simple electrophilic addition of HX.
A free radical (unpaired electron) is the intermediate in peroxide-catalysed anti-Markovnikov addition, a different (radical) mechanism, not the ionic one described here.
A carbanion carries a negative charge with a lone pair, the opposite of the electron-deficient species formed when an alkene reacts with an electrophile.

questions.question: Electrophilic addition reactions of alkenes are initiated because the C=C pi bond:
options: Is electron-deficient and attacks a nucleophile
Is electron-rich and attacks an electrophile
Is non-polar and unreactive
Undergoes homolytic fission spontaneously
questions.explanation: The loosely held, exposed pi electron cloud above and below the plane of the double bond makes alkenes electron-rich, so they readily attack electron-seeking species (electrophiles) to begin the addition.
questions.hint: Think about which reagent type (electron-seeking or electron-rich) an alkene's exposed pi cloud would naturally attract.
distractor_logic: Spontaneous homolytic fission describes radical initiation (e.g. by light/peroxide/heat), not the normal ionic electrophilic addition pathway.
An electron-deficient species attacking a nucleophile describes electrophilic behaviour, the opposite of how the electron-rich alkene actually behaves.
The pi bond is reactive, not unreactive; its exposed electron density is exactly why alkenes undergo addition readily.

questions.topic: Alkenes: Markovnikov's Rule and Peroxide Effect
questions.question: According to Markovnikov's rule, when HX adds to an unsymmetrical alkene, the hydrogen atom attaches to the carbon that:
options: Is more highly substituted
Bears the halogen in the product
Already carries the greater number of hydrogen atoms
Already carries the fewer number of hydrogen atoms
questions.explanation: Markovnikov's rule: 'the negative part of the addendum (X) goes to the carbon with fewer hydrogens,' which is equivalent to saying H adds to the carbon already richer in hydrogens — this pathway forms the more stable (more substituted) carbocation.
questions.hint: Remember the rule is often paraphrased as 'the rich get richer' in hydrogens.
distractor_logic: Where the halogen ends up in the product is the complementary fact, but it does not describe where H attaches.
This describes where X (not H) ends up, which is the reverse assignment of the rule.
The more highly substituted carbon is where X ends up (via the more stable carbocation), not where H adds.

questions.topic: Alkenes: Markovnikov's Rule and Peroxide Effect
questions.question: The peroxide effect (Kharasch effect), which reverses the normal addition regiochemistry, is observed specifically for the addition of:
options: HBr in the presence of peroxides
HCl in the presence of peroxides
H<sub>2</sub> in the presence of peroxides
HI in the presence of peroxides
questions.explanation: The peroxide effect is unique to HBr: the Br• radical chain propagation is thermodynamically favourable, giving anti-Markovnikov addition. For HCl the H−Cl bond is too strong for efficient radical initiation, and for HI the propagation step is endothermic and radical iodine tends to recombine, so neither shows the effect.
questions.hint: This effect is famously limited to just one of the three common hydrogen halides.
distractor_logic: HI does not show the peroxide effect because iodine radical addition is endothermic and reverses easily, preventing an efficient radical chain.
HCl does not show the peroxide effect because the radical chain propagation step is energetically unfavourable for chlorine under these conditions.
H<sub>2</sub> addition is a catalytic hydrogenation (syn addition on a metal surface), not a radical HX addition, so the peroxide effect concept does not apply to it.

questions.question: Ozonolysis of an alkene, followed by Zn/H<sub>2</sub>O (reductive) workup, cleaves the double bond to give:
options: Carboxylic acids only
Alkyl halides
Carbonyl compounds (aldehydes and/or ketones)
Alcohols only
questions.explanation: Ozone adds across C=C to form an ozonide, which reductive workup with Zn dust and water cleaves into two carbonyl fragments — aldehydes from =CH− carbons, ketones from fully substituted =C< carbons.
questions.hint: The reductive workup (Zn/H<sub>2</sub>O) is specifically chosen to avoid over-oxidising the products further.
distractor_logic: Alkyl halides are unrelated to ozonolysis chemistry; no halogen source is involved.
Alcohols are not the direct ozonolysis product; the double bond is cleaved and oxidised, not simply hydrated.
Carboxylic acids form only if an oxidative workup (e.g. H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>) is used instead of the reductive Zn/H<sub>2</sub>O workup, which further oxidises any aldehyde formed.

questions.question: Baeyer's reagent, used as a simple test for unsaturation, is:
options: Cold, dilute, alkaline KMnO<sub>4</sub>
Bromine water at high temperature
Hot, concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>
Ammoniacal AgNO<sub>3</sub>
questions.explanation: Cold dilute alkaline KMnO<sub>4</sub> (Baeyer's reagent) oxidises an alkene to a vicinal diol, decolourising the purple permanganate colour — a positive test for unsaturation.
questions.hint: This reagent is a mild oxidant known for its distinctive purple colour that fades when it reacts.
distractor_logic: Ammoniacal AgNO<sub>3</sub> (Tollens'-type reagent) tests for terminal alkynes (acidic C−H) or aldehydes, not general unsaturation.
Bromine water is indeed used to test unsaturation via decolourisation, but it is used cold and is a separate reagent from Baeyer's (KMnO<sub>4</sub>-based) test named here.
Hot concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> is a strong dehydrating/oxidising acid used in different contexts, not the standard mild unsaturation test.

questions.question: Catalytic hydrogenation of an alkene to the corresponding alkane commonly uses which catalyst?
options: Anhydrous AlCl<sub>3</sub>
Concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>
Peroxide
Finely divided Ni, Pd, or Pt
questions.explanation: H<sub>2</sub> adds syn (from the same face) across the C=C double bond on the surface of a finely divided metal catalyst such as Ni, Pd, or Pt, saturating the alkene to an alkane.
questions.hint: These are transition-metal catalysts, not acids or radical initiators.
distractor_logic: Peroxide initiates radical addition of HBr (anti-Markovnikov), not catalytic hydrogenation with H<sub>2</sub>.
Concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> is used for hydration or dehydration reactions, not for catalysing H<sub>2</sub> addition.
Anhydrous AlCl<sub>3</sub> is a Lewis acid catalyst used in Friedel−Crafts reactions on aromatic rings, not alkene hydrogenation.

questions.question: The addition polymer formed from many ethene (CH<sub>2</sub>=CH<sub>2</sub>) monomer units is called:
options: Natural rubber
PVC (polyvinyl chloride)
Polystyrene
Polythene (polyethylene)
questions.explanation: Repeated addition of ethene monomers under heat/pressure with a catalyst opens each C=C and links the units into a long saturated chain, −(CH<sub>2</sub>−CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>n</sub>−, called polythene.
questions.hint: This is the most common plastic, used for bags and containers, named directly after its monomer's family.
distractor_logic: PVC is the polymer of vinyl chloride (chloroethene), which carries a chlorine substituent, not plain ethene.
Natural rubber is a polymer of isoprene (2-methylbuta-1,3-diene), a naturally occurring diene, not a synthetic ethene polymer.
Polystyrene is the polymer of styrene (phenylethene), which carries a benzene ring substituent, not plain ethene.

questions.question: The carbon atoms joined by a carbon−carbon triple bond in an alkyne are:
options: sp<sup>3</sup> hybridised
sp hybridised
d<sup>2</sup>sp<sup>3</sup> hybridised
sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised
questions.explanation: Each triple-bond carbon uses two sp hybrid orbitals for linear (180°) sigma bonding and has two unhybridised p orbitals forming two mutually perpendicular pi bonds.
questions.hint: This hybridisation gives the linear geometry characteristic of a triple bond.
distractor_logic: d<sup>2</sup>sp<sup>3</sup> hybridisation describes octahedral coordination complexes, irrelevant to simple carbon hybridisation in hydrocarbons.
sp<sup>3</sup> hybridisation gives tetrahedral geometry with no p orbitals free for pi bonding, characteristic of alkanes.
sp<sup>2</sup> hybridisation gives trigonal planar geometry with one p orbital, appropriate for a double bond (alkenes), not a triple bond.

questions.question: Terminal alkynes (R−C≡C−H) show weakly acidic character because the C−H bond involved is attached to a carbon that is:
options: sp hybridised
Not hybridised
sp<sup>3</sup> hybridised
sp<sup>2</sup> hybridised
questions.explanation: An sp carbon has 50% s-character, holding its bonding electrons closer to the nucleus; this makes the sp C−H bond more polarised and the hydrogen more easily removed as H<sup>+</sup>, compared to sp<sup>2</sup> or sp<sup>3</sup> C−H bonds with less s-character.
questions.hint: Greater s-character in a hybrid orbital pulls bonding electrons closer to the carbon nucleus.
distractor_logic: sp<sup>3</sup> carbons (as in alkanes) have the least s-character (25%) among these, making alkane C−H bonds essentially non-acidic.
The carbon is definitely hybridised (sp); the acidity is a direct consequence of that specific hybridisation, not an absence of hybridisation.
sp<sup>2</sup> carbons (as in alkenes) have less s-character (33%) than sp carbons, making their C−H bonds less acidic.

questions.question: The reaction of calcium carbide (CaC<sub>2</sub>) with water produces which alkyne?
options: Ethyne (acetylene)
Benzyne
But-1-yne
Propyne
questions.explanation: CaC<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O → Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub> + HC≡CH (ethyne); this reaction is the classic industrial/laboratory route to acetylene gas.
questions.hint: This is the two-carbon parent member of the alkyne family, commonly called acetylene.
distractor_logic: Benzyne is a highly reactive aromatic triple-bond intermediate formed under very different (strong base, aryl halide) conditions, unrelated to calcium carbide hydrolysis.
Propyne (a three-carbon alkyne) is not the product of calcium carbide hydrolysis, which gives only the two-carbon alkyne.
But-1-yne (a four-carbon alkyne) is likewise not formed from this two-carbon-yielding reaction.

questions.question: Treating a vicinal or geminal dihalide with excess alcoholic KOH (double dehydrohalogenation) produces:
options: An alkene
An alkane
A diol
An alkyne
questions.explanation: Excess alcoholic KOH eliminates two molecules of HX in succession from a dihalide (one HX to give an alkenyl halide, a second HX to give the triple bond), producing an alkyne.
questions.hint: This is the same elimination chemistry used to make alkenes from monohalides, but applied twice.
distractor_logic: A diol would form from hydrolysis (substitution) of both halogens by −OH, not from base-mediated elimination.
An alkene would result from only a single elimination (one HX removed) from a monohalide, not the double elimination described here from a dihalide.
An alkane would require addition of hydrogen, the opposite of the elimination chemistry occurring here.

questions.question: Complete hydration of an alkyne (H<sub>2</sub>O, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, HgSO<sub>4</sub>) proceeds through an unstable enol intermediate that rearranges to give a:
options: Alcohol only, no rearrangement
Carbonyl compound (aldehyde or ketone)
Alkyl halide
Carboxylic acid
questions.explanation: Markovnikov addition of water to the triple bond first gives an enol (a C=C bearing −OH), which is unstable and tautomerises to the more stable carbonyl form — ethyne uniquely gives acetaldehyde, while other alkynes give ketones.
questions.hint: The initial addition product has both a double bond and an −OH on the same carbon, which is an unstable arrangement.
distractor_logic: No halogen source is present in this hydration reaction, so an alkyl halide cannot be the product.
A carboxylic acid would require further oxidation beyond simple hydration, not the mechanism described here.
The enol intermediate is not stable on its own; it always tautomerises further to the carbonyl form, so 'no rearrangement' is incorrect.

questions.question: The delocalised pi electron cloud in benzene's aromatic ring consists of how many pi electrons?
questions.explanation: Benzene has three formal C=C double bonds contributing 2 pi electrons each, giving 6 delocalised pi electrons spread over the ring — satisfying Hückel's (4n+2) rule with n = 1.
questions.hint: Count the pi electrons from the three alternating double bonds in the Kekulé structure.
distractor_logic: 8 pi electrons would satisfy 4n with n = 2 (an anti-aromatic count), not the (4n+2) aromatic count that benzene actually has.
3 pi electrons is an odd number, which cannot arise from electron pairs in pi bonds at all.
4 pi electrons would correspond to n = 0.5 in Hückel's rule, which is not an integer, so it does not satisfy the aromaticity condition and undercounts benzene's three double bonds.

questions.question: For a ring system to be aromatic by Hückel's rule, besides having (4n+2) pi electrons, it must also be:
options: Planar, cyclic, and fully conjugated
Non-planar and cyclic
Saturated with no pi electrons
Acyclic with alternating double bonds
questions.explanation: Hückel's rule applies only to rings that are planar (allowing continuous p-orbital overlap), cyclic (closed loop), and fully conjugated (uninterrupted alternating multiple/single bonds) — only then does the (4n+2) pi-electron count confer aromatic stability.
questions.hint: Continuous overlap of p orbitals around the entire ring is essential, which requires a specific molecular shape.
distractor_logic: A saturated ring has no pi electrons at all, and therefore cannot satisfy the (4n+2) pi-electron requirement in the first place.
Aromaticity specifically requires a cyclic (ring) structure; an acyclic system cannot be aromatic regardless of double bond pattern.
Non-planarity disrupts continuous p-orbital overlap around the ring, preventing true delocalisation even if the electron count matches.

questions.question: Passing ethyne through a red-hot iron tube at 873 K converts three molecules of ethyne into one molecule of benzene. This is an example of:
options: Decarboxylation
Cyclic polymerisation (trimerisation)
Friedel−Crafts alkylation
Wurtz−Fittig reaction
questions.explanation: 3HC≡CH → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub> under these conditions is a cyclic trimerisation: three alkyne units combine and cyclise to form the aromatic benzene ring.
questions.hint: Three identical small molecules are joining together and closing into a ring.
distractor_logic: Friedel−Crafts alkylation attaches an alkyl group to an existing aromatic ring using a Lewis acid catalyst; it does not build the ring itself from ethyne.
Decarboxylation removes a −COOH group as CO<sub>2</sub>, unrelated to this alkyne-to-arene cyclisation.
The Wurtz−Fittig reaction couples an aryl halide with an alkyl halide using sodium, an entirely different reagent set from this thermal trimerisation.

questions.question: Heating sodium benzoate with soda lime (NaOH + CaO) gives which product?
options: Phenol
Toluene
Benzaldehyde
Benzene
questions.explanation: This is a decarboxylation reaction: the −COONa group is replaced by −H, releasing Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> and yielding benzene (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COONa + NaOH → C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub> + Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>).
questions.hint: Soda lime decarboxylation removes the carboxylate group entirely, replacing it with hydrogen.
distractor_logic: Phenol would require the carboxylate to be replaced by −OH, not −H, which is not what decarboxylation does.
Benzaldehyde retains a carbon-bearing functional group (−CHO); decarboxylation removes carbon (as CO<sub>2</sub>-derived carbonate) rather than converting it to an aldehyde.
Toluene has an extra methyl group not present in sodium benzoate's starting skeleton, so simple decarboxylation cannot produce it.

questions.question: Benzene typically undergoes substitution reactions rather than addition reactions mainly because substitution:
options: Regenerates the stable, delocalised aromatic ring
Is always faster than addition, regardless of ring stability
Proceeds without any intermediate
Requires a weaker electrophile
questions.explanation: Addition would permanently destroy the ring's cyclic delocalisation and aromatic stabilisation energy. Substitution lets the electrophile replace a hydrogen while the ring re-aromatises (loses H<sup>+</sup> from the arenium intermediate), preserving that stability.
questions.hint: Think about what happens to the ring's special stability if two pi electrons were used up in an addition instead.
distractor_logic: Both pathways proceed through an intermediate (the arenium/sigma-complex cation for substitution); substitution is not intermediate-free.
The strength of the electrophile does not determine substitution vs. addition preference; the driving force is preserving ring aromaticity.
The preference for substitution is specifically because of aromatic stability being regained, not an unconditional, structure-independent speed rule.

questions.question: In the nitration of benzene using conc. HNO<sub>3</sub>/conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, the electrophile that actually attacks the ring is:
options: Nitrous acid, HNO<sub>2</sub>
Ammonium ion, NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>
Nitronium ion, NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>
Nitrate ion, NO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup>
questions.explanation: Conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> protonates HNO<sub>3</sub>, which loses water to generate the electrophilic nitronium ion, NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>, the actual species that attacks benzene's pi cloud.
questions.hint: This electrophile is generated in situ from nitric acid by protonation and loss of water.
distractor_logic: The ammonium ion contains no nitrogen−oxygen bonds at all and plays no role in nitration chemistry.
Nitrous acid (HNO<sub>2</sub>) is a different, lower-oxidation-state nitrogen species not generated or used in this nitration mixture.
The nitrate ion is negatively charged (a nucleophile/leaving group in other contexts), not the electrophile that attacks the electron-rich ring.

questions.topic: Aromatic Hydrocarbons: Directive Influence of Substituents
questions.question: The −OH and −NH<sub>2</sub> groups on a benzene ring are, respectively:
options: Weakly activating and meta-directing
Strongly deactivating and meta-directing
Strongly activating and ortho/para-directing
Deactivating and ortho/para-directing
questions.explanation: −OH and −NH<sub>2</sub> donate a lone pair into the ring by resonance, strongly increasing electron density (activating) and concentrating it at the ortho and para positions (ortho/para-directing).
questions.hint: These groups have a lone pair on the atom directly attached to the ring, which they can donate into the pi system.
distractor_logic: These substituents activate rather than deactivate the ring, since lone-pair donation increases electron density at ortho/para positions rather than withdrawing it.
Their activating effect is strong, not merely weak, since a full lone pair is donated directly into the ring; and the directing pattern is ortho/para, not meta.
These groups are electron-donating by resonance, so they activate (not deactivate) the ring, and they are ortho/para- (not meta-) directing.

questions.topic: Aromatic Hydrocarbons: Directive Influence of Substituents
questions.question: The −NO<sub>2</sub> group on a benzene ring is a:
options: Non-directing, neutral substituent
Strongly activating, ortho/para-directing substituent
Weakly deactivating, ortho/para-directing substituent
Strongly deactivating, meta-directing substituent
questions.explanation: −NO<sub>2</sub> withdraws electron density from the ring both inductively and by resonance (no lone pair available to donate back), strongly deactivating it, and leaves the meta position relatively least electron-poor, making it meta-directing.
questions.hint: This group has a full positive formal charge on nitrogen adjacent to the ring and no lone pair to donate back into it.
distractor_logic: −NO<sub>2</sub> withdraws electron density rather than donating it, so it deactivates (not activates) the ring, and it directs meta, not ortho/para.
