The deactivation is strong, not weak, and the directing pattern is meta, not ortho/para, since there is no lone pair to stabilise ortho/para intermediates.
Every substituent influences the ring's reactivity and orientation to some degree; −NO<sub>2</sub> is far from a neutral, non-directing group.

questions.question: A hydrocarbon has molecular formula C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>8</sub> and is known to be acyclic with exactly one multiple bond. Its degree of unsaturation and most likely structural class are:
options: Degree of unsaturation = 2; it is a diene (two C=C bonds)
Degree of unsaturation = 2; it is an alkyne
Degree of unsaturation = 3; it is an aromatic compound
Degree of unsaturation = 1; it is an alkene
questions.explanation: Degree of unsaturation = (2×5 + 2 − 8)/2 = (12 − 8)/2 = 2. Since the molecule is acyclic with only ONE multiple bond accounting for both degrees, that one multiple bond must be a triple bond (a triple bond alone contributes 2 degrees) — so it is an alkyne, e.g. pent-1-yne.
questions.hint: Use DoU = (2C + 2 − H)/2, then ask which single multiple bond type could account for a DoU of 2 by itself.
distractor_logic: Two separate C=C bonds (a diene) would require two multiple bonds, but the question specifies exactly one multiple bond.
A DoU of 3 miscalculates the formula, and aromaticity requires a ring plus alternating bonds, inconsistent with an acyclic structure.
A DoU of 1 would only account for a single double bond, but the correct calculation gives 2, not 1.

questions.question: A hydrocarbon has the general formula C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n</sub>. Which statement about it is necessarily true?
options: It must contain a triple bond
It must be an open-chain alkene
It must be a saturated monocyclic (cycloalkane) compound
It has exactly one degree of unsaturation, from either a C=C double bond or a ring
questions.explanation: For C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n</sub>, DoU = (2n + 2 − 2n)/2 = 1. That single degree of unsaturation could be satisfied either by one open-chain C=C double bond (an alkene) or by one saturated ring (a cycloalkane) — the formula alone cannot distinguish between the two possibilities.
questions.hint: Compute the degree of unsaturation first, then consider the two different structural features that can each supply exactly one degree of unsaturation.
distractor_logic: The formula is also satisfied by a saturated cycloalkane of the same formula (e.g. C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub> fits both pent-1-ene and cyclopentane), so it need not be an alkene.
Equally, the formula is also satisfied by an open-chain alkene, so it need not be a cycloalkane either — the formula alone is ambiguous between the two.
A triple bond contributes 2 degrees of unsaturation, not 1, so it cannot be the source of unsaturation in a C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n</sub> compound.

questions.question: What is the IUPAC name of CH<sub>3</sub>−CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)−CH<sub>2</sub>−CH<sub>3</sub>?
options: Pentane
2,2-Dimethylpropane
3-Methylbutane
2-Methylbutane
questions.explanation: The longest chain has 4 carbons (butane) with a methyl branch at C2 (numbering from the end nearer the branch, to give the lowest locant), so the name is 2-methylbutane.
questions.hint: Find the longest continuous carbon chain first, then number it to give the branch the lowest possible locant.
distractor_logic: Pentane would require 5 carbons all in a single unbranched chain, but this structure has only 4 in its longest chain plus one branch.
Numbering from the wrong end would give locant 3, but IUPAC rules require choosing the direction that gives the LOWEST locant, i.e. 2, not 3.
2,2-Dimethylpropane (neopentane) has a different skeleton (two methyls on the same central carbon of a 3-carbon chain), not matching this structure.

questions.question: What is the IUPAC name of CH<sub>3</sub>−C≡C−CH<sub>2</sub>−CH<sub>3</sub>?
options: Pent-3-yne
Pent-2-yne
Pent-1-yne
But-2-yne
questions.explanation: The 5-carbon chain is numbered to give the triple bond the lowest locant: numbering from the methyl end nearest the triple bond gives the bond between C2 and C3, so the name is pent-2-yne.
questions.hint: Number the 5-carbon chain from whichever end gives the triple bond the smaller locant.
distractor_logic: Pent-3-yne uses the higher of the two possible locants (numbering from the wrong end); IUPAC rules require the lower locant, 2, not 3.
Pent-1-yne would require the triple bond at the very end of the chain (a terminal alkyne), but here it is internal, between the second and third carbons.
But-2-yne has only 4 carbons, one fewer than this 5-carbon structure.

questions.question: How many structurally distinct chain (constitutional) isomers exist for the molecular formula C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub>?
options: 3 (n-pentane, isopentane, neopentane)
questions.explanation: C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub> has exactly three chain isomers: the unbranched n-pentane, the singly-branched 2-methylbutane (isopentane), and the doubly-branched 2,2-dimethylpropane (neopentane); no other distinct skeleton is possible for 5 carbons.
questions.hint: Systematically try the straight chain, then one branch, then two branches, checking each gives a genuinely new skeleton.
distractor_logic: This undercounts the isomers; besides the straight chain, there are two distinct branched skeletons possible (one methyl branch, and two methyl branches on the same carbon), not just one.
This overcounts further; there is no fourth or fifth distinct way to arrange 5 carbons into a different saturated skeleton beyond the three listed.
This overcounts; careful enumeration of 5-carbon skeletons yields exactly three distinct structures, not four.

questions.question: Which of the following alkenes is capable of showing geometrical (cis−trans) isomerism?
options: But-2-ene (CH<sub>3</sub>−CH=CH−CH<sub>3</sub>)
2-Methylbut-2-ene (CH<sub>3</sub>−C(CH<sub>3</sub>)=CH−CH<sub>3</sub>)
Propene (CH<sub>2</sub>=CH−CH<sub>3</sub>)
2-Methylpropene ((CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C=CH<sub>2</sub>)
questions.explanation: In but-2-ene, each double-bond carbon carries two DIFFERENT groups (CH<sub>3</sub> and H), satisfying the requirement for geometrical isomerism; cis-but-2-ene and trans-but-2-ene are genuinely distinct, isolable compounds.
questions.hint: Check whether both double-bond carbons in each option carry two different substituents.
distractor_logic: 2-Methylbut-2-ene has one double-bond carbon bearing two identical methyl groups, so swapping them gives back the same molecule — no distinct geometrical isomer exists.
Propene's terminal =CH<sub>2</sub> carbon carries two identical hydrogen atoms, so it cannot show geometrical isomerism.
2-Methylpropene's =CH<sub>2</sub> carbon (like propene's) carries two identical hydrogens, and its other double-bond carbon carries two identical methyl groups — neither carbon qualifies.

questions.question: Which alkane is formed when ethyl bromide (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br) undergoes the Wurtz reaction (Na, dry ether)?
options: Butane
Propane
Hexane
Ethane
questions.explanation: The Wurtz reaction couples two identical alkyl groups: 2CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Br + 2Na → CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>−CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> + 2NaBr, joining two 2-carbon ethyl groups into the 4-carbon chain butane.
questions.hint: The product chain length is double the alkyl halide's chain length, since two identical alkyl groups join together.
distractor_logic: Ethane would only form if the starting halide were methyl bromide (1 carbon each, giving a 2-carbon product), not ethyl bromide.
Propane (3 carbons, an odd number) cannot form from Wurtz coupling of two identical alkyl halides, since the product always has an even total carbon count.
Hexane (6 carbons) would require coupling two 3-carbon (propyl) groups, not the 2-carbon ethyl groups given here.

questions.question: Electrolysis of an aqueous solution of sodium acetate (CH<sub>3</sub>COONa), by Kolbe's method, produces which alkane at the anode?
options: Methane
Propane
Ethane
Butane
questions.explanation: At the anode, the acetate ion loses an electron and decarboxylates to a methyl radical (CH<sub>3</sub>•); two methyl radicals then combine to give ethane: 2CH<sub>3</sub>COO<sup>−</sup> → CH<sub>3</sub>−CH<sub>3</sub> + 2CO<sub>2</sub> + 2e<sup>−</sup>.
questions.hint: The product alkane has double the number of carbons that remain per acetate ion after CO<sub>2</sub> is lost.
distractor_logic: Propane (3 carbons, odd) cannot form from radical coupling of two identical methyl fragments, since the product always has an even carbon count in this method.
Butane (4 carbons) would result from coupling two 2-carbon (ethyl) radicals, which would require a 3-carbon acid (propanoate), not acetate.
Methane (1 carbon) would require the methyl radicals to somehow not combine with each other, which contradicts how Kolbe's method actually proceeds via radical coupling.

questions.question: Among n-pentane, 2-methylbutane (isopentane), and 2,2-dimethylpropane (neopentane) — all C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub> isomers — which has the HIGHEST boiling point?
options: n-Pentane
2-Methylbutane (isopentane)
All three have identical boiling points
2,2-Dimethylpropane (neopentane)
questions.explanation: Boiling point decreases with increasing branching for isomeric alkanes: branching makes the molecule more compact and spherical, reducing surface area of contact and weakening van der Waals (London dispersion) forces between molecules. The unbranched n-pentane, with the largest surface area, has the highest boiling point of the three.
questions.hint: Think about which shape (elongated vs. compact/spherical) maximises intermolecular contact area.
distractor_logic: Isopentane is singly branched, giving it less surface area and weaker dispersion forces than the unbranched isomer, so its boiling point is lower, not higher.
Neopentane is the most compact, nearly spherical isomer, with the least surface contact between molecules and therefore the LOWEST boiling point of the three, not the highest.
Boiling points of the three differ measurably (branching has a real, well-documented effect on intermolecular forces); they are not identical.

questions.question: In the most stable (anti, staggered) conformation of butane about the C2−C3 bond, the dihedral angle between the two terminal methyl groups is:
options: 0°
60°
questions.explanation: The anti conformation places the two bulky methyl groups as far apart as possible, at a dihedral angle of 180°, minimising both torsional strain and steric (van der Waals) repulsion between them — making it the lowest-energy, most stable conformation of butane.
questions.hint: This is the conformer where the two largest groups are positioned diametrically opposite each other.
distractor_logic: 120° does not correspond to any staggered or eclipsed conformer in the standard rotational analysis of butane about this bond.
0° would be a fully eclipsed arrangement with the methyl groups directly overlapping — the highest-energy, least stable conformation, the opposite of what is asked.
60° describes the gauche conformation, a staggered but higher-energy arrangement where the methyl groups experience some steric strain, not the most stable form.

questions.question: How many structurally different monochlorination products can propane (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>) give?
options: 2 (1-chloropropane and 2-chloropropane)
questions.explanation: Propane has two chemically distinct sets of hydrogens: the six equivalent primary H's (on C1 and C3, giving 1-chloropropane) and the two equivalent secondary H's (on C2, giving 2-chloropropane) — so exactly two structurally different monochloro products are possible.
questions.hint: Group the hydrogens of propane into sets of chemically equivalent positions first.
distractor_logic: 3 distinct products would require three different types of hydrogen environments, but propane has only two (primary and secondary).
Only 1 product would mean all hydrogens in propane are equivalent, but propane clearly has distinct primary and secondary hydrogen environments.
4 distinct products overcounts; propane's symmetry means the six primary hydrogens are all equivalent to each other, collapsing what might seem like multiple positions into just one product type.

questions.question: How many structurally different monochlorination products can 2,2-dimethylpropane (neopentane) give?
options: 1 (all 12 hydrogens are equivalent)
questions.explanation: Neopentane, C(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>4</sub>, has four identical methyl groups symmetrically arranged around the central carbon; all 12 hydrogens are chemically equivalent (all primary, related by the molecule's high symmetry), so only a single monochlorination product, neopentyl chloride, is possible.
questions.hint: Consider the high symmetry of this molecule's structure — how many chemically distinct 'kinds' of hydrogen does it actually have?
distractor_logic: 4 distinct products would suggest each methyl group gives a different product, but by the molecule's symmetry all four methyl groups (and all their hydrogens) are indistinguishable from one another.
3 distinct products overcounts the environments present; neopentane has no secondary or tertiary hydrogens at all, only equivalent primary ones.
2 distinct products would require at least two chemically different hydrogen environments, but neopentane's four equivalent methyl groups give only one.

questions.question: For the complete combustion C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub> + 5O<sub>2</sub> → 3CO<sub>2</sub> + 4H<sub>2</sub>O, how many moles of O<sub>2</sub> are required to completely burn 2 moles of propane?
options: 6 moles
10 moles
15 moles
5 moles
questions.explanation: The balanced equation shows 1 mol propane requires 5 mol O<sub>2</sub>; by simple proportion, 2 mol propane requires 2 × 5 = 10 mol O<sub>2</sub>.
questions.hint: Scale the balanced equation's O<sub>2</sub> coefficient by the same factor as the propane amount.
distractor_logic: 5 moles is the requirement for just 1 mole of propane, not 2 moles — this forgets to scale by the given amount.
15 moles would be triple, not double, the single-mole requirement, overshooting the correct proportional scaling.
6 moles does not correspond to any correct scaling of the balanced equation's 1:5 propane-to-oxygen ratio.

questions.question: For the complete combustion 2C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub> + 13O<sub>2</sub> → 8CO<sub>2</sub> + 10H<sub>2</sub>O, what mass of CO<sub>2</sub> is produced from 1 mole of butane? (Molar mass of CO<sub>2</sub> = 44 g/mol)
questions.explanation: The balanced equation shows 2 mol butane gives 8 mol CO<sub>2</sub>, so 1 mol butane gives 4 mol CO<sub>2</sub>. Mass = 4 × 44 g/mol = 176 g.
questions.hint: First find the mol-to-mol ratio of butane to CO<sub>2</sub> from the balanced equation, then convert to mass.
distractor_logic: 132 g corresponds to 3 moles of CO<sub>2</sub>, still short of the 4 moles that the correctly-scaled 1:4 ratio (from the given 2:8 equation) actually gives.
88 g corresponds to 2 moles of CO<sub>2</sub>, half of the correct amount — a likely error from mis-scaling the 2:8 ratio down incorrectly.
44 g corresponds to just 1 mole of CO<sub>2</sub>, forgetting that each mole of butane actually produces 4 moles of CO<sub>2</sub>, not 1.

questions.question: What is the IUPAC name of CH<sub>2</sub>=CH−CH<sub>2</sub>−CH<sub>3</sub>?
options: But-2-ene
Prop-1-ene
But-1-ene
2-Methylprop-1-ene
questions.explanation: The 4-carbon chain is numbered to give the double bond the lowest locant; the double bond starts at C1, so the name is but-1-ene.
questions.hint: Number the 4-carbon chain from the end nearest the double bond.
distractor_logic: Prop-1-ene has only 3 carbons, one fewer than this 4-carbon structure.
2-Methylprop-1-ene has a branched (methyl-substituted) 3-carbon chain, but this structure is a straight, unbranched 4-carbon chain.
But-2-ene would place the double bond between C2 and C3 (in the middle of the chain), but here it is at the very end, between C1 and C2.

questions.question: What is the IUPAC name of CH<sub>3</sub>−CH=CH−CH<sub>2</sub>−CH<sub>3</sub>?
options: Pent-1-ene
But-2-ene
Pent-2-ene
Pent-3-ene
questions.explanation: Numbering the 5-carbon chain from the end that gives the double bond the lower locant places it between C2 and C3, giving the lowest-locant name pent-2-ene (not the higher locant 'pent-3-ene', which would result from numbering the wrong way).
questions.hint: There are two ways to number this 5-carbon chain; pick whichever gives the double bond the smaller locant.
distractor_logic: Pent-3-ene uses the higher of the two possible locants for the same double bond position; IUPAC rules require choosing the lower one, 2.
Pent-1-ene would place the double bond at the very end of the chain (a terminal alkene), but here it is internal, between C2 and C3.
But-2-ene has only 4 carbons in its parent chain, one fewer than this 5-carbon structure.

questions.question: <svg viewBox="0 0 300 160" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:100%;height:auto"><line x1="100" y1="80" x2="200" y2="80" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="100" y1="74" x2="200" y2="74" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="100" y1="80" x2="40" y2="35" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><text x="34" y="31" font-size="15" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="end" dominant-baseline="middle">CH₃</text><line x1="100" y1="80" x2="40" y2="125" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><text x="34" y="137" font-size="15" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="end" dominant-baseline="middle">H</text><line x1="200" y1="80" x2="260" y2="35" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><text x="266" y="31" font-size="15" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="start" dominant-baseline="middle">H</text><line x1="200" y1="80" x2="260" y2="125" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><text x="266" y="137" font-size="15" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="start" dominant-baseline="middle">CH₃</text></svg> The structure shown above (with the two −CH<sub>3</sub> groups on opposite sides of the double bond) represents:
options: trans-But-2-ene
2-Methylpropene
cis-But-2-ene
But-1-ene
questions.explanation: With the two −CH<sub>3</sub> groups drawn on opposite sides of the C=C axis (one up, one down) and the two −H atoms likewise on opposite sides, the higher-priority groups (CH<sub>3</sub>) are on opposite sides — this is the trans (E) configuration of but-2-ene.
questions.hint: Compare which side of the double bond each −CH<sub>3</sub> group is drawn on.
distractor_logic: But-1-ene has its double bond at the chain terminus (a =CH<sub>2</sub> end group), which cannot show cis/trans isomerism at all, unlike the internal double bond drawn here.
2-Methylpropene has one double-bond carbon bearing two identical methyl groups, which also cannot show geometrical isomerism, unlike the structure shown.
cis-But-2-ene would require both −CH<sub>3</sub> groups to be drawn on the SAME side of the double bond, not opposite sides as shown here.

questions.question: Which of the following alkenes does NOT show geometrical (cis−trans) isomerism?
options: 2-Methylpropene ((CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C=CH<sub>2</sub>)
Pent-2-ene (CH<sub>3</sub>−CH=CH−CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>)
Hex-3-ene (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>−CH=CH−CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>)
1-Bromopropene (CH<sub>3</sub>−CH=CH−Br)
questions.explanation: In 2-methylpropene, one double-bond carbon bears two identical methyl groups (both −CH<sub>3</sub>); since swapping identical groups gives back the same molecule, no distinct geometrical isomer can exist. All three other alkenes have two different groups on each double-bond carbon.
questions.hint: Check each double-bond carbon in every option for two identical substituents.
distractor_logic: Hex-3-ene's double-bond carbons each carry an ethyl group and a hydrogen — again two different groups — so it also shows geometrical isomerism.
1-Bromopropene's double-bond carbons each carry (Br or CH<sub>3</sub>) and H, two different groups on each carbon, so it too shows geometrical isomerism.
Pent-2-ene's double-bond carbons each carry a methyl/ethyl group and a hydrogen — two different groups on each carbon — so it does show geometrical isomerism, unlike the correct answer.

questions.question: According to Zaitsev's rule, what is the major product when 2-bromobutane is heated with alcoholic KOH?
options: But-1-ene (the less substituted alkene)
n-Butane
Butan-2-ol
But-2-ene (the more substituted alkene)
questions.explanation: Zaitsev's rule states that elimination favours formation of the more highly substituted (and hence more stable) alkene. Removing HBr from 2-bromobutane can give either but-1-ene or but-2-ene; but-2-ene, with an alkyl group on each double-bond carbon, is more substituted and thus the major product.
questions.hint: Compare how many alkyl groups are attached directly to the double-bond carbons in each possible elimination product.
distractor_logic: But-1-ene is the LESS substituted (minor) elimination product under Zaitsev conditions, the opposite of what the rule predicts as major.
n-Butane would require addition of hydrogen (reduction), which does not occur under basic elimination conditions.
Butan-2-ol would form from substitution with aqueous (not alcoholic) KOH; alcoholic KOH favours elimination, not substitution.

questions.question: What is the major product when 2-methylbutan-2-ol is dehydrated with concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> and heat?
options: 2-Methylbutane (fully saturated)
2-Methylbut-2-ene (the most substituted alkene, by Zaitsev's rule)
3-Methylbut-1-ene (the least substituted alkene)
2-Methylbutan-1-ol (an isomeric alcohol)
questions.explanation: Acid-catalysed dehydration proceeds via a carbocation at the original −OH-bearing (tertiary) carbon; loss of a proton from an adjacent carbon that gives the MORE substituted double bond is favoured by Zaitsev's rule, yielding 2-methylbut-2-ene as the major product.
questions.hint: Dehydration proceeds through a carbocation, and Zaitsev's rule again favours the more substituted alkene product.
distractor_logic: 2-Methylbutane would require addition of hydrogen (reduction) to the double bond, the opposite of the elimination (loss of water) occurring here.
3-Methylbut-1-ene is the less substituted alternative elimination product, the minor product under Zaitsev-controlled dehydration, not the major one.
2-Methylbutan-1-ol is simply an isomeric alcohol, not a dehydration product at all — dehydration removes water to form a double bond, it doesn't rearrange to another alcohol.

questions.question: What is the major product of the addition of HBr (no peroxide) to propene, CH<sub>2</sub>=CH−CH<sub>3</sub>?
options: 1-Bromopropane
2-Bromopropane
Propane
1,2-Dibromopropane
questions.explanation: By Markovnikov's rule, H<sup>+</sup> adds to the terminal CH<sub>2</sub> carbon (already bearing more hydrogens), generating the more stable secondary carbocation at C2; Br<sup>−</sup> then attacks this carbon, giving 2-bromopropane as the major product.
questions.hint: Determine which carbon would form the more stable carbocation upon protonation, then place the halide there.
distractor_logic: Propane would result from addition of H<sub>2</sub>, not HBr; no bromine appears in this product at all.
1-Bromopropane is the anti-Markovnikov product, which would only dominate under radical (peroxide) conditions, not the plain ionic addition described here.
1,2-Dibromopropane would require addition of Br<sub>2</sub> (two bromine atoms), not HBr (one hydrogen and one bromine).

questions.question: What is the major product of the addition of HCl to 2-methylpropene, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C=CH<sub>2</sub>?
options: 2-Methylpropane
1-Chloro-2-methylpropane
2-Chloro-2-methylpropane (tert-butyl chloride)
2-Chloropropane
questions.explanation: Protonation of the terminal =CH<sub>2</sub> carbon generates a tertiary carbocation at the central carbon (much more stable than the alternative primary carbocation); Cl<sup>−</sup> then attacks this tertiary centre, giving tert-butyl chloride as the major (Markovnikov) product.
questions.hint: Compare the stability of the two possible carbocation intermediates — tertiary versus primary.
distractor_logic: 1-Chloro-2-methylpropane would require the chloride to attack the less stable primary carbocation, contrary to the strong preference for the tertiary intermediate.
2-Chloropropane has only 3 carbons, one fewer than this 4-carbon starting alkene, so it cannot be the addition product.
2-Methylpropane would result from addition of H<sub>2</sub>, not HCl; no chlorine appears in this product.

questions.topic: Alkenes: Markovnikov's Rule and Peroxide Effect
questions.question: What is the major product when propene reacts with HBr in the PRESENCE of peroxides?
options: 1-Bromopropane (anti-Markovnikov)
Propan-2-ol
1,2-Dibromopropane
2-Bromopropane (Markovnikov)
questions.explanation: Peroxides initiate a radical chain mechanism: Br• adds first to the terminal (less hindered) carbon, generating the more stable secondary radical at C2; this radical then abstracts H from HBr, placing Br at C1 — the reverse (anti-Markovnikov) regiochemistry compared to ionic addition.
questions.hint: Peroxides switch the mechanism from ionic (carbocation-based) to radical (based on the more stable radical intermediate).
distractor_logic: 1,2-Dibromopropane would require Br<sub>2</sub> addition, not the radical HBr addition occurring here.
Propan-2-ol would require water as the nucleophile, not HBr; no oxygen source is present in this reaction.
2-Bromopropane is the normal Markovnikov product formed WITHOUT peroxides via the ionic mechanism; peroxides specifically reverse this regiochemistry.

questions.topic: Alkenes: Markovnikov's Rule and Peroxide Effect
questions.question: What is the major product when propene reacts with HCl in the presence of peroxides?
options: Propan-1-ol
1,2-Dichloropropane
1-Chloropropane (anti-Markovnikov, as with HBr)
2-Chloropropane (normal Markovnikov product; peroxide effect does not apply to HCl)
questions.explanation: The peroxide (Kharasch) effect is specific to HBr; the H−Cl bond is too strong for efficient radical chain initiation, so even in the presence of peroxides, HCl still adds via the normal ionic (Markovnikov) pathway, giving 2-chloropropane.
questions.hint: Recall which single hydrogen halide actually shows the peroxide effect — does HCl belong to that group?
distractor_logic: 1,2-Dichloropropane would require Cl<sub>2</sub> addition, not HCl addition.
1-Chloropropane assumes the peroxide effect applies to HCl the same way it does to HBr, but the effect is specific to HBr and does not occur with HCl.
Propan-1-ol would require water as the nucleophile, not HCl; there is no oxygen source in this reaction.

questions.question: Ozonolysis of 2-methylpropene, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C=CH<sub>2</sub>, followed by Zn/H<sub>2</sub>O workup, gives which pair of products?
options: Acetaldehyde (CH<sub>3</sub>CHO) and formaldehyde (HCHO)
Acetic acid and formic acid
Two molecules of acetone
Acetone [(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C=O] and formaldehyde (HCHO)
questions.explanation: Ozonolysis cleaves the C=C bond, converting each doubly-bonded carbon into a C=O. The fully substituted carbon [(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C=] becomes a ketone, acetone; the =CH<sub>2</sub> carbon becomes an aldehyde, formaldehyde (HCHO).
questions.hint: Mentally split the double bond in half and cap each fragment with an oxygen where the bond used to be.
distractor_logic: Two molecules of acetone would require both alkene carbons to be identically disubstituted, but one carbon here is =CH<sub>2</sub> (disubstituted with H's), giving formaldehyde, not another acetone.
Acetaldehyde would require a =CH(CH<sub>3</sub>) fragment, but this alkene has a fully substituted (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C= carbon on one side, not a mono-substituted one.
Carboxylic acids (acetic/formic acid) would form only under OXIDATIVE workup (e.g. H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>), not the reductive Zn/H<sub>2</sub>O workup specified here.

questions.question: Ozonolysis of but-2-ene, CH<sub>3</sub>−CH=CH−CH<sub>3</sub>, followed by Zn/H<sub>2</sub>O workup, gives:
options: Two molecules of formaldehyde
Two molecules of acetaldehyde (CH<sub>3</sub>CHO)
One molecule of acetone and one of formaldehyde
One molecule of propanal and one of formaldehyde
questions.explanation: But-2-ene is symmetric: both double-bond carbons carry one methyl group and one hydrogen. Cleaving the C=C and capping each fragment with oxygen gives two identical CH<sub>3</sub>CHO (acetaldehyde) molecules.
questions.hint: Notice that this particular alkene is symmetric about its double bond — both halves are identical.
distractor_logic: Two formaldehyde molecules would result from ozonolysis of ethene (CH<sub>2</sub>=CH<sub>2</sub>), which has no methyl substituents at all, unlike but-2-ene.
Propanal and formaldehyde would result from an unsymmetrical alkene like pent-1-ene, not the symmetric but-2-ene given here.
Acetone and formaldehyde would result from cleaving an alkene with one fully-substituted carbon and one =CH<sub>2</sub> carbon, not this symmetric mono-substituted alkene.

questions.question: How many moles of H<sub>2</sub> are required to completely hydrogenate 1 mole of hexa-1,3,5-triene (three C=C double bonds)?
options: 2 moles
3 moles
1 mole
6 moles
questions.explanation: Each C=C double bond consumes exactly 1 mole of H<sub>2</sub> on complete catalytic hydrogenation; with three double bonds present, 3 × 1 = 3 moles of H<sub>2</sub> are required to fully saturate the molecule to hexane.
questions.hint: Count the number of double bonds, since each one independently consumes one mole of H<sub>2</sub>.
distractor_logic: 1 mole would only saturate one of the three double bonds, leaving the molecule still unsaturated (a diene), not fully hydrogenated.
2 moles would leave one double bond unreacted, still short of the 3 moles needed to saturate all three.
6 moles overcounts; each double bond needs exactly one H<sub>2</sub> molecule (not two), so three double bonds need only 3, not 6, moles.

questions.question: The monomer used to manufacture PVC (polyvinyl chloride) is:
options: Styrene (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>−CH=CH<sub>2</sub>)
Tetrafluoroethene (CF<sub>2</sub>=CF<sub>2</sub>)
Vinyl chloride (chloroethene, CH<sub>2</sub>=CHCl)
Ethene (CH<sub>2</sub>=CH<sub>2</sub>)
questions.explanation: PVC is formed by addition polymerisation of chloroethene (vinyl chloride), −(CH<sub>2</sub>−CHCl)<sub>n</sub>−, where the repeating unit carries one chlorine substituent per two carbons, matching PVC's composition.
questions.hint: The name 'polyvinyl chloride' directly names the halogen-substituted monomer it is built from.
distractor_logic: Styrene is the monomer of polystyrene, which carries a phenyl (benzene ring) substituent rather than a chlorine atom.
Tetrafluoroethene is the monomer of PTFE (Teflon), which is fully fluorinated, not chlorinated.
Ethene is the monomer of polythene (polyethylene), which contains no chlorine, unlike PVC.

questions.question: Does pent-1-yne (CH≡C−CH<sub>2</sub>−CH<sub>2</sub>−CH<sub>3</sub>) give a positive test (white precipitate) with ammoniacal AgNO<sub>3</sub>?
options: Yes, because it has a terminal ≡C−H that can be replaced by Ag
Yes, but only after complete hydrogenation to pentane first
No, because it has no acidic hydrogens at all
No, because it is a symmetrical alkyne
questions.explanation: Pent-1-yne is a TERMINAL alkyne, possessing an acidic ≡C−H bond at C1. Ammoniacal AgNO<sub>3</sub> replaces this hydrogen with silver, forming an insoluble white precipitate of silver pentynylide (RC≡CAg).
questions.hint: Check whether the triple bond sits at the very end of the carbon chain (terminal) or in the middle (internal).
distractor_logic: The terminal ≡C−H bond IS weakly acidic, due to the high s-character of the sp carbon; the molecule does have an acidic hydrogen, just not a strongly acidic one.
Pent-1-yne is not symmetrical (it has a terminal ≡CH on one side and a propyl chain on the other), but that is irrelevant anyway — the key requirement is a terminal ≡C−H, which this molecule has.
The test is performed directly on the alkyne itself and does not require any prior hydrogenation; hydrogenating it would remove the triple bond needed for this specific test entirely.

questions.question: Does pent-2-yne (CH<sub>3</sub>−C≡C−CH<sub>2</sub>−CH<sub>3</sub>) give a positive test (white precipitate) with ammoniacal AgNO<sub>3</sub>?
options: No, because silver only reacts with alkenes, not alkynes
Yes, because it contains an acidic C−H on its methyl groups
No, because it is an internal alkyne with no terminal ≡C−H
Yes, because all alkynes react with ammoniacal AgNO<sub>3</sub>
questions.explanation: In pent-2-yne, the triple bond is internal (between C2 and C3); both carbons of the triple bond are attached to alkyl groups, not hydrogen, so there is no acidic ≡C−H bond available to be replaced by silver — the test is negative.
questions.hint: Locate the triple bond's position in the chain; is either of its two carbons directly bonded to a hydrogen?
distractor_logic: This test is specific to TERMINAL alkynes only, not all alkynes; internal alkynes like pent-2-yne give a negative result.
The methyl group hydrogens are ordinary sp<sup>3</sup> C−H bonds with essentially no acidity; the special acidity in alkynes comes only from an sp-hybridised ≡C−H, which is absent here.
This is backwards: ammoniacal AgNO<sub>3</sub> specifically tests for terminal alkynes (via their acidic ≡C−H), and does not react with simple alkenes at all.

questions.question: What alkyne is formed when 1,2-dibromopropane is treated with excess alcoholic KOH?
options: Propene
Ethyne
Propyne
But-1-yne
questions.explanation: 1,2-Dibromopropane (CH<sub>3</sub>−CHBr−CH<sub>2</sub>Br) is a vicinal dihalide; excess alcoholic KOH removes two molecules of HBr in succession, forming the triple bond and giving propyne (CH<sub>3</sub>−C≡CH).
questions.hint: Count the carbons in the starting dihalide — the alkyne product retains the same carbon count.
distractor_logic: Propene would result from only a SINGLE elimination (one HBr removed), but excess alcoholic KOH drives a second elimination to complete the triple bond, giving the alkyne, not the alkene.
Ethyne has only 2 carbons, one fewer than the 3-carbon starting material, so it cannot be the product of this specific dihalide's elimination.
But-1-yne has 4 carbons, one more than the 3-carbon starting dihalide provides.

questions.question: What alkyne is formed when 1,2-dibromobutane is treated with excess alcoholic KOH?
options: Ethyne
But-2-yne
But-1-yne
Propyne
questions.explanation: 1,2-Dibromobutane (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>−CHBr−CH<sub>2</sub>Br) has its two bromines on C1 and C2; double dehydrohalogenation forms the triple bond specifically between C1 and C2, giving the terminal alkyne but-1-yne (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>−C≡CH).
questions.hint: The triple bond forms exactly where the two leaving bromine atoms were originally located.
distractor_logic: Propyne has only 3 carbons, one fewer than the 4-carbon starting dihalide.
But-2-yne would place the triple bond between C2 and C3, but the bromines here are on C1 and C2, so the triple bond must form there instead.
Ethyne has only 2 carbons, two fewer than the 4-carbon starting material; elimination does not remove any carbons from the chain.

questions.question: <svg viewBox="0 0 300 160" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:100%;height:auto"><line x1="100" y1="80" x2="200" y2="80" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="100" y1="74" x2="200" y2="74" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="100" y1="80" x2="40" y2="35" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><text x="34" y="31" font-size="15" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="end" dominant-baseline="middle">CH₃</text><line x1="100" y1="80" x2="40" y2="125" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><text x="34" y="137" font-size="15" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="end" dominant-baseline="middle">H</text><line x1="200" y1="80" x2="260" y2="35" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><text x="266" y="31" font-size="15" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="start" dominant-baseline="middle">CH₃</text><line x1="200" y1="80" x2="260" y2="125" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><text x="266" y="137" font-size="15" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="start" dominant-baseline="middle">H</text></svg> When but-2-yne is hydrogenated using H<sub>2</sub> over Lindlar's (poisoned Pd) catalyst, the product formed is:
options: cis-But-2-ene (shown above), from syn addition of H<sub>2</sub>
trans-But-2-ene, from anti addition of H<sub>2</sub>
But-1-ene, an unreacted terminal alkene
n-Butane, from complete saturation
questions.explanation: Lindlar's catalyst is a poisoned (partially deactivated) palladium catalyst that delivers both hydrogen atoms to the SAME face of the triple bond (syn addition) and stops after one equivalent of H<sub>2</sub>, giving the cis-alkene selectively.
questions.hint: Lindlar's catalyst is specifically chosen to add both new hydrogens from the same face and to stop the reaction after only one addition.
distractor_logic: n-Butane would require a second equivalent of H<sub>2</sub> to add across the resulting alkene; Lindlar's catalyst is specifically poisoned to stop after just the first addition.
But-1-ene would require the triple bond to be terminal or for isomerisation to occur; but-2-yne's internal triple bond hydrogenates in place to give but-2-ene, not a positional isomer.
trans-But-2-ene results from an ANTI addition mechanism (as with Na/liquid NH<sub>3</sub>), not the syn addition characteristic of Lindlar's catalyst.

questions.question: <svg viewBox="0 0 300 160" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:100%;height:auto"><line x1="100" y1="80" x2="200" y2="80" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="100" y1="74" x2="200" y2="74" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="100" y1="80" x2="40" y2="35" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><text x="34" y="31" font-size="15" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="end" dominant-baseline="middle">CH₃</text><line x1="100" y1="80" x2="40" y2="125" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><text x="34" y="137" font-size="15" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="end" dominant-baseline="middle">H</text><line x1="200" y1="80" x2="260" y2="35" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><text x="266" y="31" font-size="15" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="start" dominant-baseline="middle">H</text><line x1="200" y1="80" x2="260" y2="125" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><text x="266" y="137" font-size="15" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="start" dominant-baseline="middle">CH₃</text></svg> When but-2-yne is reduced with sodium metal in liquid ammonia, the product formed is:
options: n-Butane, from complete saturation
trans-But-2-ene (shown above), from anti addition
cis-But-2-ene, from syn addition
But-2-yne remains unreacted
questions.explanation: Na/liquid NH<sub>3</sub> reduces alkynes by a stepwise electron-transfer (radical anion) mechanism in which the two new C−H bonds are added to opposite faces of the (former) triple bond, giving the thermodynamically more stable trans-alkene selectively.
questions.hint: This dissolving-metal reduction proceeds through a different mechanism than catalytic hydrogenation, adding the two hydrogens to opposite faces.
distractor_logic: cis-But-2-ene is the product of catalytic syn addition (e.g. Lindlar's catalyst), a mechanistically different pathway from the anti addition that Na/NH<sub>3</sub> follows.
n-Butane would require full saturation (addition of two equivalents of H), but Na/liquid NH<sub>3</sub> reduction of an alkyne stops cleanly at the alkene stage.
Na/liquid NH<sub>3</sub> is a well-established reducing system that does reduce alkynes to alkenes; it does not leave the alkyne untouched.

questions.question: The cyclopentadienyl anion (C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>5</sub><sup>−</sup>) is a planar, fully conjugated 5-membered ring with 6 pi electrons. Based on Hückel's rule, it is:
options: Non-aromatic, since it is a 5-membered ring
Non-aromatic, since it carries a negative charge
Anti-aromatic, since 6 = 4n with n = 1.5
Aromatic, since 6 = 4n + 2 with n = 1
questions.explanation: Hückel's rule depends only on pi-electron count in a planar, cyclic, conjugated system, not ring size or charge. With 6 pi electrons fitting the (4n + 2) pattern at n = 1, the cyclopentadienyl anion is aromatic, despite being 5-membered and negatively charged.
questions.hint: Apply the (4n+2) formula directly to the given electron count; ring size and charge are not part of the rule itself.
distractor_logic: Hückel's rule makes no requirement about ring size (5-, 6-, or 7-membered rings can all be aromatic); a 5-membered ring is not automatically excluded.
Charge alone does not determine aromaticity; only the pi-electron count and conjugation/planarity matter, and a negatively charged ring can absolutely be aromatic if the electron count fits (4n+2).
6 does not equal 4n for any integer n (4n = 6 gives the non-integer n = 1.5), so this option's own arithmetic is inconsistent with the 4n anti-aromatic pattern it claims.

questions.question: Cyclooctatetraene (C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>8</sub>) has a cyclic, conjugated system with 8 pi electrons, but it is known to be non-planar (tub-shaped). Is it aromatic?
options: Yes, because 8 pi electrons is enough for aromaticity
No, because it contains too few carbon atoms
No, mainly because its non-planar shape prevents continuous p-orbital overlap around the ring
Yes, because it is cyclic and conjugated, regardless of pi-electron count
questions.explanation: Even though cyclooctatetraene is technically cyclic and formally conjugated, its natural tub shape twists the ring out of planarity, breaking the continuous overlap of p orbitals needed for true delocalisation. (Its 8 pi electrons also fit 4n, not 4n+2, reinforcing its non-aromatic character.) It behaves chemically like a simple polyene, not an aromatic system.
questions.hint: Hückel's rule requires planarity as a precondition — check whether that geometric requirement is actually met here.
distractor_logic: 8 pi electrons fits the (4n) pattern, not the aromatic (4n+2) pattern, so the electron count itself doesn't support aromaticity even before considering planarity.
Carbon count (ring size) is not the limiting factor here; the issue is specifically the molecule's non-planar geometry, not an insufficient number of atoms.
Being cyclic and conjugated is necessary but not SUFFICIENT for aromaticity; the ring must also be planar, and cyclooctatetraene's tub shape fails this requirement.

questions.question: What is the major product of the Friedel−Crafts alkylation of benzene with CH<sub>3</sub>Cl in the presence of anhydrous AlCl<sub>3</sub>?
options: Benzyl chloride
Xylene (dimethylbenzene)
Toluene (methylbenzene)
Chlorobenzene
questions.explanation: AlCl<sub>3</sub> polarises CH<sub>3</sub>Cl to generate an electrophilic methyl cation (CH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup>), which attacks the benzene ring; loss of H<sup>+</sup> restores aromaticity, giving toluene as the direct mono-alkylation product.
questions.hint: The methyl group from the alkyl halide is transferred directly onto the ring, replacing one ring hydrogen.
distractor_logic: Xylene would require a SECOND methylation (over-alkylation), but the question asks for the direct/major mono-substitution product, toluene.
Benzyl chloride (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>Cl) would require chlorination of toluene's methyl group afterward; it is not the direct product of this alkylation.
Chlorobenzene would result from an electrophilic chlorination (Cl<sup>+</sup> attacking the ring), not from a Friedel−Crafts alkylation with a methyl-donating reagent.

questions.question: In the bromination of benzene using Br<sub>2</sub>/FeBr<sub>3</sub>, what is the actual electrophile that attacks the ring?
options: FeBr<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup>
Br<sup>+</sup> (generated by FeBr<sub>3</sub> polarising Br−Br)
Br<sub>2</sub> itself, unmodified
Br<sup>−</sup>
questions.explanation: FeBr<sub>3</sub>, a Lewis acid, accepts a lone pair from one bromine of Br<sub>2</sub>, polarising and weakening the Br−Br bond so that it heterolyses to release the electrophilic Br<sup>+</sup> (as part of an FeBr<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup>/Br<sup>+</sup> complex), which the ring's pi electrons then attack.
questions.hint: FeBr<sub>3</sub> acts as a Lewis acid catalyst, and its role is to generate a positively charged, electrophilic bromine species.
distractor_logic: FeBr<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> is the counter-anion formed alongside Br<sup>+</sup> in this process; it is not itself the species that attacks the ring.
Br<sup>−</sup> is a nucleophile (electron-rich), the opposite of the electron-seeking species needed to attack benzene's electron-rich ring.
Unmodified Br<sub>2</sub> is too weak an electrophile to react directly with benzene's ring under normal conditions; the FeBr<sub>3</sub> catalyst is needed to activate it first.

questions.topic: Aromatic Hydrocarbons: Directive Influence of Substituents
questions.question: Nitrobenzene is treated with Br<sub>2</sub>/FeBr<sub>3</sub>. Since −NO<sub>2</sub> is a meta-directing, deactivating group, which structure best represents the major mono-bromination product?
options: meta-Bromonitrobenzene
para-Bromonitrobenzene
An approximately statistical 1:2:1 mixture of ortho, meta, and para products, since −NO<sub>2</sub> has no real directing influence
ortho-Bromonitrobenzene
questions.explanation: −NO<sub>2</sub> withdraws electron density from the ring by both induction and resonance, most strongly depleting electron density at the ortho and para positions; the meta position is relatively (though still only mildly) electron-richer, so the incoming electrophile is directed predominantly there.
questions.hint: Recall which single position a strongly deactivating, resonance-withdrawing substituent like −NO<sub>2</sub> leaves relatively least electron-poor.
distractor_logic: This places Br ortho to −NO<sub>2</sub>, a position the resonance-withdrawing nitro group depletes most strongly of electron density, making it a disfavoured (minor) site.
This places Br para to −NO<sub>2</sub>, the other position most strongly deactivated by the nitro group's resonance withdrawal, also a disfavoured (minor) site.

This incorrectly assumes −NO<sub>2</sub> has no directing influence; in reality it strongly and specifically favours meta substitution, giving a product mixture heavily skewed toward the meta isomer, not a statistical 1:2:1 spread.

questions.topic: Aromatic Hydrocarbons: Directive Influence of Substituents
questions.question: Chlorobenzene is nitrated with conc. HNO<sub>3</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>. Even though −Cl is a deactivating group overall, the major products are:
options: An equal statistical mixture of ortho, meta, and para products
meta-Chloronitrobenzene only, since all deactivating groups are meta-directors
ortho- and para-Chloronitrobenzene (Cl still directs ortho/para, despite deactivating the ring)
No reaction occurs, since −Cl deactivates the ring completely
questions.explanation: Halogens are a special exception: they deactivate the ring inductively (electronegative, withdraws sigma electron density) but still direct ortho/para, because their lone pairs can donate into the ring by resonance, stabilising the ortho/para arenium intermediates more than the meta one — even though this donation is weaker than the inductive withdrawal overall.
questions.hint: Halogens are the classic exception to the rule that 'deactivating' and 'meta-directing' always go together.
distractor_logic: Deactivation lowers the RATE of reaction compared to benzene itself, but the ring still reacts (just more slowly, and needing typically more forcing conditions); it does not mean no reaction occurs at all.
This wrongly assumes ALL deactivating groups are meta-directors; halogens are a well-known exception that deactivate yet still direct ortho/para through resonance donation of their lone pairs.
A statistical mixture ignores the real (if partial) resonance donation that halogens provide, which does meaningfully favour the ortho/para positions over meta.

questions.question: A hydrocarbon X has molecular formula C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>10</sub>. It is known to be an open (acyclic) chain compound, it decolourises bromine water instantly, and it also gives a white precipitate with ammoniacal AgNO<sub>3</sub>. What is the most likely class and structural feature of X?
options: A conjugated diene, since two isolated double bonds together give a positive AgNO<sub>3</sub> test
A terminal alkyne (e.g. hex-1-yne); the triple bond accounts for both degrees of unsaturation
An alkene with a ring, since C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>10</sub> requires 2 degrees of unsaturation
A cyclohexene, since bromine water addition confirms one ring plus one double bond
questions.explanation: DoU for C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>10</sub> = (2×6+2−10)/2 = 2. Decolourising bromine water confirms unsaturation capable of addition (true of both alkenes and alkynes), but the positive ammoniacal AgNO<sub>3</sub> test specifically indicates a TERMINAL ≡C−H. Since X is acyclic and needs 2 degrees of unsaturation from a single functional feature, a terminal triple bond (which alone contributes 2 degrees) fits perfectly — e.g. hex-1-yne.
questions.hint: The AgNO<sub>3</sub> test is decisive here: which functional group specifically gives that positive result?
distractor_logic: This again contradicts the given acyclic condition, and cyclohexene (an internal alkene) would not give a positive AgNO<sub>3</sub> test either.
A diene would decolourise bromine water, but simple alkenes (isolated or conjugated) do NOT react with ammoniacal AgNO<sub>3</sub> at all — that positive test specifically requires a terminal alkyne.
This option is explicitly excluded by the problem statement, which says X is acyclic (open chain); a ring cannot be part of the answer.

questions.question: For the structure CH<sub>3</sub>−CH<sub>2</sub>−CH(C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>)−CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)−CH<sub>3</sub>, which of the following is the correct IUPAC name?
options: 3-Ethyl-4-methylpentane
2-Ethyl-3-methylpentane
2-Methyl-3-ethylpentane
3-Ethyl-2-methylpentane
questions.explanation: The longest chain has 5 carbons (pentane) with an ethyl branch at C3 and a methyl branch at C2 (numbering from the end that gives the lower locant SET, {2,3}, rather than {3,4} from the other end). Substituents are then cited in ALPHABETICAL order in the name (ethyl before methyl), giving 3-ethyl-2-methylpentane.
questions.hint: First fix the numbering direction using the lowest-locant-set rule, then arrange the substituent names alphabetically (this does not change the locants already assigned).
distractor_logic: This uses the correct locants {2,3} but cites the substituents in the wrong order; IUPAC rules require strict alphabetical order (ethyl before methyl) in the name, not the order encountered along the chain.
This numbers the chain from the wrong end, giving locants {3,4} instead of the lower set {2,3}; the lowest-locant rule requires choosing the numbering direction that gives the smaller set of locants.
This correctly alphabetises the substituents but assigns the wrong locants (2 and 3 are swapped between the two substituents) — the ethyl group is at C3 and methyl at C2, not the reverse.

questions.question: Counting BOTH constitutional and geometrical isomers, how many distinct open-chain alkenes exist with molecular formula C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>?
options: 5, including a fifth constitutional isomer
2 (but-1-ene, but-2-ene)
3 (but-1-ene, but-2-ene, 2-methylpropene)
4 (but-1-ene, cis-but-2-ene, trans-but-2-ene, 2-methylpropene)
questions.explanation: There are 3 constitutional skeletons for C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub> open-chain alkenes: but-1-ene, but-2-ene, and 2-methylpropene. But-1-ene and 2-methylpropene each have a =CH<sub>2</sub> or doubly-methylated carbon and so show NO geometrical isomerism. But-2-ene's two double-bond carbons each carry a different pair of groups (CH<sub>3</sub> and H), so it DOES show geometrical isomerism, splitting into cis- and trans-but-2-ene. Total distinct isomers = 2 (non-geometrical) + 2 (cis/trans of but-2-ene) = 4.
questions.hint: First list the constitutional skeletons, then check each one individually for whether it additionally splits into cis/trans forms.
distractor_logic: This undercounts by treating but-2-ene as a single isomer, missing that it further splits into two distinct, isolable geometrical isomers (cis and trans).
There is no fifth constitutional (skeletal) isomer possible for C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub> open-chain alkenes; only three skeletons exist, one of which further splits geometrically.
This undercounts further, missing the geometrical isomer split entirely, and only counts constitutional skeletons.

questions.question: A student attempts to prepare pure propane by reacting a mixture of methyl bromide (CH<sub>3</sub>Br) and ethyl bromide (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>Br) together with sodium metal in dry ether (Wurtz reaction). Why is this NOT a good method to obtain pure propane?
options: The Wurtz reaction only works for identical alkyl halides, so no reaction occurs at all
The reaction statistically also couples each halide with itself, giving a mixture of ethane, butane, AND propane, requiring difficult separation
Propane cannot be formed by any Wurtz-type coupling, regardless of the halides used
Sodium metal does not react with methyl bromide at all, so only butane forms
questions.explanation: When two DIFFERENT alkyl halides are used together (an 'unsymmetrical' or 'crossed' Wurtz reaction), all three possible couplings occur simultaneously and statistically: CH<sub>3</sub>−CH<sub>3</sub> (ethane, from two methyls), C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>−C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub> (butane, from two ethyls), and CH<sub>3</sub>−C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub> (propane, the desired cross product) — making it inefficient and hard to purify the desired product from this mixture.
questions.hint: Consider all the possible pairwise combinations of radicals/anions that could combine when two different alkyl halides are both present.
distractor_logic: Propane IS one of the three products formed (from cross-coupling of the methyl and ethyl fragments); the actual problem is that it forms alongside ethane and butane, not that it cannot form at all.
Sodium metal does react readily with methyl bromide (as with any simple alkyl halide) under Wurtz conditions; this option's premise is factually incorrect.

The Wurtz reaction does proceed with a mixture of different halides; it just gives a statistical mixture of all three possible coupling products rather than a single clean product, so the reaction is not blocked entirely.

questions.question: A Grignard reagent, CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr, is treated with water. What alkane is formed, and which type of reaction does this represent?
options: Ethane; a Wurtz-type coupling of two methyl groups
No alkane forms; water only destroys the Grignard reagent without forming a new C−H bond
Methane; an oxidation of the Grignard reagent by water
Methane; protonolysis of the highly polar, basic C−Mg bond by a proton source
questions.explanation: The C−Mg bond in a Grignard reagent is highly polar (carbon is effectively carbanion-like) and strongly basic; even a weak proton source like water immediately protonates the carbanion-like carbon, replacing −MgBr with −H and releasing Mg(OH)Br — converting CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr directly into methane, with no coupling of two alkyl groups involved.
questions.hint: This is an acid−base (proton transfer) reaction, not a coupling of two separate alkyl fragments.
distractor_logic: This is a protonation (acid−base), not a redox (oxidation) process; the carbon's oxidation state is essentially unchanged, it simply gains a proton in place of the −MgBr group.

A new C−H bond IS formed (replacing the C−Mg bond) when the carbanion-like carbon is protonated by water; the reaction does productively form methane, it does not merely destroy the reagent unproductively.

Ethane would require two methyl groups to couple together (as in a Wurtz-type mechanism), but this reaction involves only a single proton transfer to the one methyl group already present, giving methane, not a doubled product.

questions.question: For rotation about the C2−C3 bond of butane, four representative conformations are: (i) anti-staggered, (ii) gauche-staggered, (iii) eclipsed with methyls overlapping two hydrogens, and (iv) fully eclipsed with the two methyl groups directly overlapping each other. Arrange these in order of INCREASING potential energy (most stable first).
options: anti < fully eclipsed < gauche < partially eclipsed
fully eclipsed < partially eclipsed < gauche < anti
anti < gauche < partially eclipsed < fully eclipsed (methyl−methyl)
gauche < anti < fully eclipsed < partially eclipsed
questions.explanation: Staggered conformations are always lower in energy than eclipsed ones (no eclipsing torsional strain). Between the two staggered forms, anti (methyls 180° apart) is more stable than gauche (methyls 60° apart, some steric strain). Between the two eclipsed forms, the one with methyl groups directly overlapping each other is the highest-energy conformation of all four, due to maximal steric clash, while the eclipsed conformation with methyls overlapping hydrogens (not each other) is somewhat less strained. Overall: anti < gauche < partially eclipsed < fully eclipsed (Me−Me).
questions.hint: Rank staggered forms below eclipsed forms first, then rank within each pair by how close the bulky methyl groups are positioned to each other.
distractor_logic: This incorrectly interleaves an eclipsed conformation between the two staggered ones; the two staggered (anti, gauche) forms are always lower in energy than either eclipsed form.
This incorrectly places both eclipsed forms below the staggered gauche conformation; ALL eclipsed conformations are higher in energy than ANY staggered conformation, without exception.
This incorrectly places gauche below anti; despite both being staggered, gauche has more steric strain from the closer methyl groups (60° apart) than anti (180° apart), so anti is always more stable.

questions.question: How many constitutionally different monochlorination products (ignoring stereochemistry) can 2-methylbutane (isopentane) give?
questions.explanation: 2-Methylbutane, CH<sub>3</sub>−CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)−CH<sub>2</sub>−CH<sub>3</sub>, has four chemically distinct hydrogen environments: (i) the two equivalent methyl groups directly attached to the tertiary carbon (C1 and the branch methyl, related by the molecule's local symmetry), (ii) the single tertiary C−H, (iii) the C3 methylene (−CH<sub>2</sub>−) hydrogens, and (iv) the C4 terminal methyl (which is NOT equivalent to the C1/branch methyls, since it sits one carbon further away). Substitution at each distinct environment gives a distinct product, so 4 monochloro isomers are possible.
questions.hint: Carefully separate the two 'terminal methyl' environments in this molecule — are they really all equivalent, or does one sit in a different position from the others?
distractor_logic: This overcounts; the two methyl groups directly attached to the tertiary carbon (C1 and the branch methyl) are equivalent to each other by the molecule's symmetry and give only ONE product between them, not two separate ones.
This also undercounts; besides overlooking the C4/C1-branch distinction, it may also miss the tertiary C−H as a separate environment from the methylene hydrogens.

This undercounts; it likely conflates the C4 terminal methyl with the C1/branch methyls, but C4 is attached to the CH<sub>2</sub> group (one bond further from the tertiary centre), making it a genuinely different environment.

questions.question: Free radical chlorination of 2-methylbutane gives some 2-chloro-2-methylbutane (tertiary chloride) as a significant product, even though the tertiary position has only 1 hydrogen compared to 6 equivalent primary hydrogens (from the two methyls on the tertiary carbon) and 2 secondary hydrogens. What does this reveal about the chlorination process?
options: The tertiary product forms exclusively via a completely different, ionic (not radical) mechanism
Chlorination is purely statistical, and the significant tertiary product formation actually contradicts the accepted mechanism
Tertiary hydrogens are chemically identical in reactivity to primary hydrogens; the product ratio is coincidental
Product distribution depends on BOTH the number of hydrogens available (statistical factor) and their relative reactivity (tertiary > secondary > primary), not on hydrogen count alone
questions.explanation: If chlorination were governed by hydrogen count alone, the vastly more numerous primary hydrogens (6 of them) would dominate the product mixture. The fact that the single tertiary hydrogen still contributes a significant share shows that tertiary C−H bonds are intrinsically MORE reactive per hydrogen (due to the greater stability of the resulting tertiary radical, formed via a weaker, more easily broken tertiary C−H bond), compensating for their lower statistical abundance.
questions.hint: If only the number of available hydrogens mattered, would the single tertiary hydrogen be expected to contribute much product at all?
distractor_logic: This is factually backwards: tertiary hydrogens are considerably MORE reactive than primary hydrogens toward radical abstraction (due to the greater stability of the resulting tertiary radical), not equally reactive.

Chlorination of alkanes (including at tertiary positions) proceeds via the same free-radical chain mechanism throughout; there is no separate ionic pathway responsible for the tertiary product specifically.

This misreads the observation: the significant tertiary product is fully CONSISTENT with the accepted free-radical mechanism (which accounts for both statistical abundance and relative radical stability), not a contradiction of it.

questions.question: 0.1 mol of an unknown straight-chain alkane, C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub>, requires exactly 0.65 mol of O<sub>2</sub> for complete combustion. What is n, and hence what is the alkane?
options: n = 4 (butane)
n = 6 (hexane)
n = 5 (pentane)
n = 3 (propane)
questions.explanation: The balanced combustion equation is C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub> + [(3n+1)/2]O<sub>2</sub> → nCO<sub>2</sub> + (n+1)H<sub>2</sub>O. Given 0.1 mol alkane needs 0.65 mol O<sub>2</sub>: 0.1 × (3n+1)/2 = 0.65, so (3n+1)/2 = 6.5, giving 3n + 1 = 13, so n = 4 — butane.
questions.hint: Set up the mole ratio from the general balanced equation and solve algebraically for n.
distractor_logic: n = 5 would require 0.1 × (3×5+1)/2 = 0.1 × 8 = 0.8 mol O<sub>2</sub>, not the given 0.65 mol.
n = 3 would require 0.1 × (3×3+1)/2 = 0.1 × 5 = 0.5 mol O<sub>2</sub>, not the given 0.65 mol.
n = 6 would require 0.1 × (3×6+1)/2 = 0.1 × 9.5 = 0.95 mol O<sub>2</sub>, far more than the given 0.65 mol.

questions.question: For the structure CH<sub>3</sub>−CH<sub>2</sub>−C(CH<sub>3</sub>)=CH−CH<sub>3</sub>, which locant set and name correctly follow IUPAC's 'lowest locant to the principal characteristic group (here, the double bond)' rule?
options: 3-Methylpent-2-ene (double bond locant 2, methyl locant 3)
4-Methylpent-2-ene
2-Methylpent-3-ene (double bond locant 3, methyl locant 2)
3-Methylpent-3-ene
questions.explanation: Numbering from the end nearer the double bond (the right-hand CH<sub>3</sub> end) gives: C1(CH<sub>3</sub>)−C2(H)=C3(CH<sub>3</sub>)−C4(H<sub>2</sub>)−C5(H<sub>3</sub>). The double bond is between C2 and C3 (cited as the lower locant, 2), and the methyl substituent sits on C3. This gives 3-methylpent-2-ene, correctly prioritising the lowest locant for the double bond over the substituent.
questions.hint: IUPAC rules give the double bond priority for the lowest locant over a simple alkyl substituent; number from whichever end achieves that.
distractor_logic: This locant set (3,3) does not correctly describe this structure at all; the double bond and the methyl substituent are on adjacent, not the same, pair of numbered carbons.
This numbers from the wrong end, giving the double bond the higher locant (3) instead of the lower one (2); the double bond should get priority for the lowest possible locant.

This uses locant 4 for the methyl group, which would only be correct if numbering from the wrong end AND for a different substitution pattern; it does not match this structure under lowest-locant numbering.

questions.question: Hexa-2,4-diene, CH<sub>3</sub>−CH=CH−CH=CH−CH<sub>3</sub>, has two independent double bonds, each individually capable of a cis or trans arrangement. Accounting for the molecule's own symmetry, how many DISTINCT geometrical isomers does it actually have?
options: 2 (only E,E and Z,Z are possible)
3 (the E,E and Z,Z forms, plus a single E,Z form that is identical to its own Z,E mirror-numbering)
4 (all combinations E,E / E,Z / Z,E / Z,Z are distinct)
1 (the molecule cannot show geometrical isomerism at all, since it has two double bonds)
questions.explanation: Naively, 2 independent double bonds give 2<sup>2</sup> = 4 combinations. However, hexa-2,4-diene is symmetric (CH<sub>3</sub>−CH=CH−CH=CH−CH<sub>3</sub>reads the same from either end), so labelling one double bond 'E' and the other 'Z' (the E,Z combination) describes the EXACT SAME molecule as labelling them in the opposite order (Z,E) — they are related by simply flipping the molecule end-to-end. This collapses the 4 naive combinations into 3 genuinely distinct isomers: E,E; Z,Z; and the single (E,Z = Z,E) form.
questions.hint: Before concluding there are 4 isomers, check whether swapping the labels of the two double bonds (reading the molecule from the other end) actually gives a different molecule or the same one.
distractor_logic: This misses the molecule's own end-to-end symmetry, which makes the E,Z and Z,E combinations identical to each other rather than two separate isomers.
This undercounts by missing the mixed E,Z form entirely; besides the two 'matched' forms (E,E and Z,Z), there genuinely is a third, distinct 'mismatched' form.

Hexa-2,4-diene absolutely can show geometrical isomerism; each of its two double bonds independently carries two different groups (CH<sub>3</sub>/H on the end carbons, and H/−CH=CH− fragment on the inner carbons), satisfying the requirement for cis/trans isomerism at both sites.

y2="125" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><text x="266" y="137" font-size="15" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="start" dominant-baseline="middle">CH₃</text></svg>, which has a net molecular dipole moment of (approximately) zero, and why?
options: trans-But-2-ene — its two C−CH<sub>3</sub> bond dipole vectors point in opposite directions and cancel by the molecule's symmetry
cis-But-2-ene — its two C−CH<sub>3</sub> bond dipole vectors reinforce each other, which coincidentally sums to zero
Neither isomer has any net dipole moment, since but-2-ene is an overall non-polar hydrocarbon
trans-But-2-ene — because it contains no bonds capable of having a dipole moment at all
questions.explanation: Each C−CH<sub>3</sub> bond has a small dipole moment (methyl groups are weakly electron-donating relative to the sp<sup>2</sup> vinylic carbon). In trans-but-2-ene, the two methyl groups point to opposite sides of the double bond axis, so their bond dipole vectors point in opposite directions and cancel by the molecule's symmetry, giving a net dipole close to zero. In cis-but-2-ene, both methyls are on the same side, so the two bond dipoles partially reinforce, giving cis-but-2-ene a small but genuinely non-zero net dipole moment.
questions.hint: Think of each C−CH<sub>3</sub> bond as a small vector arrow; add the two arrows together for each isomer and see which sum is (near) zero.
distractor_logic: This ignores that cis-but-2-ene does have a small but measurable net dipole moment, since its two C−CH<sub>3</sub> bond dipoles do not fully cancel by symmetry the way trans-but-2-ene's do.
This correctly describes cis-but-2-ene's bond dipoles as reinforcing (giving a small NON-zero dipole), but then wrongly claims this sums to zero — reinforcing vectors add up, they do not cancel.

This is factually wrong; C−C and C−H bonds between atoms of different electronegativity do have small dipole moments, and more importantly cis/trans-but-2-ene's near-zero (trans) vs. small (cis) dipole difference arises from vector geometry, not an absence of any dipole-capable bonds.

questions.question: 2-Bromo-2-methylbutane is heated with alcoholic KOH. Two elimination products are possible: 2-methylbut-2-ene (removing a beta-H from C3) or 3-methylbut-1-ene (removing a beta-H from one of the two equivalent methyl groups on C2). Which is the major product, and why?
options: 2-Methylbut-2-ene, because it is the more highly substituted (trisubstituted), more stable alkene, favoured by Zaitsev's rule
Neither forms; tertiary halides do not undergo elimination with alcoholic KOH
3-Methylbut-1-ene, because primary C−H bonds are always removed preferentially in elimination
Both form in exactly equal amounts, since the leaving group is the same tertiary bromide either way
questions.explanation: 2-Methylbut-2-ene has three alkyl groups (two methyls and one from the original chain) directly attached to its double-bond carbons, making it trisubstituted and more stable than the monosubstituted 3-methylbut-1-ene. Zaitsev's rule predicts the more substituted, more stable alkene predominates in this E1/E2 elimination from a tertiary halide, so 2-methylbut-2-ene is the major product.
questions.hint: Compare how many alkyl groups are attached directly to the double-bond carbons in each of the two possible products.
distractor_logic: Tertiary alkyl halides are actually the BEST substrates for E1/E2 elimination with alcoholic KOH (readily forming a stable tertiary carbocation or undergoing facile E2), not unreactive toward it.

This is backwards; Zaitsev's rule favours removing a beta-H that leads to the MORE substituted alkene, which in this case is a beta-H from C3 (giving the trisubstituted product), not preferential removal of primary hydrogens.
The two products are NOT formed in equal amounts under Zaitsev-controlled elimination; the more substituted alkene is significantly favoured, not an even 50:50 split.

questions.question: Propan-1-ol is first converted to 1-bromopropane using HBr, and the 1-bromopropane is then heated with alcoholic KOH. What is the final major product of this two-step sequence, and why is there no ambiguity about which alkene forms?
options: Propan-2-ol; alcoholic KOH substitutes the bromide with hydroxide instead of eliminating
But-1-ene; the carbon chain is extended by one carbon during the HBr step
Propane; alcoholic KOH reduces the C−Br bond directly to C−H
Propene; 1-bromopropane has only one type of beta-hydrogen available (on C2), so elimination can give only one possible alkene
questions.explanation: Step 1: propan-1-ol + HBr → 1-bromopropane (simple substitution, no change in carbon count). Step 2: 1-bromopropane, CH<sub>3</sub>−CH<sub>2</sub>−CH<sub>2</sub>Br, has beta-hydrogens only on C2 (C1 bears the leaving Br and has no adjacent carbon beyond C2 on that side); elimination can only remove an H from C2, giving a single unambiguous product, propene — there is no second elimination pathway to compete via Zaitsev's rule here.
questions.hint: First identify the actual product of the substitution step, then check which carbons are adjacent (beta) to the leaving group in that specific molecule.
distractor_logic: No step in this sequence adds a carbon atom; HBr substitution and KOH elimination both preserve the original 3-carbon chain, so a 4-carbon product (but-1-ene) is not possible here.
Alcoholic KOH acts as a base promoting elimination (loss of HBr), not as a reducing agent; it does not simply replace C−Br with C−H without removing an additional hydrogen to form a double bond.

Alcoholic (not aqueous) KOH strongly favours elimination over substitution; the alcoholic medium was specifically chosen in this sequence to drive the second step toward the alkene, not a substitution product.

questions.question: Propene is first treated with HBr (no peroxide) to form 2-bromopropane, which is then heated with alcoholic KOH. What is the final product of this two-step sequence, relative to the starting material?
options: Propene is regenerated, since 2-bromopropane has only equivalent beta-hydrogens (on C1 and C3) that eliminate back to the same alkene
Propan-2-ol forms, since alcoholic KOH substitutes rather than eliminates
But-2-ene forms, since the carbon chain is extended during the addition step
Propane forms, since two sequential reactions fully saturate any remaining unsaturation
questions.explanation: Step 1 (Markovnikov addition of HBr to propene) gives 2-bromopropane. Step 2 (elimination with alcoholic KOH) removes a beta-hydrogen from either C1 or C3 (both primary methyls, chemically equivalent by the molecule's symmetry), regenerating the identical alkene, propene, that the sequence started from — illustrating that simple Markovnikov addition followed by elimination can be a net 'round trip'.
questions.hint: Work out the structure after each individual step, then compare the final structure to what you started with.
distractor_logic: The second step is an elimination (forming a new double bond), not a reduction; it does not add hydrogen to saturate the molecule further, so propane is not the product.
No step in this two-reaction sequence adds a carbon atom; both the HBr addition and the KOH elimination act on the same 3-carbon skeleton throughout, so a 4-carbon product is not possible.
Alcoholic (not aqueous) KOH conditions favour elimination over substitution, which is exactly why this sequence regenerates the alkene rather than forming an alcohol.

questions.question: Addition of HCl to 3-methylbut-1-ene, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CH−CH=CH<sub>2</sub>, gives a significant amount of 2-chloro-2-methylbutane as the major product, rather than the 'simple' Markovnikov product 2-chloro-3-methylbutane. What explains this outcome?
options: This indicates the reaction actually proceeds by anti-Markovnikov addition instead
The starting alkene must have been contaminated with a positional isomer before the reaction began
The initially-formed secondary carbocation rearranges via a hydride shift to a more stable tertiary carbocation before Cl<sup>−</sup> attacks
Chlorine atoms are known to migrate spontaneously along a carbon chain after addition is complete
questions.explanation: Markovnikov protonation of the terminal =CH<sub>2</sub> carbon initially gives a secondary carbocation at C2. Since the adjacent C3 carbon bears a hydrogen and is itself attached to two methyl groups, a 1,2-hydride shift from C3 to C2 converts this into a MORE stable tertiary carbocation at C3; Cl<sup>−</sup> then attacks this rearranged, more stable cation, giving 2-chloro-2-methylbutane as the major (rearranged) product.
questions.hint: Consider whether the initially-formed carbocation is the most stable possible cation, or whether a neighbouring hydrogen could shift to create a more stable one.
distractor_logic: It is hydride ions (H<sup>−</sup>, with their bonding electron pair), not chlorine atoms, that migrate in this rearrangement, and this occurs at the carbocation intermediate stage, before Cl<sup>−</sup> ever attacks — not as a separate step after addition is 'complete'.

This is still fundamentally Markovnikov addition (H<sup>+</sup> added first, generating a carbocation that Cl<sup>−</sup> subsequently attacks); the unusual product arises from cation rearrangement, not a change in overall addition regiochemistry.
The rearranged product is a genuine, well-precedented consequence of carbocation stability differences in THIS reaction; no impurity or contamination needs to be invoked to explain it.

questions.topic: Alkenes: Markovnikov's Rule and Peroxide Effect
questions.question: A chemist needs to prepare 1-bromobutane selectively, starting from but-1-ene. Which single set of conditions achieves this, and why?
options: HBr with no peroxides, since Markovnikov's rule already favours the terminal carbon for but-1-ene
HBr in the presence of peroxides, since the resulting radical mechanism places Br at the terminal (less hindered, less substituted) carbon
This product cannot be obtained selectively from but-1-ene by any HBr-based method
HBr with no peroxides AND a large excess of the alkene, to force the anti-Markovnikov product
questions.explanation: Without peroxides, HBr would add via Markovnikov's rule, placing Br at C2 (giving the more stable secondary-carbocation-derived 2-bromobutane), NOT the desired terminal product. With peroxides, the radical mechanism adds Br• first to the terminal, less hindered carbon (forming the more stable secondary radical at C2), which upon completion places Br at C1 — the anti-Markovnikov outcome that is actually needed here.
questions.hint: Work out where Br ends up under NORMAL (no peroxide) Markovnikov addition first, then decide whether that matches the terminal position wanted.
distractor_logic: Using excess alkene has no bearing on regiochemistry (Markovnikov vs. anti-Markovnikov); only the presence or absence of a radical initiator like peroxide determines which carbon the bromine ends up on.
Without peroxides, Markovnikov addition would place the bromine at C2 (the more substituted carbon), giving 2-bromobutane, not the terminal 1-bromobutane that is actually wanted.
1-Bromobutane IS obtainable selectively from but-1-ene, precisely by using the peroxide-catalysed radical addition pathway described in the correct option.

questions.topic: Alkenes: Markovnikov's Rule and Peroxide Effect
questions.question: But-2-ene, CH<sub>3</sub>−CH=CH−CH<sub>3</sub>, is reacted with HBr, once with peroxides present and once without. What is observed?
options: No reaction occurs without peroxides, since but-2-ene lacks a terminal double bond
The same product, 2-bromobutane, forms in both cases, since the molecule's symmetry makes Markovnikov and anti-Markovnikov addition indistinguishable here
The peroxide effect causes complete double addition of HBr across the double bond in this case
Two different products form: 1-bromobutane without peroxide, and 2-bromobutane with peroxide
questions.explanation: But-2-ene is a symmetric internal alkene: both double-bond carbons are equivalent secondary centres attached to identical CH<sub>3</sub> groups. Whether H<sup>+</sup> (ionic pathway) or Br• (radical pathway) adds first, both possible addition directions lead to the SAME product, 2-bromobutane, since the two carbons are chemically indistinguishable — the peroxide effect has no visible consequence for this particular (symmetric) alkene.
questions.hint: Check whether the two double-bond carbons of but-2-ene are actually different from each other, the way they are in an unsymmetrical alkene like propene.
distractor_logic: The peroxide effect changes the REGIOCHEMISTRY of single HBr addition (via a radical rather than ionic mechanism); it does not cause a second equivalent of HBr to add across the same double bond.
