This assumes but-2-ene behaves like an unsymmetrical alkene (such as propene), where the two carbons genuinely differ; but but-2-ene's symmetry means both addition directions converge on the identical product.
But-2-ene is a perfectly reactive internal alkene toward HBr addition; the absence of a TERMINAL double bond does not prevent electrophilic (or radical) addition from occurring at all.

questions.question: Ozonolysis (Zn/H<sub>2</sub>O workup) of an unknown alkene X gives ONLY acetone, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C=O, as the sole detectable carbonyl product (no other compound formed). What must the structure of X be?
options: Propene, CH<sub>2</sub>=CH−CH<sub>3</sub> — giving one formaldehyde and one acetaldehyde fragment
2,3-Dimethylbut-2-ene, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C=C(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> — a symmetric alkene giving two identical acetone fragments
But-2-ene, CH<sub>3</sub>−CH=CH−CH<sub>3</sub> — giving two acetaldehyde fragments
2-Methylpropene, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C=CH<sub>2</sub> — giving one acetone and one formaldehyde fragment
questions.explanation: Since only ONE product (acetone) is obtained, BOTH halves of the cleaved double bond must independently generate acetone — meaning both double-bond carbons must each bear two methyl groups. This requires the fully symmetric alkene (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C=C(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> (2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene), which cleaves into two identical (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C=O fragments.
questions.hint: For only ONE product to form from cleaving a double bond, both halves of the alkene must be identically substituted.
distractor_logic: Propene's double bond is highly unsymmetrical (one =CH<sub>2</sub> carbon, one =CH(CH<sub>3</sub>) carbon), giving two DIFFERENT products (formaldehyde and acetaldehyde), and neither of them is acetone at all.

2-Methylpropene has an unsymmetrical double bond: one carbon bears two methyls (giving acetone) but the other bears two hydrogens (giving formaldehyde, a second, different product), contradicting the single-product observation.
But-2-ene's double-bond carbons each bear one methyl and one hydrogen, giving two molecules of acetaldehyde (not acetone) — a mono-, not di-, substituted carbonyl product.

questions.question: <svg viewBox="0 0 300 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:100%;height:auto"><line x1="150.0" y1="45.0" x2="193.3" y2="70.0" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="152.6" y1="54.6" x2="183.7" y2="72.6" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="193.3" y1="70.0" x2="193.3" y2="120.0" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="193.3" y1="120.0" x2="150.0" y2="145.0" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="150.0" y1="145.0" x2="106.7" y2="120.0" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="106.7" y1="120.0" x2="106.7" y2="70.0" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="106.7" y1="70.0" x2="150.0" y2="45.0" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="150.0" y1="45.0" x2="150.0" y2="17.0" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><text x="150.0" y="5.0" font-size="15" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle">CH₃</text></svg> 1-Methylcyclohexene (shown above) undergoes ozonolysis with Zn/H<sub>2</sub>O workup. Since the double bond is part of a RING rather than an open chain, what is the outcome?
options: Two separate carbonyl products form, exactly as with an open-chain alkene
No reaction occurs, since ozone cannot cleave a bond that is part of a ring
The ring is cleaved but immediately re-closes, regenerating the starting material
A single open-chain dicarbonyl product forms (6-oxoheptanal), since cleaving one bond of a ring opens it into one chain rather than splitting it into two separate fragments
questions.explanation: Ozonolysis chemically cleaves the C=C bond regardless of whether it is in a ring or an open chain. For an open-chain alkene, cutting the one C=C bond produces two separate molecular fragments. But for a RING alkene, the C=C is the only bond connecting that part of the ring closed; cutting it does not disconnect the molecule into two pieces — it simply opens (unzips) the ring into a single longer open chain bearing a carbonyl group at EACH end. Here, the ring carbon bearing −CH<sub>3</sub> (fully substituted) becomes a ketone terminus, and the =CH− ring carbon becomes an aldehyde terminus, connected by the remaining 4-carbon ring chain — giving the single product 6-oxoheptanal (CH<sub>3</sub>−CO−CH<sub>2</sub>−CH<sub>2</sub>−CH<sub>2</sub>−CH<sub>2</sub>−CHO).
questions.hint: Think about whether cutting just one bond of a closed loop actually separates it into two independent pieces, the way cutting a bond in a straight chain does.
distractor_logic: Ozonolysis is not a reversible ring-opening/ring-closing process; the C=C bond is chemically transformed into two separate C=O bonds, which cannot spontaneously re-form the original double bond and ring.

Ozone reacts with the C=C pi bond itself, and it makes no difference whether that pi bond happens to be part of a ring or an open chain; the ring system does not somehow shield the double bond from ozone.

This is the outcome for an OPEN-CHAIN alkene, where the two ends were never otherwise connected; a ring's carbons remain joined by the rest of the ring even after the double bond is cleaved, so the two carbonyl ends stay part of one single molecule.

questions.question: The heat of hydrogenation of but-1-ene is about 127 kJ/mol, while that of but-2-ene is about 120 kJ/mol (both give the same product, butane). Using this data, which alkene is more stable, and what general trend about alkene substitution does this illustrate?
options: But-2-ene is LESS stable, since a smaller heat of hydrogenation means less bond energy was available to release in the first place

But-2-ene is more stable; a smaller heat of hydrogenation means the starting alkene was already at a lower (more stable) energy level, consistent with more substituted alkenes being generally more stable
But-1-ene is more stable; releasing less energy would mean starting from a higher-energy, less stable alkene, which is inconsistent with this data
Both alkenes are equally stable, since they hydrogenate to the identical product, butane
questions.explanation: Since both alkenes hydrogenate to the SAME final product (butane), a SMALLER heat of hydrogenation means the starting alkene was already closer in energy to that final, common product — i.e., the alkene itself was at a LOWER energy (more stable) to begin with. But-2-ene (disubstituted, an internal alkene with an alkyl group on each double-bond carbon) releasing less heat (120 vs. 127 kJ/mol) than but-1-ene (monosubstituted, terminal) confirms the general trend that more substituted alkenes are more stable, consistent with hyperconjugative and inductive stabilisation from the additional alkyl groups.
questions.hint: Since both reactions end at the same energy level (butane), a smaller energy release must mean a smaller energy 'drop' — which alkene, then, started higher up?
distractor_logic: This misinterprets what 'more bond energy available to release' would mean; the heat of hydrogenation reflects the energy DIFFERENCE between the specific starting alkene and the common product, not some independent quantity of stored bond energy unrelated to the alkene's own stability.

This reasoning inverts the logic: since the final product (butane) is identical for both, a LARGER heat release (but-1-ene, 127 kJ/mol) means but-1-ene started at a HIGHER (less stable) energy, not that it was the more stable one.

Having the same final product does not make the starting alkenes equally stable; it is precisely BECAUSE they reach the same endpoint that their differing heats of hydrogenation directly reveal their differing starting stabilities.

questions.question: Ranking the acidity of a terminal alkyne's ≡C−H, an alkene's =C−H, and an alkane's −C−H (all else being comparable), and given that sodium amide (NaNH<sub>2</sub>) is a strong enough base to deprotonate a terminal alkyne but not an alkene or alkane C−H bond, what does this reveal about the relationship between hybridisation and acidity?
options: Acidity is unrelated to hybridisation; NaNH<sub>2</sub> simply reacts faster with alkynes for unrelated steric reasons

Acidity increases with increasing s-character of the hybrid orbital holding the C−H bonding pair (sp > sp<sup>2</sup> > sp<sup>3</sup>), and NaNH<sub>2</sub> is strong enough to cross only the sp threshold
NaNH<sub>2</sub> deprotonates all three equally well; the terminal alkyne reaction is simply easier to observe experimentally
Acidity decreases with increasing s-character, so alkane C−H bonds should actually be the most acidic of the three
questions.explanation: Greater s-character (sp, 50% s > sp<sup>2</sup>, 33% s > sp<sup>3</sup>, 25% s) holds the bonding electrons closer to the carbon nucleus, stabilising the resulting carbanion and making that C−H bond more acidic. This is exactly why terminal alkynes (pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 25) are acidic enough for the moderately strong base NaNH<sub>2</sub> (conjugate acid NH<sub>3</sub>, pK<sub>a</sub> ≈ 38) to deprotonate them essentially completely, while alkenes and alkanes (pK<sub>a</sub> in the 44−50 range) are far too weakly acidic for NaNH<sub>2</sub> to touch.
questions.hint: Recall the relative percentage of s-character in sp, sp<sup>2</sup>, and sp<sup>3</sup> hybrid orbitals, and how that affects how tightly the bonding electrons are held.
distractor_logic: This ignores a well-established, mechanistically grounded trend; hybridisation-dependent acidity is a direct, quantifiable consequence of how close bonding electrons sit to the nucleus in orbitals of differing s-character, not a coincidental steric effect.

NaNH<sub>2</sub> is a strong base, but not strong enough to deprotonate the far less acidic alkene or alkane C−H bonds to any significant extent (they are simply too weakly acidic, by many pK<sub>a</sub> units); this is a genuine reactivity difference, not merely an observational convenience.
This reverses the actual trend; MORE s-character (not less) correlates with greater acidity, since the electrons are held closer to the nucleus, better stabilising the resulting negative charge.

questions.question: Suggest a two-step reagent sequence to convert but-1-yne (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>−C≡CH) into pent-1-yne (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>−C≡CH), extending the chain by one carbon at the terminal position.
options: (1) O<sub>3</sub> then Zn/H<sub>2</sub>O, to cleave the triple bond; (2) NaBH<sub>4</sub>, to add back one carbon
(1) NaNH<sub>2</sub>, to form the sodium acetylide; (2) CH<sub>3</sub>Br, to alkylate the acetylide anion with a methyl group
(1) H<sub>2</sub>/Lindlar's catalyst, to reduce to an alkene; (2) HBr/peroxide, to add a bromine that later becomes a methyl group
(1) Br<sub>2</sub>, to add across the triple bond; (2) Mg/dry ether, to form a Grignard reagent that extends the chain
questions.explanation: NaNH<sub>2</sub> deprotonates the acidic terminal ≡C−H of but-1-yne, forming the nucleophilic sodium alkynide (acetylide) anion, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>−C≡C<sup>−</sup>Na<sup>+</sup>. This carbanion then performs an S<sub>N</sub>2 attack on the electrophilic carbon of a primary alkyl halide like CH<sub>3</sub>Br, forming a new C−C bond and extending the chain by exactly one carbon, giving pent-1-yne while regenerating the terminal ≡C−H.
questions.hint: The key step is generating a nucleophilic carbanion at the terminal alkyne carbon, which can then attack a simple alkyl halide.
distractor_logic: Simple addition of Br<sub>2</sub> across the triple bond does not create a site for chain extension in the way needed, and forming a Grignard reagent from a vicinal dibromide under these conditions would not cleanly extend the original alkyne chain by one carbon while preserving the triple bond.

Reducing the triple bond to an alkene (step 1) moves in the wrong direction, since the target is still an alkyne; the alkyne functionality would need to be destroyed and could not be simply regenerated by an HBr/peroxide addition.

Ozonolysis cleaves and destroys the triple bond entirely (breaking the carbon skeleton apart), which is the opposite of the chain-EXTENSION needed here; NaBH<sub>4</sub> is a reducing agent, not a carbon-chain-building reagent.

questions.question: How many total moles of Br<sub>2</sub> are required to completely saturate (convert to the fully saturated tetrabromoalkane) 1 mole of but-1-yne?
options: 1 mole
4 moles
2 moles
3 moles
questions.explanation: The triple bond of but-1-yne first adds 1 mole of Br<sub>2</sub> to give a dibromoalkene (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>−CBr=CHBr); this remaining double bond then adds a SECOND mole of Br<sub>2</sub> to give the fully saturated tetrabromoalkane (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>−CBr<sub>2</sub>−CHBr<sub>2</sub>). Total Br<sub>2</sub> consumed = 1 + 1 = 2 moles.
questions.hint: Break the process into its two sequential addition stages: triple bond to double bond, then double bond to single bond.
distractor_logic: 3 moles overcounts; only two sequential additions (triple → double, then double → single) are needed, each consuming exactly one mole of Br<sub>2</sub>, not three.

1 mole of Br<sub>2</sub> only converts the triple bond to a double bond (a dibromoalkene); the resulting alkene still has one more degree of unsaturation that requires a second equivalent of Br<sub>2</sub> to fully saturate.
4 moles substantially overcounts the stoichiometry required; each addition step consumes only one mole of Br<sub>2</sub>, and only two such steps are needed to fully saturate one triple bond.

questions.question: The cycloheptatrienyl (tropylium) cation, C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>7</sub><sup>+</sup>, is unusually stable for a carbocation. Using Hückel's rule, explain why.
options: Carbocations are inherently stable regardless of ring size or electron count, so this is unrelated to aromaticity
It is planar, cyclic, and fully conjugated with 6 delocalised pi electrons (4n+2, n=1), satisfying Hückel's rule for aromaticity despite being a cation
It is stabilised only by simple inductive electron donation from the seven CH groups, with no aromatic contribution
It has 7 pi electrons, one for each ring carbon, which happens to satisfy the (4n+2) rule for n=1.25
questions.explanation: Removing a hydride from cycloheptatriene leaves an empty p orbital on the former sp<sup>3</sup> carbon, which becomes part of a fully conjugated, planar, cyclic pi system. Counting electrons: the resulting cation has 7 ring carbons but only 6 pi ELECTRONS (each of the three remaining formal double bonds contributes 2 electrons, and the cationic centre contributes an empty p orbital, not electrons). Six pi electrons satisfies Hückel's (4n+2) rule with n=1, making the tropylium cation aromatic and unusually stabilised, unlike a typical localised carbocation.
questions.hint: Be careful to distinguish the number of ring CARBONS (7) from the number of pi ELECTRONS actually present (which is fewer, since one carbon is cationic and contributes no electrons to the pi system).
distractor_logic: Ordinary (non-aromatic) carbocations are generally quite unstable and reactive; tropylium's exceptional stability specifically requires the special aromatic stabilisation described, it is not a general property of all carbocations.

This conflates the number of ring CARBONS (7) with the number of pi ELECTRONS (6); the cationic carbon contributes an empty p orbital, not an electron, and 7 does not fit the (4n+2) pattern for any integer n in any case.

While the ring carbons do have some inductive effects, the tropylium cation's remarkable extra stability (far beyond a typical carbocation) is specifically attributed to its aromatic delocalisation satisfying Hückel's rule, not simple induction alone.

questions.question: Benzene is first converted to toluene by Friedel−Crafts methylation (CH<sub>3</sub>Cl/anhydrous AlCl<sub>3</sub>). The resulting toluene is then treated with hot, concentrated, alkaline KMnO<sub>4</sub>, followed by acidification. What is the final product of this ENTIRE two-step sequence, starting from benzene?
options: Benzaldehyde (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CHO), from partial oxidation stopping at the aldehyde stage
Benzoic acid (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>COOH), from complete oxidation of the methyl side chain
Toluene itself, since KMnO<sub>4</sub> does not react with alkylbenzenes
Benzyl alcohol (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH), from partial oxidation of the methyl group
questions.explanation: Step 1 installs a methyl group on the ring (benzene → toluene). Step 2 uses hot, concentrated alkaline KMnO<sub>4</sub>, a strong oxidant that oxidises a benzylic C−H-bearing side chain (regardless of its original length) all the way to a ring-attached −COOH group; the aromatic ring itself is untouched. Acidification of the resulting carboxylate salt gives benzoic acid as the final isolated product.
questions.hint: Hot, concentrated alkaline KMnO<sub>4</sub> is a strong enough oxidant to NOT stop at an intermediate oxidation state of the side chain.
distractor_logic: Hot alkaline KMnO<sub>4</sub> is specifically known to oxidise alkylbenzene side chains (this is a standard, well-established reaction of toluene and similar compounds), not leave them untouched.

Benzaldehyde is likewise only a partial oxidation intermediate; the vigorous hot, concentrated alkaline KMnO<sub>4</sub> conditions carry the oxidation through to completion, giving the carboxylic acid, not stopping at the aldehyde.

Benzyl alcohol would be only a partial oxidation product; under the strongly oxidising hot KMnO<sub>4</sub> conditions specified, oxidation proceeds all the way to the carboxylic acid, not stopping at the alcohol stage.

questions.question: Rank the relative rates of nitration (HNO<sub>3</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>) for benzene, toluene, and nitrobenzene, from FASTEST to SLOWEST.
options: Toluene > benzene > nitrobenzene
All three react at the same rate, since nitration always proceeds through the same NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> electrophile
Nitrobenzene > benzene > toluene
Benzene > toluene > nitrobenzene
questions.explanation: The rate of electrophilic aromatic substitution depends heavily on the ring's electron density, set by any existing substituent. Toluene's −CH<sub>3</sub> group is activating (electron-donating via hyperconjugation), speeding up attack by the electrophile relative to unsubstituted benzene. Nitrobenzene's −NO<sub>2</sub> group is strongly deactivating (electron-withdrawing by both induction and resonance), making its ring much less reactive than even plain benzene. This gives the order toluene > benzene > nitrobenzene.
questions.hint: Think about whether each ring's existing substituent makes it more or less electron-rich than plain benzene, then rank accordingly.
distractor_logic: This places toluene as slower than plain benzene, ignoring that the methyl group's electron-donating (activating) effect makes toluene's ring MORE reactive than unsubstituted benzene, not less.

While the same electrophile (NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>) does attack all three rings, the RATE at which it does so depends strongly on each ring's electron density, which differs substantially between an activated ring (toluene), a neutral one (benzene), and a strongly deactivated one (nitrobenzene).

This places the strongly deactivated nitrobenzene as fastest and the activated toluene as slowest, the complete reverse of how electron density (governed by each ring's substituent) actually affects electrophilic attack rate.

questions.question: Sulfonation of benzene with fuming H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (or SO<sub>3</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>) gives benzenesulfonic acid; heating this product with superheated steam reverses the reaction, regenerating benzene. What does this reversibility reveal about the electrophilic substitution mechanism?
options: This is unique to sulfonation; no other electrophilic aromatic substitution can ever be reversed

The reaction proceeds through a genuine arenium ion (sigma-complex) intermediate that can lose EITHER the electrophile OR H<sup>+</sup> to re-aromatise, making the overall process a true equilibrium under appropriate conditions
The reversibility shows benzene's ring is permanently destroyed and randomly re-forms by chance under steam
Sulfonation must not actually be an electrophilic substitution at all, since true substitutions are always irreversible
questions.explanation: After SO<sub>3</sub>H<sup>+</sup>-type electrophile attacks the ring, the resulting arenium (Wheland) intermediate can either lose H<sup>+</sup> to give the substitution product (forward direction, favoured under fuming H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>) or, since the C−SO<sub>3</sub>H bond formation is itself reversible under forcing conditions, lose the −SO<sub>3</sub>H group instead (effectively the reverse reaction, favoured when diluted with excess water/steam, which shifts the equilibrium back toward benzene). This demonstrates that the arenium ion intermediate is a genuine, reversible branch point in the mechanism, not simply a one-way pathway to substitution.
questions.hint: Think about the arenium ion intermediate as a fork in the road, with two different groups that could each potentially be expelled to restore the aromatic ring.
distractor_logic: The ring is not 'destroyed and randomly re-formed'; the mechanism proceeds through a specific, well-defined arenium ion intermediate whose breakdown pathway (losing H<sup>+</sup> vs. losing −SO<sub>3</sub>H) is what determines the direction of the reaction, not random chance.

While sulfonation's reversibility under steam is a particularly well-known textbook example, the underlying arenium-ion mechanism (and hence, in principle, the possibility of reversibility under suitable conditions) is common to electrophilic aromatic substitution generally, not exclusive to sulfonation alone.

This is a real, well-documented example of electrophilic aromatic substitution; being reversible under specific, forcing conditions does not disqualify a mechanism from being classified as substitution — it instead reveals detail about the mechanism's intermediate.

questions.topic: Aromatic Hydrocarbons: Directive Influence of Substituents
questions.question: <svg viewBox="0 0 300 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:100%;height:auto"><line x1="150.0" y1="45.0" x2="193.3" y2="70.0" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="152.6" y1="54.6" x2="183.7" y2="72.6" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="193.3" y1="70.0" x2="193.3" y2="120.0" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="193.3" y1="120.0" x2="150.0" y2="145.0" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="183.7" y1="117.4" x2="152.6" y2="135.4" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="150.0" y1="145.0" x2="106.7" y2="120.0" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="106.7" y1="120.0" x2="106.7" y2="70.0" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="113.7" y1="113.0" x2="113.7" y2="77.0" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="106.7" y1="70.0" x2="150.0" y2="45.0" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="150.0" y1="45.0" x2="150.0" y2="17.0" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><text x="150.0" y="5.0" font-size="15" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle">CH₃</text><line x1="150.0" y1="145.0" x2="150.0" y2="173.0" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><text x="150.0" y="185.0" font-size="15" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle">NO₂</text></svg> para-Nitrotoluene (shown above, −CH<sub>3</sub> and −NO<sub>2</sub> para to each other) undergoes further bromination (Br<sub>2</sub>/FeBr<sub>3</sub>). Reconciling both substituents' directing effects on the four remaining open ring positions, where does Br predominantly attack?
options: Ortho to −CH<sub>3</sub> (which is simultaneously meta to −NO<sub>2</sub>) — both directing effects reinforce at this position
Meta to −CH<sub>3</sub> (which is simultaneously ortho to −NO<sub>2</sub>) — the more strongly deactivating group's directing effect always overrides the other
An equal statistical mixture across all four open positions, since the two directing effects of different strengths simply cancel out
Exclusively at the position already occupied by −CH<sub>3</sub> or −NO<sub>2</sub>, displacing whichever group is the weaker director
questions.explanation: Of the four open ring positions, two are simultaneously ORTHO to −CH<sub>3</sub> (an o/p-director) AND META to −NO<sub>2</sub> (a meta-director) — both groups favour substitution there. The other two open positions are simultaneously META to −CH<sub>3</sub> and ORTHO to −NO<sub>2</sub>, positions disfavoured by both groups (meta is the less-favoured position for an o/p-director, and ortho is a strongly disfavoured position for a meta-director). Since the directing effects reinforce rather than conflict here, bromination occurs predominantly ortho to the methyl group (equivalently, meta to the nitro group).
questions.hint: For each of the four open ring positions, work out its relationship to BOTH existing substituents, then see which position(s) both groups actually agree on.
distractor_logic: In this specific case the two directing effects REINFORCE rather than conflict (both favour the same pair of ring positions), so there is no need to invoke one substituent overriding the other, and the product is not an even statistical spread across all four positions.

This identifies the position disfavoured by BOTH substituents (meta to the o/p-directing methyl, and ortho to the meta-directing nitro group) as the major site, the opposite of where reinforcing directing effects actually point.

Ipso attack (displacing an existing substituent) is not the typical pathway for simple electrophilic bromination under these conditions; the electrophile instead adds at one of the available (unsubstituted) ring positions, as the correct option describes.

questions.topic: Aromatic Hydrocarbons: Directive Influence of Substituents
questions.question: tert-Butylbenzene undergoes nitration to give predominantly the PARA product, with only a small amount of ortho product, whereas toluene gives substantial amounts of BOTH ortho and para products. Both −CH<sub>3</sub> and −C(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub> are electronically similar (o/p-directing, activating, by hyperconjugation/induction). What explains the shift away from ortho specifically for the bulkier group?
options: The tert-butyl group is actually meta-directing, unlike the methyl group, which explains the reduced ortho product
tert-Butylbenzene does not undergo electrophilic substitution at all under standard nitration conditions
The ortho product is electronically forbidden for any substituent larger than methyl, regardless of sterics
Steric hindrance: the bulky tert-butyl group physically crowds the adjacent (ortho) position, disfavouring electrophilic attack there even though it remains electronically activated
questions.explanation: Both groups activate the ring similarly and remain o/p-directors electronically. However, the much bulkier tert-butyl group creates significant steric hindrance (steric strain in the transition state and product) at the immediately adjacent ortho position, discouraging the incoming electrophile from attacking there, while the more distant para position remains sterically unhindered. This shifts the o/p product ratio heavily toward para for tert-butylbenzene, purely as a steric (not electronic) effect layered on top of the same underlying electronic directing behaviour.
questions.hint: The electronic character (activating, o/p-directing) is stated to be the same for both groups; look instead for a purely spatial/steric reason specific to the bulkier substituent.
distractor_logic: This contradicts the question's own premise, which states both groups are similarly o/p-directing electronically; the shift toward para is a steric effect layered on top of unchanged electronic behaviour, not a change in directing character itself.

There is no absolute electronic prohibition on ortho substitution for bulkier alkyl groups; the ortho position remains electronically favourable, it is simply sterically disfavoured relative to the unhindered para position for a sufficiently bulky substituent.

tert-Butylbenzene undergoes nitration readily (it is, if anything, still an activated ring due to the alkyl group); the question explicitly describes it forming a major, isolable para product, which would be impossible if no reaction occurred.

questions.question: Ethyl bromide is first converted to ethane via the Wurtz reaction (Na/dry ether), and this ethane is then subjected to monochlorination. What is the key limitation shared by BOTH steps when scaling this two-step route to make pure ethyl chloride?
options: Both steps give only ONE possible monosubstituted/coupled product from ethyl bromide/ethane, so purity is not the issue — but the Wurtz step fails for odd-carbon targets, and the chlorination step is hard to stop at mono-substitution
Free-radical chlorination of ethane cannot occur because ethane has no C−H bonds available for abstraction
The Wurtz reaction cannot use ethyl bromide at all, so the entire route is invalid from step one
Both steps proceed with 100% selectivity and no side products, making this the industrially preferred method
questions.explanation: Ethyl bromide + Na/ether gives butane (self-coupling of two ethyl groups), not ethane — the Wurtz reaction only cleanly makes SYMMETRICAL alkanes with an EVEN number of carbons from a single halide, doubling the chain length. Separately, even granting ethane were available, free-radical chlorination of ethane's six equivalent H's proceeds via a chain mechanism that keeps abstracting H from already-formed ethyl chloride, giving a statistical mixture of mono-, di-, tri- substituted products alongside unreacted ethane — controlling for pure monochloroethane requires large excess ethane and low conversion.
questions.hint: First check what the Wurtz reaction on a SINGLE alkyl halide actually produces, then think about why radical chain halogenation is hard to stop at one substitution.
distractor_logic: Ethane has six equivalent primary C−H bonds and DOES undergo free-radical chlorination readily; this option's premise is false.
Ethyl bromide is a perfectly valid substrate for Wurtz coupling; it just gives butane, not ethane, since only one halide is used.

This wrongly claims purity isn't an issue; in fact self-coupling gives butane (not ethane) from ethyl bromide alone, and uncontrolled chlorination gives a polysubstituted mixture — both are real limitations.

questions.question: Propane, made industrially from petroleum, is chlorinated under UV light. Considering the relative number of 1° and 2° hydrogens AND their relative reactivity (2° H reacts about 3.8× faster than 1° H per H, at room temperature for Cl<sub>2</sub>), what is the approximate ratio of 1-chloropropane to 2-chloropropane formed?
options: 6 (1° H count) × 1 : 2 (2° H count) × 3.8 ≈ 6 : 7.6, i.e. roughly comparable amounts of both isomers
Exactly 3:1, matching the raw statistical ratio of 1° to 2° hydrogens alone
Only 1-chloropropane forms, since there are more 1° hydrogens available
Only 2-chloropropane forms, since 2° radicals are always exclusively favoured
questions.explanation: Propane has 6 equivalent 1° H's and 2 equivalent 2° H's. Product ratio = (count × relative rate) for each type: 1°-Cl : 2°-Cl = (6×1) : (2×3.8) = 6 : 7.6 ≈ 44% : 56%. So BOTH products form in comparable, non-negligible amounts — this is exactly why chlorination (low selectivity) gives poor synthetic control compared to bromination (high selectivity, which would favour 2° far more strongly).
questions.hint: Multiply hydrogen COUNT by relative RATE for each type, don't use raw statistics alone.
distractor_logic: This ignores the intrinsic rate difference and uses raw H-count only, missing that 2° radicals form significantly faster per hydrogen.
2-Chloropropane does not form exclusively; chlorination's LOW selectivity (unlike bromination) means the more numerous 1° hydrogens still contribute substantially.
1-Chloropropane does not form exclusively; the reactive but less numerous 2° hydrogens also contribute significantly to product.

questions.question: Sodium propanoate is subjected to decarboxylation by heating with soda lime (NaOH/CaO). The ethane product is then completely combusted. Which sequence of reaction types correctly describes these two steps?
options: Step 1: decarboxylation (loses CO<sub>2</sub>, replacing −COONa with −H); Step 2: complete combustion (oxidation to CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O)
Step 1: Wurtz coupling; Step 2: free-radical halogenation
Step 1: decarboxylation giving propane directly; Step 2: incomplete combustion giving only CO
Step 1: hydrogenation; Step 2: ozonolysis
questions.explanation: CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COONa + NaOH →(CaO, Δ) CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> (ethane) + Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> — the carboxylate carbon is lost as carbonate, and the remaining chain (one carbon shorter than the acid) gains an H in its place; this is decarboxylation. Ethane then undergoes complete combustion in excess O<sub>2</sub>: C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub> + 7/2 O<sub>2</sub> → 2CO<sub>2</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub>O.
questions.hint: Sodium propanoate has 3 carbons; count how many carbons remain in the alkane product to identify what's lost in step 1.
distractor_logic: Decarboxylation of sodium propanoate (3 carbons, losing the carboxyl carbon) gives ETHANE (2 carbons), not propane (3 carbons) — propane would require decarboxylation of a 4-carbon acid.

Combustion is described as 'complete' in the question (implying excess O<sub>2</sub>), which gives CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O, not CO; incomplete combustion (limited O<sub>2</sub>) would be needed for CO.
There is no alkyl halide present, so no Wurtz coupling or radical halogenation is occurring here; this is the soda-lime decarboxylation reaction.

questions.question: 2-Methylbutane (isopentane) is monobrominated under free-radical conditions (Br<sub>2</sub>/hν, high selectivity). Accounting for both the NUMBER of structurally distinct products and their relative amounts, which statement is correct?
options: 4 distinct monobromo constitutional isomers are possible; the major product is 2-bromo-2-methylbutane, since bromination strongly favours the sole 3° hydrogen despite it being just 1 of 12 total H's
3 distinct monobromo products are possible, and the major one comes from a 1° hydrogen since there are the most of those
Only 1 monobromo product is possible, since isopentane has just one type of hydrogen environment
5 distinct monobromo products are possible due to the branched skeleton
questions.explanation: Isopentane, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CH−CH<sub>2</sub>−CH<sub>3</sub>, has FOUR distinct H-environments: the two equivalent methyls on C2 (1°), the C2−H itself (3°, just 1 H), the C3−H<sub>2</sub> (2°), and the terminal C4 methyl (1°, chemically distinct from the C2 methyls). This gives 4 constitutional monobromo products. Despite only 1 of the 12 H's being 3°, bromination's very high 3°:2°:1° selectivity (roughly 1600:82:1 at room temperature) makes 2-bromo-2-methylbutane the dominant product.
questions.hint: Carefully map out all chemically distinct hydrogen environments in the branched skeleton first — don't just count 1°/2°/3° broadly, check if all 1° H's are actually equivalent to each other.
distractor_logic: Isopentane does NOT have just one H-environment; it has four distinct ones (two different types of 1° H, one type of 2°, and one 3°), since the molecule is unsymmetrical.
Overcounts; only 4 chemically distinct H-environments exist in this structure, giving 4 (not 5) monobromo constitutional isomers.

Undercounts the products; there are 4, not 3, distinct monobromo isomers, and the major product is from the single 3° hydrogen (favoured by bromination's high selectivity), not the more numerous 1° hydrogens.

questions.question: Both n-butane and isobutane are chlorinated under free-radical conditions. Which pair correctly matches each starting alkane to the NUMBER of distinct monochloro constitutional isomers it can form?
options: n-Butane → 1 isomer; isobutane → 4 isomers
n-Butane → 4 isomers; isobutane → 1 isomer
Both give exactly 3 isomers each, since both have 4 carbons
n-Butane → 2 isomers (1-chloro and 2-chloro); isobutane → 2 isomers (1-chloro and 2-chloro, i.e. tertiary)
questions.explanation: n-Butane, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, is symmetric, so its two ends are equivalent: substitution at C1 (or equivalently C4) gives 1-chlorobutane, and substitution at C2 (or C3) gives 2-chlorobutane — only 2 distinct products. Isobutane, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>CH, has 9 equivalent 1° H's (giving isobutyl chloride) and 1 unique 3° H (giving tert-butyl chloride) — also 2 distinct products, though in very different proportions (the 3° product favoured despite being 1 of 10 H's).
questions.hint: Use the molecule's own symmetry to identify which hydrogens are chemically equivalent to each other before counting.
distractor_logic: n-Butane's count is right only by coincidence in this option; isobutane does NOT give 3 products — recount its hydrogen environments (9 equivalent 1° + 1 unique 3° = only 2 environments).
Isobutane does give 2 distinct products (1° and 3°), not just 1; its nine 1° hydrogens and one 3° hydrogen are two chemically different environments.
n-Butane's symmetry means only 2 (not 4) distinct products form, since C1≡C4 and C2≡C3 by the molecule's own symmetry.

questions.question: Which of the following laboratory routes correctly produces METHANE specifically (not a general alkane), and why does this method NOT extend to making ethane by the same logic?
options: The Wurtz reaction on CH<sub>3</sub>Br directly gives methane in one step

CH<sub>3</sub>COONa + NaOH →(CaO,Δ) CH<sub>4</sub> + Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> (decarboxylation of a 2-carbon acid salt loses one carbon); extending this to ethane would require decarboxylating a 3-carbon acid salt (sodium propanoate) instead
Hydrolysis of methylmagnesium bromide gives ethane, not methane
Kolbe electrolysis of sodium acetate gives methane as the major product
questions.explanation: Decarboxylation of sodium acetate (CH<sub>3</sub>COONa, 2 carbons) with soda lime removes the carboxyl carbon as carbonate, leaving just CH<sub>4</sub> (1 carbon) — each decarboxylation shortens the chain by exactly one carbon relative to the starting acid salt. To make ethane this way you'd need to start from a 3-carbon acid (sodium propanoate), not repeat the same reagent on methane's own salt (which doesn't exist as a useful precursor here).
questions.hint: Track how many carbons the starting carboxylate has versus how many end up in the alkane product.
distractor_logic: The Wurtz reaction COUPLES two alkyl halide molecules, so CH<sub>3</sub>Br + CH<sub>3</sub>Br would give ethane (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>), not methane — Wurtz cannot give a 1-carbon product from a 1-carbon halide.
Hydrolysis (protonolysis) of CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr gives methane (the Grignard's own carbon chain plus one H from water), not ethane; no C−C coupling occurs in a simple protonolysis.

Kolbe electrolysis of sodium acetate gives ETHANE (via coupling of two CH<sub>3</sub>• radicals released at the anode), not methane; this is analogous to Wurtz in outcome though different in mechanism.

questions.question: Both free-radical halogenation of alkanes and the peroxide-catalysed addition of HBr to alkenes proceed via RADICAL chain mechanisms. What is the key mechanistic difference between them in terms of what the radical intermediate does?
options: In alkane halogenation the radical ABSTRACTS a hydrogen atom from the substrate (substitution); in peroxide-effect HBr addition, the Br• radical ADDS across the C=C double bond (addition), generating the more stable secondary/tertiary carbon radical
There is no real difference; both simply substitute one hydrogen for one halogen atom
Both mechanisms involve the radical adding across a double bond; alkanes just happen to have hidden double bonds
In alkane halogenation the radical adds across a C−H single bond; in the peroxide effect it abstracts a hydrogen from the alkene
questions.explanation: Alkane free-radical halogenation: X• abstracts an H from C−H (propagation step 1), then the resulting carbon radical abstracts X from X<sub>2</sub> (step 2) — net SUBSTITUTION. Peroxide-catalysed HBr addition to an alkene: Br• (generated from peroxide-initiated homolysis) ADDS to the terminal, less-hindered alkene carbon, placing the radical on the MORE substituted carbon (more stable 2°/3° radical) — this is why the product is anti-Markovnikov (Br ends up on the terminal carbon) — then this carbon radical abstracts H from H−Br to propagate. Both are radical CHAIN mechanisms, but one is substitution (no double bond involved) and the other is addition (requires a C=C).
questions.hint: Alkanes have no double bond to add across; think about what's structurally different between the two substrates.
distractor_logic: This reverses the two mechanisms: alkane halogenation involves H-abstraction (not addition across a single bond, which isn't a defined reaction), and the peroxide effect involves Br• ADDING to the alkene (not abstracting H from it, which would just make an allylic radical, not lead to HBr addition).
The two ARE mechanistically distinct: one is substitution on a saturated C−H bond, the other is addition across an unsaturated C=C bond, even though both are initiated by radicals.
Alkanes are fully saturated and have no C=C double bond at all, so radical addition across a 'hidden' double bond is not chemically possible.
mixed_topics: Alkenes: Markovnikov's Rule and Peroxide Effect

questions.question: Propyne (HC≡C−CH<sub>3</sub>) has hydrogens on three different types of carbon: the terminal ≡C−H, and the CH<sub>3</sub> hydrogens. Why is it misleading to predict propyne's reactivity toward Na metal by simply comparing 'terminal vs. non-terminal' C−H bond dissociation energies, the way you would rank radical halogenation selectivity?
options: BDE-based reasoning is equally valid for both reactions since both ultimately break a C−H bond
Propyne's methyl hydrogens are actually more acidic than the terminal alkyne hydrogen

The terminal alkyne C−H reacts with Na via ACID-BASE deprotonation (driven by the high s-character/electronegativity of the sp carbon stabilising the resulting carbanion), an entirely different mechanism from the RADICAL H-abstraction used to explain BDE-based halogenation selectivity
Sodium metal reacts with alkanes and alkynes by exactly the same free-radical mechanism
questions.explanation: Radical halogenation selectivity (1°<2°<3°) is governed by the STABILITY of the carbon RADICAL formed upon homolytic C−H cleavage. But Na metal reacting with a terminal alkyne is an ACID-BASE reaction: Na donates an electron, and the terminal ≡C−H proton is removed as H<sup>+</sup>-equivalent (forming NaC≡CCH<sub>3</sub> + ½H<sub>2</sub>), favoured because the sp carbanion (50% s-character, electrons held close to the nucleus) is unusually stable — a completely different stability criterion (carbanion stability, not radical stability) governs this reactivity, so BDE/radical-based reasoning doesn't directly transfer.
questions.hint: Ask what KIND of intermediate each reaction actually forms — a radical, or a carbanion — before comparing their 'stability'.
distractor_logic: This is exactly the flawed assumption the question asks you to identify as incorrect — the two reactions form different intermediates (radical vs. carbanion) governed by different stability rules.

The methyl (sp<sup>3</sup>) hydrogens are far LESS acidic than the terminal sp C−H; sp carbons hold bonding electrons closer to the nucleus (higher effective electronegativity), making that C−H the most acidic in the molecule.

Na with alkanes (if it reacted at all under normal conditions) would not proceed this way; more importantly, Na with a terminal alkyne is a straightforward acid-base deprotonation, not a radical chain process.

questions.question: 2-Bromobutane is treated with alcoholic KOH (dehydrohalogenation, E1/E2 favouring the Zaitsev product) to give an alkene, which is then treated with HBr in the absence of peroxide. What is the overall relationship between the starting halide and the final product?
options: The final product is a completely different halide, 1-bromobutane, due to peroxide effects even though none was mentioned

Elimination gives predominantly but-2-ene (Zaitsev, more substituted alkene); Markovnikov addition of HBr to but-2-ene regenerates 2-bromobutane (both double-bond carbons are equivalent by symmetry, so only one addition product is possible)
Elimination gives but-1-ene exclusively; Markovnikov addition then gives 1-bromobutane
Both steps are addition reactions, so no new bonds are broken in either step
questions.explanation: E2 elimination from 2-bromobutane can give but-1-ene or but-2-ene; Zaitsev's rule favours the more substituted (more stable) alkene, but-2-ene, as major product. But-2-ene, CH<sub>3</sub>CH=CHCH<sub>3</sub>, is symmetric about its double bond — both carbons bear one CH<sub>3</sub> and one H, so Markovnikov addition of HBr (no peroxide, ionic mechanism, H to the carbon that gives the more stable carbocation) is non-selective by symmetry and gives back 2-bromobutane as the sole addition product, regenerating the original halide.
questions.hint: Check the symmetry of but-2-ene's double bond before deciding whether Markovnikov's rule can even distinguish between the two carbons.
distractor_logic: The first step (alcoholic KOH, E2) is an ELIMINATION (loses HBr, forms a new π bond), and the second step (HBr addition) is an ADDITION; describing both as addition is incorrect.
But-1-ene is the MINOR (anti-Zaitsev) elimination product, not the exclusive one; Zaitsev's rule favours the more substituted but-2-ene as major.

No peroxide is present in this problem (explicitly stated), so ionic Markovnikov addition applies, not the radical anti-Markovnikov pathway; furthermore but-2-ene's symmetry means Markovnikov addition regenerates the SAME halide (2-bromobutane), not 1-bromobutane.

questions.question: 3-Methylbut-1-ene reacts with HCl via the standard Markovnikov ionic mechanism. Considering that the initially formed secondary carbocation can rearrange via a hydride shift to a more stable tertiary carbocation, how many distinct monochloride CONSTITUTIONAL isomers can reasonably form as products?
options: 4 products form due to both hydride and alkyl shifts occurring simultaneously
Only 1 product forms, since Markovnikov's rule always predicts a single unambiguous outcome
2: the 'direct' Markovnikov product (2-chloro-3-methylbutane, from the unrearranged 2° cation) AND the rearranged product (2-chloro-2-methylbutane, from the hydride-shifted 3° cation)
3 products form, including one from a methyl shift that is not chemically favourable here
questions.explanation: H<sup>+</sup> adds to the terminal =CH<sub>2</sub> (Markovnikov), generating a 2° carbocation at C2 of the resulting chain, adjacent to the 3° C3−H. A 1,2-hydride shift from C3 to C2 converts this into a MORE STABLE 3° carbocation at C3. Cl<sup>−</sup> can capture either cation: the unrearranged 2° cation gives 2-chloro-3-methylbutane, while the rearranged 3° cation gives 2-chloro-2-methylbutane (the major product, since the 3° cation is lower energy and forms preferentially once the shift is favourable). Both are commonly reported as the product mixture in this classic rearrangement example.
questions.hint: Identify the initially formed carbocation's position, then check if an adjacent C−H can hydride-shift to give a more stable cation.
distractor_logic: This overcounts; a methyl (alkyl) shift is not favoured here because a simple 1,2-hydride shift already reaches the most stable available (3°) cation, so no further alkyl shift product is expected.

This ignores the well-known carbocation rearrangement in this specific substrate; when a more stable cation is accessible via a 1,2-shift, Markovnikov's rule alone does not fully predict the product mixture.
This overcounts further; only a hydride shift (not an additional alkyl shift) is relevant here, since the hydride shift alone already achieves the thermodynamically most stable 3° cation.

questions.question: Propan-2-ol is dehydrated with hot concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> to give propene, which is then polymerised. What is the correct identity of the two products, in order?
options: Propane (not propene) from dehydration, which cannot be polymerised at all
Propene (CH<sub>2</sub>=CH−CH<sub>3</sub>) from acid-catalysed dehydration (E1, loss of water via a 2° carbocation); polypropylene from addition polymerisation of propene
Propene from dehydrogenation (loss of H<sub>2</sub>, not water); polypropylene from condensation polymerisation
But-1-ene from dehydration; polybutylene from polymerisation
questions.explanation: Propan-2-ol, on protonation of −OH by H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> followed by loss of water, forms a 2° carbocation at C2 which loses a β-H (E1) to give propene, CH<sub>2</sub>=CH−CH<sub>3</sub>. Propene monomers then undergo ADDITION polymerisation (radical or Ziegler-Natta catalysed, opening the π bond repeatedly) to form polypropylene, −[CH<sub>2</sub>−CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)]<sub>n</sub>−.
questions.hint: Propan-2-ol has only 3 carbons; the alkene product must also have 3 carbons, not 4.
distractor_logic: Propan-2-ol has only 3 carbons, so it cannot give a 4-carbon alkene like but-1-ene; the carbon count must be conserved in a simple dehydration.
Dehydration of an alcohol removes water to form an ALKENE (propene), not an alkane (propane); alkenes readily undergo addition polymerisation, so this option's claim is incorrect on both counts.

This is DEHYDRATION (loss of H<sub>2</sub>O, an acid-catalysed elimination), not dehydrogenation (loss of H<sub>2</sub>, a different reaction typically needing a metal catalyst); and alkene polymerisation is ADDITION type (opening π bonds), not condensation (which would need small-molecule byproducts like water).

questions.question: But-1-ene is treated separately with (a) HCl and (b) HBr in the presence of peroxide. Why do these two experiments give DIFFERENT regiochemical outcomes even though HCl and HBr are both hydrogen halides?
options: The H−Br bond is weak enough for peroxide to homolyse it into Br• radicals that propagate a radical chain (anti-Markovnikov), but the much stronger H−Cl bond is not cleaved this way by peroxide, so HCl still adds via the normal ionic Markovnikov pathway regardless of peroxide
HCl and HBr are chemically identical in this respect and both give anti-Markovnikov addition with peroxide present
Peroxide only affects reactions of alkynes, not alkenes, so neither HCl nor HBr addition is affected
HCl gives anti-Markovnikov addition because Cl is more electronegative than Br
questions.explanation: The peroxide (anti-Markovnikov) effect is specific to HBr because the H−Br bond is weak enough to be homolysed by radical initiators (from peroxide decomposition) to generate Br•, which then adds to the LESS hindered terminal carbon of the alkene (placing the radical on the more stable, more substituted carbon), reversing the usual regiochemistry. H−Cl and H−I bonds are respectively too strong or too weak (or the resulting radical chain is thermodynamically unfavourable) for this radical pathway to compete, so they add via the standard ionic (Markovnikov) mechanism regardless of peroxide.
questions.hint: The peroxide effect is a named, HBr-specific exception in NCERT — check whether it extends to HCl.
distractor_logic: This is factually backwards; the peroxide effect specifically does NOT extend to HCl (or HI) — only HBr shows anti-Markovnikov addition with peroxides.

Peroxide effect is a phenomenon specific to ALKENE + HBr addition, not alkynes; alkynes can also show a peroxide effect with HBr but that is a separate case, not the reason HCl behaves differently here.
Electronegativity of the halogen is not the deciding factor; the relevant property is H−X bond strength/homolysis feasibility, which is why HBr (not HCl) shows the anomalous effect.
mixed_topics: Alkenes: Markovnikov's Rule and Peroxide Effect

questions.question: But-2-yne is partially hydrogenated over Lindlar's catalyst to give an alkene, which is then treated with HBr (no peroxide). Which final product forms, and via what stereochemical/mechanistic pathway?
options: But-2-yne is fully reduced to butane directly by Lindlar's catalyst, so no alkene intermediate exists
cis-But-2-ene forms, but HBr cannot add to it at all due to its geometry

cis-But-2-ene forms first (syn addition of H<sub>2</sub> over Lindlar's catalyst); Markovnikov addition of HBr then gives 2-bromobutane (both alkene carbons equivalent by symmetry, so stereochemistry of the alkene doesn't affect which constitutional isomer forms)
trans-But-2-ene forms first; anti-Markovnikov addition of HBr then gives 1-bromobutane
questions.explanation: Lindlar's catalyst (Pd poisoned with Pb/quinoline) selectively delivers H<sub>2</sub> in a SYN fashion to alkynes, stopping at the alkene stage and giving the CIS alkene specifically — here, cis-but-2-ene. Since but-2-ene is symmetric about its double bond (CH<sub>3</sub> and H on each carbon regardless of cis/trans), Markovnikov (ionic, no peroxide) addition of HBr gives a single constitutional product, 2-bromobutane, irrespective of whether the starting alkene was cis or trans.
questions.hint: Lindlar's catalyst is specifically known for giving ONE stereochemical outcome (not the other) at the alkene stage — and check if that stereochemistry even matters for the next step's product identity.
distractor_logic: cis-But-2-ene is a perfectly normal alkene and readily undergoes Markovnikov addition with HBr like any other alkene; its cis geometry does not block the reaction.
Lindlar's catalyst gives the CIS alkene (syn addition), not trans; trans-but-2-ene would instead form from Na/liquid NH<sub>3</sub> reduction (anti addition), a different named method.

Lindlar's catalyst is specifically chosen to STOP at the alkene stage (poisoned to prevent over-reduction to the alkane); full reduction to butane would require an unpoisoned Pd/Pt/Ni catalyst instead.

questions.question: Both the addition of Br<sub>2</sub> to an alkene and the bromination of benzene (Br<sub>2</sub>/FeBr<sub>3</sub>) are described as 'electrophilic' reactions. What is the essential mechanistic difference in how the aromatic ring reaction proceeds compared to the alkene reaction?
options: Alkene + Br<sub>2</sub> is an ADDITION (both new C−Br bonds form, saturating the double bond, no catalyst strictly required for simple alkenes); benzene + Br<sub>2</sub> is a SUBSTITUTION (one ring H is replaced by Br, the aromatic sextet is regenerated after the arenium-ion intermediate loses a proton, and a Lewis acid catalyst like FeBr<sub>3</sub> is needed to generate a strong enough electrophile)
Both reactions are identical additions that simply happen to occur on different substrates
Alkenes require FeBr<sub>3</sub> catalyst for bromination just as benzene does
Benzene undergoes addition of Br<sub>2</sub> just like an alkene, permanently destroying its aromaticity
questions.explanation: A simple alkene reacts with Br<sub>2</sub> via direct electrophilic ADDITION (bromonium ion intermediate, then Br<sup>−</sup> opens it, giving a vicinal dibromide) — no catalyst is needed since alkene π electrons are reactive enough alone. Benzene's aromatic ring, however, is markedly LESS reactive toward simple Br<sub>2</sub> (stabilised by delocalisation/aromaticity), so a Lewis acid catalyst (FeBr<sub>3</sub>) is required to polarise Br<sub>2</sub> into a stronger electrophile; and critically, after the electrophile adds to give the resonance-stabilised arenium (Wheland) intermediate, the ring loses H<sup>+</sup> to RESTORE aromaticity rather than trapping a second Br<sup>−</sup> — giving net substitution, not addition.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to the ring's aromaticity/stability at the end of each reaction — is it retained or destroyed?
distractor_logic: Simple alkenes react with Br<sub>2</sub> readily without any Lewis acid catalyst; FeBr<sub>3</sub> is specifically needed for benzene's comparatively unreactive aromatic system, not for ordinary alkenes.

The two reactions are mechanistically distinct in outcome (addition vs. substitution) precisely because of the thermodynamic drive to restore aromaticity in the benzene case, which has no analogue in a simple alkene.

If benzene simply added Br<sub>2</sub> like an alkene, it would lose its aromatic stabilisation, which is thermodynamically unfavourable; the observed reaction is substitution, which preserves aromaticity.

questions.question: 2-Bromobutane undergoes E2 elimination with alcoholic KOH via an ANTI-PERIPLANAR transition state. For the major (Zaitsev) product but-2-ene, this stereospecific mechanism has a consequence for which geometric isomer predominates from a given starting stereoisomer. What does this mean in practice for a student analysing the product?
options: The product is always exclusively cis-but-2-ene regardless of the starting halide's configuration, due to anti-periplanar geometry
E2 elimination never has any stereochemical consequence; only E1 does

The anti-periplanar requirement means a SPECIFIC diastereomer of the starting halide leads preferentially to a SPECIFIC alkene geometry (cis or trans), so E2 is stereospecific — not merely a matter of thermodynamic (Zaitsev) preference for which REGIOCHEMICAL alkene forms
Anti-periplanar geometry is only relevant to addition reactions, not eliminations
questions.explanation: Zaitsev's rule addresses REGIOCHEMISTRY (which alkene, but-1-ene vs. but-2-ene, is thermodynamically favoured as major product), while the anti-periplanar requirement of E2 addresses STEREOCHEMISTRY (which specific geometric isomer, cis or trans, results from a given spatial arrangement of leaving group and β-H in the starting material) — these are two separate, complementary aspects of the same elimination, and E2 is genuinely stereospecific (a defined starting configuration gives a defined, predictable alkene geometry), unlike E1 which proceeds through a planar carbocation and is not stereospecific.
questions.hint: Distinguish between 'which alkene regiochemistry forms' (Zaitsev) and 'which alkene stereochemistry forms' (anti-periplanar E2) — these are different questions.
distractor_logic: This is backwards; E2 IS distinctly stereospecific due to its concerted, anti-periplanar transition state, while E1 (via a planar carbocation intermediate) is generally NOT stereospecific.

Anti-periplanar geometry is a defining mechanistic feature of E2 ELIMINATIONS specifically (concerted removal of H and leaving group from opposite faces); it is not a general requirement for additions.

The specific geometric outcome (cis or trans) depends on the STARTING halide's spatial arrangement, not a fixed universal answer; without knowing the specific diastereomer's 3D structure, you cannot assume cis is always the result.

questions.question: Propene and propyne are both treated with dilute H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> in the presence of HgSO<sub>4</sub> (used specifically to hydrate the alkyne). Why is a mercury(II) catalyst specifically needed for the alkyne's hydration but not typically emphasised for the alkene's acid-catalysed hydration?
options: Alkenes are less reactive than alkynes toward electrophiles, which is why alkenes need the extra Hg<sup>2+</sup> catalyst instead
Hg<sup>2+</sup> is required for both reactions equally and this is just a coincidental difference in how textbooks present them
Alkynes cannot be hydrated by any method, making the premise of the question false

Alkyne π bonds are less nucleophilic/more electron-poor toward simple protonation than alkene π bonds (due to the sp carbons' higher electronegativity/s-character), so Hg<sup>2+</sup> is used to activate the triple bond as a better electrophile-acceptor, forming a mercurinium-like intermediate before water attacks; simple alkenes are nucleophilic enough to be directly protonated by H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> without needing this activation
questions.explanation: Alkyne π electrons are held more tightly by the higher-s-character (sp) carbons, making a simple alkyne somewhat less prone to direct protonation than an alkene under the same mild acidic conditions used for alkene hydration; Hg<sup>2+</sup> coordinates to the triple bond, polarising it and helping stabilise the developing positive charge (forming a bridged mercurinium ion) so that water can attack efficiently, ultimately tautomerising (via an enol) to a ketone (Markovnikov, giving acetone from propyne). A simple terminal alkene like propene undergoes direct Markovnikov acid-catalysed hydration to an alcohol (isopropanol) without needing this extra activation.
questions.hint: Compare how tightly each type of π bond's electrons are held, based on the hybridisation of the carbons involved.
distractor_logic: This reverses the actual reactivity comparison; alkenes are generally MORE reactive toward simple protonation than alkynes (due to more available, less tightly held π electrons), which is why alkenes don't need the extra Hg<sup>2+</sup> activation that alkynes do.
Hg<sup>2+</sup> catalysis (oxymercuration-type activation) is specifically associated with alkyne hydration in the NCERT syllabus, not a routine requirement for simple alkene hydration.
Alkynes CAN be hydrated (this is a standard NCERT reaction, giving carbonyl compounds via Markovnikov addition and enol-keto tautomerism); the premise that they cannot is false.

questions.question: Kolbe's electrolysis of sodium hex-3-enoate (a salt with the double bond already present, far from the carboxyl group) is attempted to make an alkene by radical coupling. Why is this a poor experimental design compared to using a saturated acid salt like sodium butanoate to reach a target alkene?
options: This is in fact the standard, most efficient way to synthesise alkenes and is preferred over dehydration/dehydrohalogenation methods

Kolbe electrolysis couples two radicals derived from the ACID's own alkyl portion (losing CO<sub>2</sub> from each), so starting from an unsaturated acid just carries the existing double bond through unchanged into a longer, still-unsaturated coupled product, rather than being a sensible way to INTRODUCE a new double bond — the standard synthetic use of Kolbe is coupling saturated acids to build simple symmetric alkanes, not alkenes
The electrolysis converts the alkene into an alkyne under these conditions
Kolbe electrolysis cannot be performed on any carboxylate salt containing a double bond, so the reaction simply fails
questions.explanation: Kolbe electrolysis (2 RCOO<sup>−</sup> → R−R + 2CO<sub>2</sub> + 2e<sup>−</sup>, via radical coupling at the anode) is a standard method for making simple, symmetric ALKANES from saturated carboxylate salts. If the starting acid already contains a C=C double bond elsewhere in the chain, that double bond is simply carried through into the coupled product unchanged (now in a longer, doubled chain) — the reaction doesn't create or move the double bond, so it's not a sensible or standard route specifically for SYNTHESISING new alkenes; dehydration of alcohols or dehydrohalogenation of alkyl halides are the standard alkene-forming methods instead.
questions.hint: Ask what Kolbe electrolysis is normally used to make, and whether starting with an already-unsaturated acid actually helps create anything new.
distractor_logic: There is no mechanistic pathway by which Kolbe electrolysis converts an existing alkene into an alkyne; the double bond, if present in the starting acid, is simply carried through unchanged.
Kolbe electrolysis is the standard method for making simple ALKANES via radical coupling, not a preferred general route to alkenes; alkenes are normally made via elimination reactions instead.
Kolbe electrolysis does not have a specific restriction against unsaturated acid salts; the reaction can proceed, it's just not a useful or standard way to deliberately introduce unsaturation.

questions.question: Pent-1-yne is first deprotonated with NaNH<sub>2</sub> and then alkylated with CH<sub>3</sub>Br to give hex-2-yne, which is then fully hydrogenated with excess H<sub>2</sub>/Ni. What overall transformation, in terms of both chain length change and hybridisation change, has occurred across all three steps?
options: Chain length stays the same throughout, and only a stereochemical change occurs
Complete hydrogenation with Ni gives an alkene, not an alkane, as the final product
The deprotonation step alone adds a carbon, and hydrogenation removes one, giving no net change

Chain lengthens by one carbon (C5→C6, via the alkylation step) and the internal carbons' hybridisation changes from sp (triple bond) to sp<sup>3</sup> (fully saturated alkane, hexane) upon complete hydrogenation
questions.explanation: Step 1: NaNH<sub>2</sub> deprotonates the acidic terminal ≡C−H of pent-1-yne (sp carbanion, stabilised by high s-character) to give sodium pent-1-ynide, releasing NH<sub>3</sub>. Step 2: this acetylide anion attacks CH<sub>3</sub>Br in an S<sub>N</sub>2 alkylation, forming a new C−C bond and extending the chain by one carbon to hex-2-yne (6 carbons, internal triple bond). Step 3: excess H<sub>2</sub>/Ni fully saturates the triple bond (sp) all the way to a single bond (sp<sup>3</sup>), giving n-hexane. Net: +1 carbon, and hybridisation of C2/C3 changes sp → sp<sup>3</sup>.
questions.hint: Track the carbon count through the alkylation step specifically, and separately track what 'excess H<sub>2</sub>/Ni' does to a triple bond.
distractor_logic: The alkylation step (acetylide + CH<sub>3</sub>Br) explicitly forms a new C−C bond, adding a carbon and changing the chain length; this is not merely a stereochemical change.

The deprotonation step (NaNH<sub>2</sub>) removes only a proton (H<sup>+</sup>), not a carbon, from the molecule; only the subsequent alkylation with CH<sub>3</sub>Br adds a carbon, and hydrogenation adds only hydrogens, not removing any carbon.

Excess H<sub>2</sub> over an active hydrogenation catalyst like Ni does NOT stop at the alkene stage (that selective stopping requires Lindlar's poisoned catalyst); with plain Ni and excess H<sub>2</sub>, the triple bond is fully reduced all the way to the alkane.

questions.question: But-1-yne is treated with excess HBr (2 equivalents, no peroxide, standard ionic Markovnikov addition both times). What is the final GEM-dihalide product, and why does the second HBr addition follow the same regiochemical logic as the first?
options: 1,2-Dibromobutane; both additions occur anti-Markovnikov since alkynes always react opposite to alkenes
The reaction stops after the first addition and cannot add a second HBr under any conditions

2,2-Dibromobutane; the first HBr adds Markovnikov (H to terminal C1, Br to C2, forming the more stable 2° vinyl-derived cation pathway), and the second HBr addition to the resulting bromoalkene (2-bromobut-1-ene) again places the incoming H on the less-substituted terminal carbon and Br on C2 (now stabilised further by the adjacent Br's lone pair via resonance/inductive effects), giving both Br's on the same carbon
1,1-Dibromobutane forms, with both bromines on the terminal carbon
questions.explanation: First HBr addition to but-1-yne (HC≡C−CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>) follows Markovnikov's rule: H adds to the terminal (less substituted) carbon, Br to C2, giving 2-bromobut-1-ene, CH<sub>2</sub>=C(Br)−CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>. This intermediate is itself an alkene; a second Markovnikov HBr addition again places H on the terminal CH<sub>2</sub>= carbon and Br on C2 (which is additionally favoured because a partial positive charge at C2 is stabilised by the adjacent, already-present bromine's lone-pair donation), giving the GEM-dihalide 2,2-dibromobutane, with both Br's on C2.
questions.hint: Apply Markovnikov's rule twice in succession: once to the alkyne (giving a bromoalkene), then again to that resulting alkene.
distractor_logic: Alkynes readily add a SECOND equivalent of HX under excess reagent, proceeding through the intermediate bromoalkene to a gem-dihalide; the reaction does not stop after one addition.
Alkynes do NOT universally react opposite (anti-Markovnikov) to alkenes; without peroxide, ordinary ionic Markovnikov addition applies to alkynes just as it does to alkenes.
Both bromines end up on C2 (giving a 2,2-, not 1,1-, dihalide), since the terminal carbon (C1) is where hydrogen is added in BOTH Markovnikov additions, not bromine.
mixed_topics: Alkenes: Markovnikov's Rule and Peroxide Effect

questions.question: Ethyne's terminal C−H bond dissociation energy is actually HIGHER than a typical alkane's 1° C−H BDE, yet ethyne's terminal hydrogen is far MORE acidic (readily removed by NaNH<sub>2</sub>) than any alkane hydrogen. How do you reconcile these two seemingly contradictory facts?
options: BDE and acidity always correlate directly, so a high-BDE bond must always be a weak acid
This is a contradiction and one of the two premises must be experimentally wrong
Acidity in organic chemistry has nothing to do with the C−H bond at all, only with oxygen-containing groups

BDE measures the energy to homolytically cleave a bond into two RADICALS (relevant to radical halogenation selectivity), while acidity measures the ease of heterolytic cleavage into H<sup>+</sup> and a CARBANION (relevant to base-mediated deprotonation) — these are different bond-breaking processes governed by different stabilities (radical stability vs. carbanion stability), so a bond can simultaneously have a high BDE and be comparatively acidic
questions.explanation: BDE (radical stability) and acidity (carbanion stability) are answers to two DIFFERENT questions about the same bond: 'how easily does it split into two radicals' vs. 'how easily does it split into H<sup>+</sup> and a carbanion'. The sp carbon in ethyne holds its carbanion lone pair in an orbital with high s-character (closer to the nucleus, lower energy, more stable carbanion) — explaining the high acidity — while the same bond's radical-cleavage energy (BDE) depends on different factors (radical stabilisation, which sp carbons do NOT provide well, unlike 3° alkyl radicals). There is no contradiction; they're simply uncorrelated properties in general.
questions.hint: Ask precisely what species results from EACH type of bond-breaking (BDE vs. acidity) — are they the same kind of intermediate?
distractor_logic: BDE and pKa (acidity) do NOT always correlate; this exact ethyne example is a classic illustration of how they can diverge, since they reflect stability of different intermediates (radical vs. carbanion).

Both facts (high terminal-alkyne BDE and high terminal-alkyne acidity) are independently well-established; there's no need to discard either, since they answer different questions about bond cleavage.

C−H acidity is a real, well-studied phenomenon (terminal alkynes are a textbook example, with pKa around 25, much more acidic than alkane C−H at pKa ≈ 50); acidity is not restricted to O−H-type bonds.

questions.question: Pent-2-yne is treated with excess KMnO<sub>4</sub> (hot, oxidative cleavage conditions, analogous to how KMnO<sub>4</sub> cleaves alkenes but going further for alkynes) which cleaves the triple bond completely to two carboxylic acid fragments. What are the two fragments, and how does this compare to ozonolysis of the corresponding alkene (pent-2-ene) at the same carbon position?
options: Pent-2-yne (CH<sub>3</sub>−C≡C−CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>) cleaves to CH<sub>3</sub>COOH (ethanoic acid) and CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOH (propanoic acid); this is analogous to how ozonolysis of pent-2-ene at the SAME C2≡C3 (or C2=C3) position would give a ketone/aldehyde pair (CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>3</sub> fragment logic doesn't directly apply here since the carbon skeleton differs) — but the key parallel is that BOTH reactions cleave the multiply-bonded carbons into two separate oxidised fragments, reflecting where the unsaturation was located
The triple bond cannot be cleaved by KMnO<sub>4</sub> under any conditions, unlike a double bond
Both fragments must be identical, since triple bonds always cleave symmetrically
The reaction gives a single carboxylic acid with all 5 carbons intact, since oxidative cleavage doesn't break C−C bonds
questions.explanation: Hot, vigorous (oxidative) KMnO<sub>4</sub> cleaves an internal alkyne fully across the C≡C bond, oxidising each resulting fragment all the way to a carboxylic acid: pent-2-yne, CH<sub>3</sub>−C≡C−CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, cleaves between C2 and C3 to give CH<sub>3</sub>COOH (from the C1−C2 fragment) and CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>COOH (from the C3−C4−C5 fragment). The broader parallel with ozonolysis (which cleaves C=C in alkenes) is that both reaction types locate the position of unsaturation in an unknown structure by identifying which two fragments result — a core structure-elucidation strategy used for both alkenes (ozonolysis) and, analogously, alkynes (oxidative cleavage).
questions.hint: Break the molecule at the triple bond position (between C2 and C3) and figure out what each resulting piece oxidises to.
distractor_logic: The two fragments need not be identical; cleavage occurs at the position of the triple bond, and the resulting fragment identities simply depend on which carbons are on each side — here, unequal fragments (2 carbons and 3 carbons) result since the triple bond is not centrally symmetric.
Oxidative cleavage of a multiple bond by hot KMnO<sub>4</sub> specifically DOES break the carbon skeleton at that bond, giving two separate smaller acid fragments, not one intact 5-carbon product.
Internal alkynes ARE cleaved by hot, concentrated KMnO<sub>4</sub> (an oxidative cleavage reaction, analogous in spirit to ozonolysis of alkenes); the premise that cleavage cannot occur is incorrect.

questions.question: A student claims: 'Since ethyne (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>2</sub>) has the general formula C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n−2</sub>, and cyclohexene (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>10</sub>) also fits C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n−2</sub> (n=6), both compounds must belong to the same functional class.' What is wrong with this reasoning?
options: This reasoning is actually completely correct, and all C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n−2</sub> compounds are alkynes
Ethyne and cyclohexene cannot both have degree of unsaturation 2; one of the formulas given must be wrong

Molecular formula alone (degree of unsaturation) does NOT uniquely determine functional class; C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n−2</sub> is satisfied by BOTH open-chain alkynes/dienes (2 degrees of unsaturation from multiple bonds) AND by cycloalkenes (2 degrees, one from the ring and one from the double bond) — you must know the actual connectivity, not just the formula, to classify a compound
General formulas apply only to acyclic compounds, so cyclohexene cannot be discussed using DoU at all
questions.explanation: Degree of unsaturation (DoU) for C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n−2</sub> is (2n+2−(2n−2))/2 = 2. But DoU only tells you the COUNT of rings+π-bonds, not their type or arrangement: 2 degrees could mean one triple bond (alkyne), two double bonds (diene), or one ring plus one double bond (cycloalkene) — all consistent with the same molecular formula pattern but structurally and chemically very different classes. Ethyne (open-chain, one triple bond) and cyclohexene (one ring, one double bond) both have DoU=2 by pure coincidence of formula, but are entirely different functional classes.
questions.hint: Calculate the degree of unsaturation for both, and then ask whether a single DoU value can correspond to more than one type of structural feature.
distractor_logic: General (degree-of-unsaturation-based) formulas apply perfectly well to cyclic compounds too, since a ring itself contributes one degree of unsaturation, just like a π bond does; DoU reasoning is not restricted to acyclic molecules.

Both formulas ARE correct (ethyne C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>2</sub> and cyclohexene C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>10</sub> both genuinely have DoU=2); the student's error is assuming matching DoU implies matching functional class, not an arithmetic error in the formulas themselves.
Not all C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n−2</sub> compounds are alkynes; this formula is shared by alkynes, dienes, and cycloalkenes alike, which is exactly the point of the question.

questions.question: But-2-yne is treated with Na/liquid NH<sub>3</sub> (dissolving-metal reduction) to give trans-but-2-ene. This trans alkene is then subjected to catalytic hydrogenation (H<sub>2</sub>/Ni, excess). What happens to the STEREOCHEMICAL information (cis/trans) established in the first step, after the second step?
options: The trans stereochemistry is fully preserved in the butane product as a permanent structural feature
Hydrogenation of an alkene always converts trans to cis, never fully saturating it

The trans (E) stereochemistry is completely destroyed/erased; catalytic hydrogenation saturates the double bond entirely, converting sp<sup>2</sup> carbons to sp<sup>3</sup>, so the resulting butane has no double bond left and therefore no cis/trans descriptor applies at all
Butane itself can exist as cis and trans isomers depending on which alkene it came from
questions.explanation: Na/NH<sub>3</sub> reduction of an internal alkyne is a stereospecific ANTI addition of H<sub>2</sub> equivalents, giving specifically the TRANS alkene (unlike Lindlar's syn addition, which gives cis). However, once that trans-but-2-ene is FULLY hydrogenated (excess H<sub>2</sub>/Ni saturates the remaining C=C completely), both alkene carbons become sp<sup>3</sup> and identical in connectivity to each other's substituents on a straight 4-carbon chain — butane has no stereocentre or double bond, so the 'cis/trans' descriptor, which only has meaning for a restricted-rotation C=C (or a ring), simply ceases to apply; the stereochemical information is lost upon full saturation.
questions.hint: Cis/trans (geometric) isomerism specifically requires restricted rotation around a double bond (or a ring) — ask whether that restriction still exists after complete hydrogenation.
distractor_logic: Butane (an acyclic, fully saturated alkane with free rotation about every C−C bond) has no possible cis/trans isomers; the geometric distinction is a property specific to restricted-rotation systems like alkenes or rings, not simple alkanes.

Hydrogenation with excess H<sub>2</sub> over an active catalyst does not stop partway or invert geometry; it proceeds to full saturation, removing the double bond (and any associated cis/trans label) entirely.

Geometric isomerism requires a C=C double bond (or ring) to restrict rotation; once that double bond is fully hydrogenated to a single bond, free rotation is restored and the cis/trans distinction becomes meaningless — it is not preserved.
