questions.question: Comparing the C−H bond angle and hybridisation across ethane (sp<sup>3</sup>), ethene (sp<sup>2</sup>), and ethyne (sp), which trend correctly links increasing s-character to bond properties, and what is its chemical consequence for acidity?
options: s-Character decreases from ethane to ethyne, making ethyne's C−H the least acidic of the three
sp<sup>2</sup> carbons (ethene) have the highest s-character and are therefore the most acidic of the three
Bond angle and acidity are unrelated to hybridisation entirely; acidity depends only on the number of hydrogens present

s-Character increases sp<sup>3</sup>(25%) < sp<sup>2</sup>(33%) < sp(50%); higher s-character pulls bonding/lone-pair electron density CLOSER to the more electronegative-behaving carbon nucleus, so the sp C−H bond in ethyne is both the shortest/strongest C−H bond AND the most acidic, since the resulting carbanion's lone pair is best stabilised in a high-s-character orbital
questions.explanation: Hybridisation s-character: sp<sup>3</sup> = 25% s, sp<sup>2</sup> = 33% s, sp = 50% s. Higher s-character means the orbital is held closer to (lower in energy relative to) the nucleus, increasing the effective electronegativity of that carbon toward its substituents. This has two consequences: (1) the C−H bond becomes shorter and stronger (higher BDE) going sp<sup>3</sup>→sp<sup>2</sup>→sp, and (2) a carbanion formed at that carbon is progressively more stabilised (lone pair held closer to nucleus), so acidity INCREASES in the same order: ethane < ethene < ethyne, with ethyne's terminal C−H being distinctly acidic enough for NaNH<sub>2</sub> to deprotonate it cleanly.
questions.hint: Recall the exact s-character percentages for sp<sup>3</sup>, sp<sup>2</sup>, and sp, and think about what 'higher s-character' does to how tightly electrons are held.
distractor_logic: This reverses the correct trend; s-character INCREASES (not decreases) from sp<sup>3</sup> to sp, and acidity increases correspondingly, making ethyne's terminal H the MOST (not least) acidic of the three.
sp<sup>2</sup> (ethene, 33% s-character) sits between sp<sup>3</sup> and sp; sp (ethyne, 50% s-character) has the HIGHEST s-character of the three and is correspondingly the most acidic, not ethene.

Hybridisation-dependent electronegativity is precisely WHY acidity varies systematically among these three hydrocarbons despite all having only C−H bonds; acidity is not simply about hydrogen count (ethane has more H's than ethyne yet is far less acidic).

questions.question: Ethyne is treated with excess Cl<sub>2</sub> gas (no catalyst, straightforward electrophilic addition, not radical conditions) to give a fully saturated tetrachloro product. Separately, ethane is treated with excess Cl<sub>2</sub> under UV light (radical substitution). Compare the maximum number of chlorine atoms that can be incorporated per molecule of starting hydrocarbon in each case, and why.
options: Both reactions are capped at exactly 2 chlorine atoms maximum, since both starting materials have only 2 carbons

Ethyne + excess Cl<sub>2</sub> (addition) → 1,1,2,2-tetrachloroethane (4 Cl atoms, two additions across the triple bond, no hydrogens lost); ethane + excess Cl<sub>2</sub> (substitution) can in principle go all the way to hexachloroethane (6 Cl atoms, replacing all 6 H's one at a time), since substitution just keeps replacing remaining H's rather than being capped by a fixed number of π bonds
Ethane's reaction with Cl<sub>2</sub> is an addition reaction, just like ethyne's, so both follow the same addition-based atom-economy logic
Ethyne can incorporate at most 2 Cl atoms since it only has 2 hydrogens to begin with
questions.explanation: Ethyne's addition chemistry is capped by its TWO π bonds: each Cl<sub>2</sub> adds across one π bond without removing any atoms, so 2 equivalents of Cl<sub>2</sub> (4 Cl atoms total) fully saturate it to 1,1,2,2-tetrachloroethane, Cl<sub>2</sub>CH−CHCl<sub>2</sub> — no more addition is possible once fully saturated. Ethane's chemistry is SUBSTITUTION: each Cl<sub>2</sub> molecule replaces one H with one Cl (releasing HCl), and since ethane starts with 6 H's, substitution can in principle proceed stepwise all the way to hexachloroethane, C<sub>2</sub>Cl<sub>6</sub>, with excess Cl<sub>2</sub> and UV light — a fundamentally different atom-count ceiling because substitution isn't limited by a fixed number of π bonds the way addition is.
questions.hint: Addition is capped by the number of π bonds available; substitution is capped by the number of hydrogens available. Count each separately for the two molecules.
distractor_logic: Both reactions are NOT capped at the same number; ethyne's addition is limited by its 2 π bonds (max 4 Cl), while ethane's substitution is limited by its 6 hydrogens (max 6 Cl) — two different mechanisms with two different ceilings.

Ethyne has only 2 HYDROGENS but its addition chemistry doesn't remove or replace those hydrogens at all; Cl<sub>2</sub> adds ACROSS the π bonds without touching the existing C−H bonds, so the H-count is irrelevant to the addition ceiling here.

Ethane, being fully saturated, has NO π bond to add across; its reaction with Cl<sub>2</sub> under UV light is necessarily a substitution (radical chain, H replaced by Cl), not an addition — the two hydrocarbons undergo fundamentally different reaction types with Cl<sub>2</sub>.

questions.question: Benzene is first prepared by cyclic trimerisation of ethyne (3 HC≡CH, passed through a red-hot iron/copper tube), and this benzene is then nitrated (conc. HNO<sub>3</sub>/conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>). What is the role of conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> in the second step, mechanistically?
options: H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> is the electrophile itself that directly attacks the ring
H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> acts purely as a drying/dehydrating agent and plays no direct mechanistic role in electrophile generation

Conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> protonates HNO<sub>3</sub>, helping it lose water to generate the actual electrophile, the nitronium ion NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>, which then attacks the electron-rich aromatic ring
H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> reduces HNO<sub>3</sub> to a less reactive species before the reaction proceeds
questions.explanation: Benzene's cyclic trimerisation from ethyne (via a red-hot tube, a classic NCERT-cited preparation) sets up the substrate; in nitration, conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> protonates HNO<sub>3</sub> at its −OH oxygen, which then leaves as water, generating the true electrophile NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> (nitronium ion): HNO<sub>3</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> → NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> + H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> + 2HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup>. This strong electrophile is then attacked by the ring's π electrons, forming the resonance-stabilised arenium ion, which loses H<sup>+</sup> to regenerate aromaticity as nitrobenzene.
questions.hint: Ask what species is actually attacking the ring in nitration — is it HNO<sub>3</sub> itself, or something generated from it?
distractor_logic: H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> does not reduce HNO<sub>3</sub>; it protonates it to facilitate loss of water and formation of the electrophilic nitronium ion — no change in nitrogen oxidation state occurs in this step.

The ring's electrophile is NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> (generated FROM HNO<sub>3</sub> with H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>'s help), not H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> itself, which instead serves as the proton source/acid catalyst.
H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>'s role goes beyond simple drying; it actively protonates HNO<sub>3</sub> to help generate the reactive nitronium electrophile, which is essential to the mechanism.

questions.question: Toluene undergoes Friedel-Crafts alkylation with CH<sub>3</sub>Cl/anhydrous AlCl<sub>3</sub>. Combining the fact that −CH<sub>3</sub> is an activating, ortho/para-directing group with the fact that Friedel-Crafts reactions are especially prone to POLY-alkylation (unlike nitration or halogenation, which self-limit), what practical problem is most likely to occur?
options: The reaction will exclusively give meta-xylene as the sole clean product with no over-alkylation

The initial mono-methylation product (a xylene isomer, itself even MORE activated toward further electrophilic attack than toluene was) readily undergoes further alkylation, giving a mixture of di- and poly-methylated benzenes rather than stopping cleanly at one substitution
No further reaction can occur once one methyl group is installed, since the ring becomes deactivated
AlCl<sub>3</sub> prevents any alkylation from occurring on an already-substituted ring
questions.explanation: −CH<sub>3</sub> is activating (o/p-directing) via hyperconjugation/inductive electron donation. Once toluene is mono-methylated to a xylene (dimethylbenzene), the ring now carries TWO activating alkyl groups, making it even MORE reactive toward further Friedel-Crafts alkylation than toluene itself was — this is the classic reason Friedel-Crafts alkylations are notoriously hard to stop at monosubstitution (unlike nitration/sulfonation, which are self-limiting because the incoming NO<sub>2</sub>/SO<sub>3</sub>H groups are deactivating), typically requiring a large excess of the arene substrate to favour mono-substitution statistically.
questions.hint: Ask whether the FIRST alkyl group installed makes the ring more or less reactive toward a second alkylation, compared to nitration where the first group installed is deactivating.
distractor_logic: Both ortho- and para-methylation are directed by the existing methyl group, and a mixture of isomers (not exclusively meta, which the methyl group actually disfavours) forms even before considering the poly-alkylation problem.

AlCl<sub>3</sub> is the Lewis acid catalyst that ENABLES Friedel-Crafts alkylation; it does not selectively block reaction on a substituted ring, and in fact the substituted (activated) ring reacts even more readily.

This is backwards; alkyl groups are ACTIVATING, so a mono-methylated ring is MORE reactive toward further electrophilic attack, not deactivated — the opposite of what happens with nitration's deactivating −NO<sub>2</sub> group.

HNO<sub>3</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>). −Cl is unusual: it is O,P-DIRECTING (like alkyl groups) but overall DEACTIVATING (unlike alkyl groups). Which explanation correctly accounts for BOTH observations simultaneously?
options: Cl is o/p-directing purely due to its size (steric bulk), unrelated to any electronic effect
Cl withdraws electron density by resonance and donates by induction, the reverse of the correct explanation

Cl's lone pair can be donated into the ring by RESONANCE at the ortho/para positions (stabilising the arenium intermediate there, hence o/p-directing), but Cl's high electronegativity withdraws electron density from the ring INDUCTIVELY through the σ framework overall (hence net deactivating, since the inductive withdrawal outweighs the resonance donation in the ground state/rate)
Cl activates the ring at ALL positions equally, and 'deactivating' is a misnomer used only historically
questions.explanation: Halogens are the classic example of DUAL, opposing electronic effects: the lone pairs on Cl CAN be donated into the ring π system by resonance, which specifically stabilises the arenium ion intermediate when the electrophile attacks ortho or para to Cl (hence o/p-directing) — but this resonance donation is relatively weak because Cl's 3p orbital doesn't overlap as efficiently with the ring's 2p orbitals (poor size/energy match). Simultaneously, Cl's high electronegativity pulls σ-bond electron density away from the ring inductively at ALL positions, net-deactivating the ring overall (making chlorobenzene react slower than benzene itself, though still faster than a purely deactivating, meta-directing group like −NO<sub>2</sub>).
questions.hint: Halogens show two competing electronic effects (inductive vs. resonance) that point in DIFFERENT directions for rate vs. regiochemistry — identify which effect governs which observation.
distractor_logic: This reverses the correct assignment; Cl DONATES by resonance (weakly, but enough to direct o/p) and WITHDRAWS by induction (strongly enough to net-deactivate), not the other way around.
Cl's directing effect is electronic (resonance donation into the ring at o/p positions stabilising the intermediate), not primarily a steric phenomenon.

Cl is net deactivating overall (slower reaction than benzene), even though it directs to specific (o/p) positions when reaction does occur; these are not contradictory once you separate the rate effect (inductive, deactivating) from the regiochemical effect (resonance, o/p-directing).

questions.question: n-Hexane is converted to benzene by catalytic reforming (aromatisation: cyclisation + dehydrogenation, Pt/Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>3</sub> catalyst, high temperature/pressure). This benzene is then completely combusted. Compare the degree of unsaturation of n-hexane, benzene, and the immediate cyclohexane intermediate typically invoked in this mechanism.
options: n-Hexane has a higher DoU than benzene, since it has more hydrogens
All three compounds have the same DoU, since they have the same number of carbons
Cyclohexane and benzene have identical DoU because both are 6-membered rings

n-Hexane: DoU = 0 (fully saturated, acyclic); cyclohexane (cyclisation step): DoU = 1 (one ring, no π bonds yet); benzene (after dehydrogenation, losing 3 H<sub>2</sub>): DoU = 4 (one ring + three π bonds)
questions.explanation: DoU = (2C+2−H)/2. n-Hexane, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>14</sub>: DoU = (14−14)/2 = 0 (fully saturated, acyclic, matches general alkane formula). Cyclisation to cyclohexane, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>, forms one ring (losing H<sub>2</sub> in the process, conceptually): DoU = (14−12)/2 = 1. Aromatisation (catalytic dehydrogenation) removes 3 more H<sub>2</sub> to form benzene, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub>: DoU = (14−6)/2 = 4, reflecting the ring (1) plus 3 C=C-equivalent degrees of unsaturation from the aromatic system.
questions.hint: Compute DoU = (2C + 2 − H)/2 for each of the three molecular formulas (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>14</sub>, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub>) separately.
distractor_logic: n-Hexane, being fully saturated, has DoU = 0, the LOWEST of the three, not the highest; more hydrogens (for a fixed carbon count) corresponds to a LOWER degree of unsaturation, not higher.

Cyclohexane (DoU=1, just a ring) and benzene (DoU=4, a ring plus three degrees of unsaturation from the aromatic π system) are chemically very different despite both being 6-membered rings; benzene's aromaticity adds substantial additional unsaturation beyond the ring itself.

All three do NOT share the same carbon count coincidence leading to equal DoU; each loses hydrogens progressively through the reforming process, increasing DoU at each stage despite constant carbon count.

questions.question: Both benzene sulfonation (conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> or fuming H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>/SO<sub>3</sub>) and alkene hydration (dil. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>) use sulfuric acid, but play very different mechanistic roles in each. Contrast these roles.
options: H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> plays an identical role (as the direct electrophile) in both reactions
In both reactions, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> acts purely as a solvent with no mechanistic involvement

In sulfonation, SO<sub>3</sub> (from fuming H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>) IS the electrophile itself, attacked directly by the ring to form the arenium intermediate, which then loses H<sup>+</sup> (substitution, aromaticity restored); in alkene hydration, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> instead supplies a proton (H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>) that adds to the alkene as the electrophile, and water later adds as the nucleophile (Markovnikov addition, no aromaticity concern since alkenes aren't aromatic)
Sulfonation is an addition reaction just like alkene hydration, both saturating a π system fully
questions.explanation: In aromatic sulfonation, electrophilic SO<sub>3</sub> (present in fuming H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, or generated from H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> itself) is attacked by the ring's π electrons, forming an arenium intermediate that loses H<sup>+</sup> to regenerate aromaticity, giving benzenesulfonic acid — net substitution. In alkene hydration, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> instead protonates the alkene (H<sup>+</sup> is the electrophile here, added across the π bond to form the more stable carbocation, Markovnikov), and water then acts as the NUCLEOPHILE attacking that carbocation to give the alcohol — net addition, since there's no aromatic system to restore.
questions.hint: Identify the actual electrophilic species in each reaction (is it H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>/SO<sub>3</sub> itself, or something H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> helps generate/donate) and whether the final step is addition or substitution.
distractor_logic: Sulfonation is a SUBSTITUTION (aromaticity is restored after H<sup>+</sup> loss, net replacing a ring H with −SO<sub>3</sub>H), while alkene hydration is a genuine ADDITION (both new bonds, to H and OH, are retained in the saturated product); they are not the same reaction type.

The two roles are mechanistically distinct: SO<sub>3</sub> acts as a direct electrophile in sulfonation, while in hydration H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> acts as a proton (acid) donor, not as the electrophile itself in the same sense.

H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> is directly, mechanistically involved in both reactions (as electrophile-source in sulfonation, as proton/acid catalyst in hydration), not merely acting as an inert solvent in either case.

Given that −CH<sub>3</sub> is o,p-directing, and assuming statistically THREE times as many ortho positions are 'available' relative to the single para position (2 ortho vs. 1 para, before accounting for any steric preference), but that steric hindrance from the adjacent methyl disfavours ortho attack, what is the typical observed major/minor product distribution for mononitration of toluene?
options: Nitration of toluene gives a single, exclusively pure product with no isomer mixture
Ortho and para form in exactly the statistical 2:1 ratio predicted by position count alone, with no steric effect at all

Para-nitrotoluene forms as a substantial fraction (often comparable to or exceeding ortho despite the 2:1 statistical position ratio), because steric hindrance suppresses ortho attack even though ortho is statistically favoured 2:1 by position count alone; only a small amount of meta-nitrotoluene forms since −CH<sub>3</sub> disfavours meta
Only meta-nitrotoluene forms, since −CH<sub>3</sub> is meta-directing
questions.explanation: −CH<sub>3</sub> is o,p-directing (both activated by hyperconjugation/induction), so ortho- and para-nitrotoluene dominate, with only a small amount of meta-nitrotoluene (the minor, non-directed product). While there are twice as many ortho positions as the single para position, the bulky electrophile (NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup>, and the incoming group's proximity to the existing methyl) experiences STERIC hindrance specifically at the ortho positions, reducing the actual ortho yield below the naive 2:1 statistical prediction — so para product forms in a substantial, often comparable or even majority, share among the o/p products, illustrating that directing rules predict WHICH positions are favoured in principle, while steric effects modulate the exact ortho:para ratio.
questions.hint: Directing rules tell you WHICH positions (ortho+para vs. meta) are favoured; steric bulk further adjusts the ratio WITHIN the favoured set (ortho vs. para) — these operate at different levels.
distractor_logic: The observed ratio deviates from the naive 2:1 statistical prediction specifically because of steric hindrance disfavouring ortho attack; a pure statistical (position-count-only) prediction ignores this real steric effect.
−CH<sub>3</sub> is o,p-directing, NOT meta-directing (that classification applies to deactivating groups like −NO<sub>2</sub>, −COOH, −CN); meta-nitrotoluene is actually the MINOR product here.

Electrophilic aromatic substitution reactions typically give a MIXTURE of isomers (here, predominantly ortho and para, in some experimentally-determined ratio, plus a small amount of meta), not a single exclusively pure product.

questions.question: Benzene, prepared industrially from the catalytic reforming of petroleum naphtha (rather than from ethyne trimerisation, which is mainly a laboratory-scale/historical method), is then Friedel-Crafts ACYLATED with CH<sub>3</sub>COCl/AlCl<sub>3</sub> to give acetophenone. Why is Friedel-Crafts ACYLATION generally preferred over ALKYLATION when a single, clean mono-substitution product is the synthetic goal?
options: Acyl chlorides can never react with benzene under any Friedel-Crafts conditions

The acyl group (−COCH<sub>3</sub>) installed is DEACTIVATING (due to the electron-withdrawing carbonyl), so once one acyl group is on the ring, the ring becomes LESS reactive toward a second Friedel-Crafts reaction, naturally limiting the reaction to mono-substitution (unlike alkylation, where the installed alkyl group is activating and promotes over-substitution)
Acylation and alkylation behave identically with respect to over-substitution risk, so there's no preference either way
Acylation is preferred simply because AlCl<sub>3</sub> is not required as a catalyst for acylation
questions.explanation: Friedel-Crafts acylation installs a carbonyl-containing group (−COR), which is electron-WITHDRAWING (deactivating, meta-directing) due to the carbonyl's resonance/inductive pull — so after one acylation, the ring is deactivated toward further electrophilic attack, naturally stopping the reaction at mono-substitution. This contrasts sharply with alkylation, where the installed alkyl group is activating, making the ring MORE prone to a second (poly-)alkylation, a well-known practical problem. This self-limiting behaviour is a major reason acylation (sometimes followed by a separate Clemmensen/Wolff-Kishner reduction to remove the carbonyl if a simple alkyl group is ultimately desired) is often the preferred synthetic route.
questions.hint: Compare the electronic nature (activating vs. deactivating) of the group left behind on the ring after each type of reaction.
distractor_logic: AlCl<sub>3</sub> (or a similar Lewis acid) IS required as a catalyst for Friedel-Crafts acylation, just as it is for alkylation; this is not the distinguishing factor between the two reaction types.
Acyl chlorides are the standard, textbook reagent for Friedel-Crafts acylation and react readily with benzene under AlCl<sub>3</sub> catalysis; this premise is factually incorrect.

The two reactions behave very differently regarding over-substitution risk precisely because the group each one installs (activating alkyl vs. deactivating acyl) has opposite effects on the ring's further reactivity.

questions.question: Both benzene (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub>) and 1,3,5-hexatriene (an open-chain conjugated triene, also C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>8</sub> — note the DIFFERENT formula) are sometimes casually confused as 'the same thing drawn differently' by students. Identify the actual relationship (or lack thereof) between them.
options: They are constitutional isomers of each other, both C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub>
Both compounds are equally aromatic since both have three alternating double bonds

Benzene (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub>) and 1,3,5-hexatriene (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>8</sub>) are DIFFERENT molecular formulas (not isomers of each other) and different classes entirely: benzene is a cyclic, planar, fully conjugated AROMATIC ring (Huckel 4n+2, n=1, delocalised, unusually stable), while hexatriene is an ACYCLIC triene with three localised (non-aromatic) alternating double bonds and no special aromatic stabilisation
Hexatriene is simply the 'open' (non-aromatic) resonance structure of benzene and interconverts freely with it
questions.explanation: Benzene, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub>, has DoU = 4 (1 ring + 3 π-equivalents) and IS aromatic (cyclic, planar, fully conjugated, 4n+2 = 6 π electrons via Huckel's rule, giving substantial extra thermodynamic stability/delocalisation energy beyond a simple triene). 1,3,5-Hexatriene, CH<sub>2</sub>=CH−CH=CH−CH=CH<sub>2</sub>, is C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>8</sub> (DoU = 3, three isolated/conjugated π bonds only, no ring) — a genuinely different molecular formula, so they are NOT isomers of each other at all, merely superficially similar in having 'three double bond equivalents' in casual description. Hexatriene, being acyclic, cannot access the special cyclic delocalisation and aromatic stabilisation that defines benzene's chemistry.
questions.hint: Compare the actual molecular formulas (count H's carefully) before assuming any isomeric relationship.
distractor_logic: Benzene's aromatic ring structure and hexatriene's open triene structure are genuinely different, stable molecules with different formulas; they do not freely interconvert as resonance structures of one single compound.

Constitutional isomers must share the SAME molecular formula; benzene (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>6</sub>) and hexatriene (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>8</sub>) have different formulas, so they cannot be isomers of each other by definition.

Only benzene, with its CYCLIC, planar, fully conjugated system satisfying Huckel's 4n+2 rule, is aromatic; hexatriene's open-chain, non-cyclic triene does not meet the structural requirements for aromaticity regardless of having conjugated double bonds.

questions.question: Both the Wurtz reaction (2 RX + 2Na → R−R) and the Fittig reaction (Wurtz's aromatic analogue, using aryl halides) form new C−C bonds via sodium-mediated coupling. Why can't the Fittig reaction be used to couple a simple alkyl halide with an aryl halide (the 'Wurtz-Fittig' reaction) to reliably give a SINGLE pure product, just like the ordinary symmetric Fittig reaction does for two identical aryl halides?
options: Using two DIFFERENT halides (one alkyl, one aryl) in a crossed Wurtz-Fittig reaction faces the same 'crossed coupling' problem as an unsymmetrical Wurtz reaction: all possible statistical couplings occur (alkyl-alkyl, aryl-aryl, AND the desired alkyl-aryl), giving a product mixture rather than one clean compound
The Fittig reaction cannot use alkyl halides under any circumstances, so the Wurtz-Fittig reaction does not actually exist
Sodium metal reacts only with aryl halides, never with alkyl halides, making cross-coupling impossible
The Wurtz-Fittig reaction always gives 100% selectivity for the alkyl-aryl cross product with no side products
questions.explanation: The Wurtz-Fittig reaction (an alkyl halide + an aryl halide + Na) does exist and is a genuine named method for making alkylbenzenes (e.g. bromobenzene + methyl bromide + Na → toluene), but like any 'crossed' radical/organometallic coupling using two different halide partners, it suffers from the same statistical mixing problem as an unsymmetrical Wurtz reaction: self-coupling of the alkyl halide (giving an alkane), self-coupling of the aryl halide (giving a biaryl, e.g. biphenyl), AND the desired cross-coupled product all form simultaneously, requiring careful stoichiometry (often excess aryl halide) and separation to isolate the desired alkylbenzene.
questions.hint: Think back to why an unsymmetrical (crossed) Wurtz reaction between two DIFFERENT alkyl halides gives a mixture — the same statistical logic applies here.
distractor_logic: The Wurtz-Fittig reaction is a genuine, named, real synthetic method (alkyl halide + aryl halide + Na) used to prepare alkylbenzenes; the premise that it cannot exist is factually incorrect.

Like the unsymmetrical Wurtz reaction, the Wurtz-Fittig reaction gives a MIXTURE of products (self-coupled alkane, self-coupled biaryl, and the cross product), not a clean 100%-selective cross-coupling.

Sodium metal reacts with BOTH alkyl and aryl halides in these coupling reactions (that's the basis of the ordinary Wurtz reaction working on alkyl halides and the Fittig reaction working on aryl halides individually); it isn't restricted to aryl halides only.

questions.question: Pentane (C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub>) has 3 constitutional isomers (n-pentane, isopentane, neopentane). Considering ALSO that n-pentane can adopt different CONFORMATIONS (anti, gauche, etc. about its C2−C3 bond) by free rotation, why are conformations NOT counted as additional isomers when answering 'how many isomers of pentane exist'?
options: Conformations and constitutional isomers are exactly the same phenomenon and should always be counted together
Constitutional isomers also interconvert freely at room temperature, just like conformations, making the distinction meaningless

Conformations interconvert freely and rapidly at room temperature via simple rotation about a single (σ) bond, with no bond breaking involved, so they represent the SAME compound in different transient shapes, not distinct, isolable substances; constitutional isomers, by contrast, differ in actual atom-to-atom connectivity (bonding pattern) and are separate, isolable compounds
n-Pentane cannot actually rotate about any of its C−C bonds due to steric strain, so conformations don't exist for it
questions.explanation: Constitutional (structural) isomers have genuinely different connectivity (different bonds to different atoms) and are distinct, separately isolable compounds with different physical/chemical properties (e.g. n-pentane bp 36°C vs. neopentane bp 9.5°C). Conformations (like anti and gauche about a C−C single bond) are simply different 3D arrangements reached by low-barrier bond ROTATION, not bond breaking — they rapidly interconvert at room temperature and are not separable, isolable species, so they are not counted as 'isomers' in the constitutional sense.
questions.hint: Ask whether interconverting between the two forms requires breaking a bond, or just rotating around one.
distractor_logic: Constitutional isomers do NOT interconvert freely at room temperature; converting one into another requires breaking and re-forming actual covalent bonds (a chemical reaction), unlike simple bond rotation.

n-Pentane, being an open (acyclic) chain with only single bonds along its backbone, rotates freely about each C−C bond at room temperature (subject only to small, easily-surmounted energy barriers); conformations do exist for it.

This conflates two genuinely different phenomena; constitutional isomers require different atom connectivity (bonds to different partners), while conformations are just rotational snapshots of the SAME connectivity.

questions.question: Hex-2-ene (CH<sub>3</sub>−CH=CH−CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>) shows cis/trans isomerism, but hex-1-ene (CH<sub>2</sub>=CH−CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>) does not, even though BOTH are constitutional isomers of the same molecular formula C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>. What is the precise structural rule that explains this difference?
options: Hex-1-ene doesn't show geometrical isomerism because it has an odd total number of carbons
Only even-numbered-position double bonds (2-ene, 4-ene, etc.) show geometrical isomerism; odd-numbered (1-ene) never do, as a general numerical rule

Geometrical isomerism requires EACH double-bond carbon to bear TWO DIFFERENT substituents; in hex-1-ene, the terminal =CH<sub>2</sub> carbon bears two IDENTICAL substituents (both H), so no cis/trans distinction is possible there, whereas in hex-2-ene both double-bond carbons (C2: CH<sub>3</sub>/H; C3: H/propyl) bear two different groups each
Both compounds actually DO show geometrical isomerism equally; the question's premise is false
questions.explanation: The general rule: a C=C shows cis/trans isomerism only if EACH of the two double-bond carbons carries two DIFFERENT groups. In hex-2-ene, C2 bears CH<sub>3</sub> and H (different), and C3 bears H and n-propyl (different) — both conditions met, so cis/trans exists. In hex-1-ene, the terminal carbon (C1, =CH<sub>2</sub>) bears two H atoms (identical to each other) — failing the 'two different groups' condition at that carbon — so no geometrical isomerism is possible, regardless of what's on the other carbon (C2: H and n-butyl, which alone would satisfy the condition but isn't sufficient on its own).
questions.hint: Check EACH of the two double-bond carbons individually for whether its two attached groups are different from each other — both carbons must pass this test.
distractor_logic: The total carbon count (6, in both cases here) is irrelevant to whether geometrical isomerism is possible; the determining factor is the specific substitution pattern at the two double-bond carbons.

There is no such general numerical rule tied to whether the locant is odd or even; the real criterion is about which specific groups are attached to each double-bond carbon, not the position number in the name.

The two compounds do NOT behave the same; hex-2-ene genuinely shows cis/trans isomerism while hex-1-ene genuinely does not, precisely because of the terminal =CH<sub>2</sub> group's two identical hydrogens.

questions.question: But-1-yne and but-2-yne are both C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>6</sub>, yet only but-1-yne reacts with ammoniacal AgNO<sub>3</sub> to give a precipitate, and only but-1-yne is deprotonated by NaNH<sub>2</sub>. Classify the isomeric relationship between these two compounds AND explain their differing reactivity in one consistent structural explanation.
options: They are geometrical (cis/trans) isomers of each other, and their differing reactivity comes from that geometric difference

They are constitutional (position) isomers, differing in WHERE the triple bond sits in the chain; only but-1-yne has a TERMINAL ≡C−H (acidic, reactive toward Ag<sup>+</sup> and NaNH<sub>2</sub>), while but-2-yne's triple bond is INTERNAL (no acidic terminal H, since both triple-bond carbons instead bear CH<sub>3</sub> groups)
They are identical compounds (not isomers at all), and the reactivity difference described must be an experimental error
They differ only in molecular formula, not structure, which explains the reactivity difference
questions.explanation: But-1-yne, HC≡C−CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, and but-2-yne, CH<sub>3</sub>−C≡C−CH<sub>3</sub>, share the same molecular formula C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>6</sub> but differ in where the triple bond is positioned along the chain — a constitutional (positional) isomer pair. Only but-1-yne retains a TERMINAL ≡C−H (acidic due to sp-hybridised carbanion stability), which is what reacts with ammoniacal AgNO<sub>3</sub> (forming a silver acetylide precipitate) and with NaNH<sub>2</sub> (deprotonation); but-2-yne's triple bond is flanked by two CH<sub>3</sub> groups (no terminal alkyne C−H at all), so it is unreactive in both tests — this is in fact a standard NCERT-cited chemical test to distinguish terminal from internal alkynes.
questions.hint: A triple bond can sit at different POSITIONS along the same 4-carbon chain; ask whether each position leaves a terminal ≡C−H or not.
distractor_logic: Alkynes cannot show cis/trans (geometrical) isomerism at all, since the two sp carbons of a triple bond are collinear with their substituents, leaving no 'sides' for cis/trans to distinguish; the relationship here is constitutional (positional), not geometrical.

The two compounds are genuinely distinct, separately isolable substances (different structures, different physical/chemical properties including this diagnostic AgNO<sub>3</sub> test); they are not identical.

Both compounds share the exact same molecular formula, C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>6</sub>; their difference is purely structural (position of the triple bond along the chain), which is precisely the definition of constitutional isomerism.

questions.question: Dibromobenzene (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>4</sub>Br<sub>2</sub>) exists as three constitutional isomers: ortho-, meta-, and para-dibromobenzene. If these three isomers are treated as a single 'mixture' rather than being separated, explain in terms of isomerism why this mixture behaves as three chemically distinct substances rather than one compound with variable properties.
options: Only ortho- and para- are real isomers; meta-dibromobenzene does not actually exist as a distinct compound

Ortho-, meta-, and para-dibromobenzene are constitutional (positional) isomers — each has genuinely different connectivity (relative POSITIONS of the two Br atoms on the ring), giving each a fixed, distinct melting point, boiling point, and reactivity; a 'mixture' of the three is physically a blend of three separate pure compounds, not one compound with a range of properties
The three forms are identical in every property and only differ in name, so treating them as a mixture is unnecessary
They are geometrical isomers of each other, arising from restricted rotation around the ring's single bonds
questions.explanation: The three dibromobenzene isomers differ in the relative ring positions of the two Br substituents (adjacent = ortho, one-carbon-apart = meta, opposite = para) — different connectivity/relative positioning, making them constitutional isomers, each a distinct pure compound with its own characteristic melting point (e.g. para-dibromobenzene, being more symmetric, packs into a crystal lattice more efficiently and has a notably higher melting point than the ortho or meta isomers) and separate chemical identity. A 'mixture' of all three, if unseparated, is simply a physical blend of three distinct pure substances, analogous to a mixture of any three different organic compounds.
questions.hint: Ask what physically distinguishes ortho from meta from para on a benzene ring, and whether that's a difference in connectivity or in molecular shape/rotation.
distractor_logic: There is no restricted rotation involved here; the ring itself is a fixed hexagonal framework, and ortho/meta/para describe fixed RELATIVE POSITIONS of substituents around that fixed ring, not a rotational/conformational relationship.

The three isomers have genuinely different physical and chemical properties (notably different melting points, with para typically highest due to better crystal packing symmetry); they are not identical compounds under different names.
All three isomers (ortho, meta, AND para) are real, well-characterised, separately isolable compounds; meta-dibromobenzene is a genuine, distinct substance, not a non-existent form.

questions.question: Cyclobutane and but-1-ene are both C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub> (DoU = 1 each), yet they are typically classified separately rather than as 'isomers of the same functional class'. Reconcile this with the general definition of isomerism.
options: Cyclobutane and but-1-ene are actually the same compound viewed from two different angles

Cyclobutane (a ring, no π bond) and but-1-ene (an open chain with one C=C) ARE constitutional isomers of each other (same molecular formula, different connectivity/bonding arrangement achieving the same DoU=1 in two structurally different ways: ring-closure vs. a double bond) — they are correctly classed in different functional FAMILIES (cycloalkane vs. alkene) while still technically being isomers of one another
They cannot be isomers because one is cyclic and the other is not; isomerism requires identical ring/chain structure
They have different molecular formulas, so the comparison is invalid from the start
questions.explanation: Both cyclobutane and but-1-ene have molecular formula C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub> (DoU=1: cyclobutane achieves this via ring closure with no π bond, while but-1-ene achieves it via one C=C π bond with no ring) — matching molecular formulas with different connectivity is EXACTLY the definition of constitutional isomerism, regardless of which 'named functional class' (cycloalkane vs. alkene) each is more conventionally filed under for teaching purposes. Isomerism doesn't require the two structures to belong to the same IUPAC-named family; it only requires the same molecular formula with different structural arrangement.
questions.hint: Check whether isomerism, by definition, requires the two compounds to be in the SAME functional-class category, or just the same molecular formula.
distractor_logic: Cyclobutane (a saturated ring) and but-1-ene (an unsaturated open chain) have distinctly different structures, reactivity, and physical properties; they are not the same compound, merely isomers of each other.

Isomerism explicitly does NOT require identical ring/chain topology; it only requires the same molecular formula with a different arrangement of atoms, which is satisfied here even though one is cyclic and the other acyclic.

Both compounds are verified to be C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub> (cyclobutane: ring of 4 CH<sub>2</sub> units; but-1-ene: CH<sub>2</sub>=CH−CH<sub>2</sub>−CH<sub>3</sub>), so the molecular formulas do match, making the comparison valid.

questions.question: A Wurtz reaction is run on 1-bromo-2-methylpropane (isobutyl bromide) with Na/dry ether. The coupled product, 2,5-dimethylhexane, is compared against n-octane (also C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub>, obtainable by Wurtz coupling of n-butyl bromide instead). What isomeric relationship do these two Wurtz products have, and why does the choice of STARTING alkyl halide's branching pattern directly control which isomer results?
options: The branching pattern of the starting halide has no influence on the product's structure at all
They are geometrical isomers, differing only in cis/trans arrangement
They are not isomers because Wurtz coupling always gives the same single product regardless of the starting halide's structure

They are constitutional isomers (both C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub>, different connectivity); since Wurtz coupling simply joins two intact alkyl groups at their former halide-bearing carbon without rearrangement, the BRANCHING of the starting halide is directly preserved and doubled in the product — a branched starting halide gives a branched product, a straight-chain halide gives a straight-chain product
questions.explanation: Wurtz coupling joins two alkyl radical/organosodium fragments directly at the carbon that bore the halogen, without any skeletal rearrangement — so 2 × isobutyl (from 1-bromo-2-methylpropane) coupled together gives 2,5-dimethylhexane (branched), while 2 × n-butyl (from 1-bromobutane) gives n-octane (straight chain). Both are C<sub>8</sub>H<sub>18</sub> (constitutional isomers of each other), and the STRUCTURE of the halide used directly and predictably determines the branching pattern of the doubled product, since no rearrangement occurs in this simple radical/ionic coupling.
questions.hint: Wurtz coupling simply joins two existing alkyl fragments together at their halide carbon; trace where each carbon of the starting halide ends up in the product.
distractor_logic: The branching pattern is directly and predictably carried through from starting halide to coupled product, since no bonds within each alkyl fragment are broken or rearranged during simple Wurtz coupling.
Wurtz coupling's product structure is directly determined by which alkyl halide is used; different halides (straight-chain vs. branched) give different, non-identical coupled products.

Alkanes with only single bonds throughout (no ring, no restricted rotation) cannot show geometrical (cis/trans) isomerism; the relationship here is constitutional, based on differing branching patterns.

questions.question: 2-Methylbut-2-ene and 3-methylbut-1-ene are both C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub> constitutional isomers. If BOTH are subjected to ozonolysis (O<sub>3</sub> then Zn/H<sub>2</sub>O), will the resulting fragment sets allow you to distinguish which original isomer you started with? Explain.
options: Yes: 2-methylbut-2-ene (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C=CH−CH<sub>3</sub> cleaves to acetone (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C=O and acetaldehyde CH<sub>3</sub>CHO, while 3-methylbut-1-ene (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CH−CH=CH<sub>2</sub> cleaves to isobutyraldehyde (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CH−CHO and formaldehyde HCHO — two entirely different fragment pairs, so ozonolysis products DO distinguish the two constitutional isomers unambiguously
Only one of the two isomers actually undergoes ozonolysis; the other has no reactive double bond
Ozonolysis cannot be performed on either compound since both are branched
No, both isomers give identical ozonolysis fragments since they have the same molecular formula
questions.explanation: Ozonolysis cleaves the C=C bond and converts each resulting carbon into a carbonyl, directly reflecting the substitution pattern AT the double bond — which differs between these two constitutional isomers. 2-Methylbut-2-ene's double bond (between a disubstituted and a monosubstituted carbon) gives acetone + acetaldehyde. 3-Methylbut-1-ene's double bond (between a monosubstituted and the terminal =CH<sub>2</sub>) gives isobutyraldehyde + formaldehyde. Since the fragment identities directly encode the original substitution pattern, ozonolysis is a genuinely useful structure-elucidation tool for distinguishing constitutional isomers that differ in where/how their double bond is substituted.
questions.hint: Draw each alkene's double bond explicitly, and convert each of the two double-bond carbons (with its attached groups) into a separate carbonyl fragment.
distractor_logic: Molecular formula alone does not determine ozonolysis fragments; the actual connectivity/substitution pattern at the double bond (which differs between these two constitutional isomers) is what determines the fragments, and here it genuinely does differ.
Branching at a carbon NOT involved in the double bond does not prevent ozonolysis; both molecules have a reactive C=C that undergoes cleavage normally.
Both compounds contain a C=C double bond (2-methylbut-2-ene between C2−C3; 3-methylbut-1-ene between C1−C2) and both react with ozone under standard ozonolysis conditions.

questions.question: Cyclopropane, propene, and propyne all relate to the general concept of 'unsaturation equivalents' but represent three DIFFERENT molecular formulas (C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>, C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>, C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>4</sub> respectively). Identify which pair (if any) among these three are true isomers of each other, and which is the odd one out.
options: Cyclopropane and propene ARE isomers of each other (both C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>, DoU=1, achieved via a ring in one case and a double bond in the other); propyne (C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>4</sub>, DoU=2) is the odd one out, since it has a different molecular formula entirely (not merely a different arrangement of the same atoms)
All three share the identical molecular formula C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub> and are therefore all isomers of one another
Propyne and propene are isomers of each other, while cyclopropane is the odd one out
None of the three are isomers of any other, since all three belong to different named functional classes
questions.explanation: Cyclopropane (a 3-membered ring, fully saturated, C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>) and propene (CH<sub>2</sub>=CH−CH<sub>3</sub>, C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>) share the exact same molecular formula (both DoU=1) but achieve it through different structural features (ring vs. double bond) — genuine constitutional isomers. Propyne (HC≡C−CH<sub>3</sub>, C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>4</sub>, DoU=2) has a DIFFERENT molecular formula (two fewer hydrogens, one more degree of unsaturation, from its triple bond) — it is NOT an isomer of either of the other two, since isomerism strictly requires an identical molecular formula, not merely 'being C<sub>3</sub> and unsaturated in some way'.
questions.hint: Write out and compare the exact molecular formula of all three compounds before deciding which pairs qualify as isomers.
distractor_logic: Isomerism is defined purely by matching molecular formula with different structure; the conventional 'named functional class' (cycloalkane vs. alkene vs. alkyne) that a compound is filed under for teaching purposes does not determine or preclude an isomeric relationship.

Propyne's molecular formula is C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>4</sub>, not C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>; it has two fewer hydrogens than cyclopropane/propene due to its additional degree of unsaturation (triple bond vs. single double bond/ring), so it does not share their formula.

Propyne (C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>4</sub>) and propene (C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>) have DIFFERENT molecular formulas and are therefore not isomers of each other; it is cyclopropane and propene (both C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>) that form the true isomeric pair.

questions.question: Equal moles of propane (C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>) and propene (C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub>) are each completely combusted. Which requires MORE O<sub>2</sub> per mole, and does this match the general trend that more UNSATURATED hydrocarbons need less oxygen per mole for complete combustion?
options: Propane needs more O<sub>2</sub> (5 mol O<sub>2</sub> per mol, vs. propene's 4.5 mol O<sub>2</sub> per mol), consistent with the general trend: more hydrogens (more saturated) means more O<sub>2</sub> is needed to fully oxidise all those extra H's to H<sub>2</sub>O, on top of the fixed CO<sub>2</sub> requirement from the 3 carbons common to both
Neither compound can be completely combusted; only CO forms from both
Both require exactly the same amount of O<sub>2</sub>, since both have 3 carbons
Propene needs more O<sub>2</sub> than propane, breaking the general trend
questions.explanation: Balanced equations: C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub> + 5O<sub>2</sub> → 3CO<sub>2</sub> + 4H<sub>2</sub>O (5 mol O<sub>2</sub>/mol fuel); C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>6</sub> + 4.5O<sub>2</sub> → 3CO<sub>2</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub>O (4.5 mol O<sub>2</sub>/mol fuel, i.e. 9/2). Both need the same O<sub>2</sub> to convert their 3 carbons to 3CO<sub>2</sub>, but propane's extra 2 hydrogens (8 vs. 6) require additional O<sub>2</sub> to form the extra H<sub>2</sub>O — so the more saturated (more hydrogen-rich) compound needs more O<sub>2</sub> per mole, a general trend across hydrocarbon combustion.
questions.hint: Balance both combustion equations fully and compare the O<sub>2</sub> coefficients directly.
distractor_logic: Both compounds have 3 carbons requiring the same O<sub>2</sub> for CO<sub>2</sub> formation, but they have DIFFERENT hydrogen counts (8 vs. 6), so their total O<sub>2</sub> requirements per mole are not equal.

This reverses the correct comparison; propane (more hydrogens, more saturated) requires MORE O<sub>2</sub> than propene, not less, since propane needs more O<sub>2</sub> to oxidise its extra hydrogens to water.

Complete combustion (as specified, implying sufficient/excess O<sub>2</sub>) gives CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O as the standard full-oxidation products for both compounds; CO only forms under incomplete (limited O<sub>2</sub>) combustion conditions.

questions.question: A hydrocarbon sample of unknown formula C<sub>x</sub>H<sub>y</sub> is combusted, producing 4 mol CO<sub>2</sub> and 5 mol H<sub>2</sub>O per mole of the compound burned. If this compound is also known to be a fully saturated, acyclic alkane (matching C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub>), determine its molecular formula and verify the combustion stoichiometry is self-consistent.
options: C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub> (n-butane or isobutane); 4 mol CO<sub>2</sub> matches x=4 directly, and 5 mol H<sub>2</sub>O implies y=10, which correctly satisfies y=2n+2=2(4)+2=10 for an alkane, confirming self-consistency
The data is inconsistent with any alkane, so no valid formula can be determined
C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>10</sub>, incorrectly assuming the CO<sub>2</sub> count equals n−1
C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>8</sub>, since 5 mol H<sub>2</sub>O simply means 8 hydrogens (a miscount ignoring the factor of 2 in H<sub>2</sub>O)
questions.explanation: Moles CO<sub>2</sub> = moles C in the original compound, so x=4. Moles H<sub>2</sub>O × 2 = moles H, so y = 5×2 = 10, giving C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>. Checking against the alkane general formula C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub> with n=4: 2(4)+2=10 ✓, confirming this is indeed a valid, self-consistent saturated alkane formula (matches either n-butane or isobutane structurally, though combustion data alone cannot distinguish these constitutional isomers).
questions.hint: Remember that each mole of H<sub>2</sub>O contains 2 moles of H atoms — don't equate moles of H<sub>2</sub>O directly to moles of H.
distractor_logic: The data IS fully consistent with a valid alkane formula (C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>, verified against C<sub>n</sub>H<sub>2n+2</sub>); there is no inconsistency once the H<sub>2</sub>O-to-H-atom conversion is done correctly.
There is no such rule that CO<sub>2</sub> count equals n−1; moles of CO<sub>2</sub> directly equal moles of carbon (n) in the original hydrocarbon, one-to-one.

This makes the common error of equating moles of H<sub>2</sub>O directly to moles of H atoms, forgetting that each H<sub>2</sub>O molecule contains TWO hydrogen atoms; the correct H count is 5×2=10, not 8.

questions.question: Ethene is catalytically hydrogenated to ethane (H<sub>2</sub>/Ni), and this ethane is then completely combusted, releasing heat ΔH<sub>combustion</sub>(ethane). Separately, ethene itself is directly combusted, releasing ΔH<sub>combustion</sub>(ethene). Using Hess's law logic (heat of hydrogenation + heat of combustion of the product = heat of combustion of the starting alkene, since both paths reach the same final oxidation products CO<sub>2</sub>+H<sub>2</sub>O), which quantity should be LARGER in magnitude, and why?
options: Heat of hydrogenation is irrelevant to combustion heat comparisons entirely
Ethane releases more heat upon combustion than the SUM of ethene's hydrogenation and combustion heats combined, violating Hess's law
Ethene and ethane release exactly identical heat upon combustion, since both eventually form the same CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O

|ΔH<sub>combustion</sub>(ethene)| is smaller in magnitude than |ΔH<sub>combustion</sub>(ethane)| + |ΔH<sub>hydrogenation</sub>|... more precisely: ΔH<sub>combustion</sub>(ethene) = ΔH<sub>hydrogenation</sub> + ΔH<sub>combustion</sub>(ethane) by Hess's law (both being negative/exothermic), so combusting ethene directly releases MORE total heat than combusting the equivalent ethane alone, because ethene also releases the hydrogenation exotherm along the way to the same final products
questions.explanation: By Hess's law, since both routes (direct ethene combustion, vs. hydrogenate-then-combust ethane) start from ethene (plus, in the second route, extra H<sub>2</sub>) and end at the same final products (CO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O, plus accounting for the H<sub>2</sub> consumed), the total enthalpy change must be path-independent: ΔH<sub>combustion</sub>(ethene) = ΔH<sub>hydrogenation</sub>(ethene→ethane) + ΔH<sub>combustion</sub>(ethane). Since hydrogenation is exothermic (ΔH<sub>hydrogenation</sub> is negative) and combustion is strongly exothermic (ΔH<sub>combustion</sub> is very negative), direct combustion of ethene releases MORE total heat (larger negative ΔH) than combustion of ethane alone, because it additionally captures the hydrogenation exotherm.
questions.hint: Set up a Hess's law cycle: ethene → (route A: direct combustion) vs. (route B: hydrogenate then combust) — both end at the same place.
distractor_logic: Heat of hydrogenation is directly relevant here; it's the connecting link in the Hess's law cycle between ethene's and ethane's combustion enthalpies.

Ethene and ethane are chemically distinct molecules with different total bond energies (ethene has a π bond, less thermodynamically stable per se), so their combustion heats are NOT identical, even though both ultimately form the same types of final products.

This directly violates Hess's law, which requires that the two paths from ethene to the same final products (CO<sub>2</sub>+H<sub>2</sub>O) sum consistently; the combustion heat of ethane plus the hydrogenation heat correctly EQUALS (not exceeds) the direct combustion heat of ethene.

questions.question: Benzene's measured heat of hydrogenation to cyclohexane (−208 kJ/mol) is significantly LESS exothermic than 3 × the heat of hydrogenation of a single, isolated C=C (like cyclohexene, −120 kJ/mol, so 3× would predict −360 kJ/mol if benzene were merely 'cyclohexatriene' with three independent double bonds). How does this combustion/hydrogenation-based evidence support benzene's aromatic (delocalised) structure rather than a simple triene structure?
options: The ~152 kJ/mol 'missing' exothermicity (360−208) represents benzene's extra thermodynamic stability (resonance/delocalisation energy) compared to a hypothetical localised cyclohexatriene; benzene sits at a LOWER energy (more stable) than three isolated double bonds would predict, precisely because its π electrons are delocalised over the whole ring rather than confined to three separate bonds
There should be no difference at all between benzene's actual and hypothetical hydrogenation enthalpies if the structure is correct, so this data suggests an experimental error
This data is unrelated to aromaticity and only reflects a difference in catalyst efficiency
The discrepancy shows benzene is actually LESS stable than predicted, contradicting the concept of aromatic stabilisation
questions.explanation: If benzene had three truly isolated, non-interacting double bonds (a hypothetical 'cyclohexatriene'), hydrogenating all three would release approximately 3×(−120) = −360 kJ/mol. The ACTUAL measured value is only −208 kJ/mol — substantially less exothermic (less heat released) — meaning benzene starts from a LOWER, more stable energy state than the hypothetical triene would. This ~152 kJ/mol energy gap is exactly the resonance/delocalisation (aromatic stabilisation) energy: benzene's real structure (delocalised π system over all 6 carbons) is more stable than three independent double bonds, and this stabilisation must be 'paid off' before hydrogenation can proceed, hence less heat is released overall — this experimental hydrogenation-enthalpy argument is a classic piece of evidence for aromatic delocalisation.
questions.hint: Less heat released upon hydrogenation means the starting material was already at LOWER energy (more stable) than the naive prediction — work out what that implies about benzene's actual ground-state stability.
distractor_logic: This is not an anomaly or experimental error; the ~152 kJ/mol gap is the well-established, real, reproducible resonance energy of benzene, a cornerstone of the experimental case for aromaticity.

This is a genuine thermodynamic (bond-energy/stability) argument based on measured enthalpies, not a reflection of catalyst efficiency, which would not systematically produce this specific, reproducible energy gap.

This gets the stability direction backwards; releasing LESS heat than predicted means benzene started from a MORE stable (lower energy), not less stable, state — supporting, not contradicting, aromatic stabilisation.

questions.question: n-Pentane (bp 36°C), isopentane (bp 28°C), and neopentane (bp 9.5°C) are all C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub> constitutional isomers, yet their boiling points differ substantially. What structural trend explains this, and how does it connect to intermolecular forces?
options: Neopentane has the highest boiling point of the three because it is the most symmetric molecule
More branching increases boiling point because branched molecules are heavier
Boiling point is unrelated to branching and depends only on molecular formula, so all three should boil at the same temperature

Increasing branching (n-pentane → isopentane → neopentane) makes the molecule progressively more compact/spherical, REDUCING the surface area available for van der Waals (London dispersion) contact between neighbouring molecules, which weakens intermolecular attraction and lowers the boiling point
questions.explanation: All three isomers have identical molecular formula (C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub>, same molar mass), so mass is not the differentiator; the relevant intermolecular force here is van der Waals (London dispersion), which depends on the surface AREA of close contact between molecules. n-Pentane's elongated, flexible chain allows extensive side-by-side contact with neighbouring molecules; as branching increases (isopentane, then the highly compact, near-spherical neopentane), the molecule's surface area for such contact shrinks, weakening the cumulative dispersion forces and lowering the boiling point — this straight-chain-to-branched, decreasing-boiling-point trend is a standard NCERT physical-property pattern.
questions.hint: All three have the same molar mass; think about molecular SHAPE and how it affects the surface area available for intermolecular contact.
distractor_logic: All three isomers share the exact same molecular formula (C<sub>5</sub>H<sub>12</sub>) and therefore the exact same molar mass; mass differences cannot explain the boiling point trend here.

Neopentane, being the most compact/spherical (and hence having the LEAST intermolecular contact area), has the LOWEST boiling point of the three, not the highest — the trend runs opposite to this option's claim.

Constitutional isomers with identical molecular formula can and do have different boiling points, precisely because their different shapes affect intermolecular contact area even though mass is unchanged.

questions.question: Ethyne (C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>2</sub>) is combusted in LIMITED oxygen (incomplete combustion, giving soot/carbon and water) in an oxy-acetylene welding torch, deliberately NOT run with excess O<sub>2</sub>. Contrast this with complete combustion of ethyne, and explain why the limited-O<sub>2</sub> version is industrially preferred here despite 'incomplete' combustion normally being viewed as undesirable.
options: Complete combustion (excess O<sub>2</sub>): C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>2</sub> + 5/2 O<sub>2</sub> → 2CO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O; the oxy-acetylene torch instead uses a carefully tuned (slightly O<sub>2</sub>-deficient or stoichiometric) flame to maximise the extremely high, sharply localised flame temperature (~3300°C) needed for metal cutting/welding, rather than to minimise soot production, which is a secondary concern here
Incomplete combustion is chosen purely to save money on oxygen gas, with no effect on flame temperature
The two combustion modes produce identical products and temperatures, making the O<sub>2</sub> ratio irrelevant
Ethyne cannot undergo complete combustion under any conditions due to its triple bond
questions.explanation: Complete combustion of ethyne (excess O<sub>2</sub>) follows C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>2</sub> + 5/2 O<sub>2</sub> → 2CO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O, releasing a large amount of heat and reaching very high flame temperatures. In an oxy-acetylene torch, the O<sub>2</sub>:C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>2</sub> ratio is precisely tuned (often close to stoichiometric or the primary combustion zone slightly O<sub>2</sub>-rich, with a secondary outer flame burning any remaining fuel with atmospheric O<sub>2</sub>) specifically to achieve the highest possible LOCALISED flame temperature (~3300°C, among the hottest of common fuel gases), which is what makes it useful for cutting/welding metal — the choice of ratio is about maximising temperature and flame characteristics for this specific industrial purpose, not primarily about avoiding wasted oxygen cost.
questions.hint: Think about WHY a welding torch needs an unusually hot flame, and what flame-tuning (not just 'more vs. less O<sub>2</sub>') achieves for that specific industrial goal.
distractor_logic: Cost of oxygen gas is not the primary driver of flame-ratio tuning in oxy-acetylene welding; achieving the specific very high flame temperature needed for metal work is the key industrial consideration.
The O<sub>2</sub>:fuel ratio significantly affects both the combustion products (complete vs. incomplete) and the flame temperature/character; the two modes are not interchangeable or equivalent.
Ethyne, like other hydrocarbons, DOES undergo complete combustion to CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O when burned in excess O<sub>2</sub>; its triple bond does not prevent full oxidation.

questions.question: A gas mixture of unknown composition, containing only methane and ethene, is completely combusted. 1 mole of the mixture requires exactly 2.5 moles of O<sub>2</sub> for complete combustion. Determine the mole fraction of methane in the original mixture.
options: 1.0 (pure methane), incorrectly ignoring that ethene requires a different amount of O<sub>2</sub>
0.5 (equimolar mixture): methane needs 2 mol O<sub>2</sub>/mol, ethene needs 3 mol O<sub>2</sub>/mol; setting up x(2) + (1−x)(3) = 2.5 gives 2x + 3 − 3x = 2.5, so −x = −0.5, x = 0.5
0.25, from an arithmetic slip in setting up the weighted-average equation
0.75, from mislabelling which gas needs more oxygen
questions.explanation: CH<sub>4</sub> + 2O<sub>2</sub> → CO<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (2 mol O<sub>2</sub> per mol methane). C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>4</sub> + 3O<sub>2</sub> → 2CO<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O (3 mol O<sub>2</sub> per mol ethene). Let x = mole fraction methane, (1−x) = mole fraction ethene. Weighted O<sub>2</sub> demand: 2x + 3(1−x) = 2.5 ⇒ 2x + 3 − 3x = 2.5 ⇒ −x = −0.5 ⇒ x = 0.5. Check: 0.5(2) + 0.5(3) = 1 + 1.5 = 2.5 ✓.
questions.hint: Set up a weighted-average equation using mole fraction x for methane and (1−x) for ethene, based on each gas's individual O<sub>2</sub> requirement per mole.
distractor_logic: Pure methane alone would require exactly 2 mol O<sub>2</sub> per mol of gas, not 2.5; the actual mixture's higher O<sub>2</sub> requirement (2.5) indicates some ethene (which needs more O<sub>2</sub> per mole) must be present.
This does not satisfy the weighted-average equation; substituting x=0.25 gives 0.25(2)+0.75(3)=0.5+2.25=2.75, not 2.5, so this value is incorrect.
This value does not satisfy the equation either; substituting x=0.75 gives 0.75(2)+0.25(3)=1.5+0.75=2.25, not 2.5 — the correct fraction is 0.5, not 0.75.

questions.question: Calcium carbide (CaC<sub>2</sub>) is treated with water to generate ethyne (used, among other things, as a fuel gas): CaC<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O → Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub> + C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>2</sub>. If 6.4 g of CaC<sub>2</sub> (molar mass 64 g/mol) reacts completely with excess water, and the resulting ethyne is then completely combusted, how many moles of CO<sub>2</sub> are ultimately produced?
options: 0.1 mol, forgetting that each ethyne molecule contains 2 carbons
0.4 mol, from an error in the initial mole calculation of CaC<sub>2</sub>
1.0 mol, using the molar mass of CO<sub>2</sub> instead of CaC<sub>2</sub> in the first step

0.2 mol: 6.4 g ÷ 64 g/mol = 0.1 mol CaC<sub>2</sub>, giving 0.1 mol C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>2</sub> (1:1 stoichiometry); combustion of C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>2</sub> gives 2 mol CO<sub>2</sub> per mol ethyne, so 0.1 × 2 = 0.2 mol CO<sub>2</sub>
questions.explanation: Moles CaC<sub>2</sub> = 6.4 g / 64 g/mol = 0.1 mol. By the 1:1 stoichiometry of CaC<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O → Ca(OH)<sub>2</sub> + C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>2</sub>, this gives 0.1 mol C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>2</sub>. Complete combustion: C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>2</sub> + 5/2 O<sub>2</sub> → 2CO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O, so each mole of ethyne gives 2 moles CO<sub>2</sub> (2 carbons per molecule). Total CO<sub>2</sub> = 0.1 × 2 = 0.2 mol.
questions.hint: Work in two clean stages: first find moles of ethyne from the carbide reaction, then use ethyne's own carbon count for the combustion step.
distractor_logic: 6.4 g ÷ 64 g/mol correctly gives 0.1 mol CaC<sub>2</sub>, not 0.4 mol; recheck the division.
This correctly finds 0.1 mol ethyne but forgets that each ethyne molecule contains TWO carbon atoms, so complete combustion gives 2 mol CO<sub>2</sub> per mol ethyne, not 1 mol.

The molar mass of CaC<sub>2</sub> (64 g/mol, as given) must be used for the first step's mole calculation, not the molar mass of CO<sub>2</sub> (44 g/mol), which is irrelevant until the final combustion stoichiometry step.

questions.topic: Alkenes: Markovnikov's Rule and Peroxide Effect
questions.question: Rank the following three carbocation/radical intermediates by DECREASING stability, and identify which one is formed as the key intermediate when HBr adds to propene WITHOUT peroxide: (i) a 2° carbocation, (ii) a 2° free radical, (iii) a 1° carbocation.
options: Stability order: 2° carbocation (i) ≈ 2° radical (ii), both more stable than 1° carbocation (iii) due to hyperconjugation/inductive donation from adjacent alkyl groups; WITHOUT peroxide, the ionic mechanism operates, so the key intermediate is the 2° CARBOCATION (i)
Without peroxide, a 2° free radical (ii) is always the key intermediate, since radicals are inherently more stable than any carbocation
The 1° carbocation (iii) is always the most stable and is the key intermediate regardless of peroxide
All three intermediates are equally stable, so Markovnikov's rule cannot be explained by intermediate stability at all
questions.explanation: Both carbocations and radicals are stabilised by adjacent alkyl groups via hyperconjugation and induction, so more-substituted (2° > 1°) versions of EITHER species are more stable than their less-substituted counterparts. Without peroxide, HBr adds to propene via the standard ionic (Markovnikov) mechanism: H<sup>+</sup> adds to the terminal carbon, generating the more stable 2° carbocation at C2, which Br<sup>−</sup> then captures — giving 2-bromopropane. The radical pathway (which would instead form via Br• addition, giving a 2° radical) only becomes dominant when peroxide is present to initiate the radical chain.
questions.hint: Without peroxide present, which type of mechanism (ionic or radical) is operative for simple alkene + HX addition?
distractor_logic: Without peroxide, the mechanism is ionic (via a carbocation), not radical; a free radical intermediate only becomes relevant when peroxide initiates a radical chain mechanism specifically for HBr addition.
The 1° carbocation is the LEAST stable of the three options listed (least alkyl substitution to hyperconjugatively stabilise the positive charge), not the most stable; it is not the key intermediate.

The three intermediates are NOT equally stable; substitution level (1° vs. 2°) and intermediate type (radical vs. cation) both affect relative stability, which is precisely the basis for both Markovnikov's rule and the peroxide effect.
mixed_topics: Alkenes: Markovnikov's Rule and Peroxide Effect

questions.topic: Alkenes: Markovnikov's Rule and Peroxide Effect
questions.question: 2-Methylpropene ((CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C=CH<sub>2</sub>) is treated with HBr both with and without peroxide. Predict the major product in EACH case and explain why this particular substrate gives an especially large regiochemical contrast between the two conditions.
options: Without peroxide gives isobutyl bromide; with peroxide gives tert-butyl bromide (the reverse of the correct assignment)
Peroxide has no effect on this particular alkene because it is not a terminal alkene

Without peroxide (Markovnikov, ionic): tert-butyl bromide (Br on the more substituted C, via the highly stable 3° carbocation); WITH peroxide (anti-Markovnikov, radical): isobutyl bromide (Br on the terminal CH<sub>2</sub>, via the 3° radical formed by Br• adding to the LESS hindered terminal carbon) — the contrast is especially stark because the substrate can access BOTH an unusually stable 3° cation AND a 3° radical, just on opposite carbons depending on mechanism
Both conditions give the identical product, tert-butyl bromide, since Markovnikov's rule is unaffected by peroxide for this substrate
questions.explanation: Without peroxide (ionic): H<sup>+</sup> adds to the terminal =CH<sub>2</sub>, generating the highly stable 3° carbocation at the central carbon; Br<sup>−</sup> captures it, giving tert-butyl bromide, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>CBr. With peroxide (radical): Br• adds FIRST, to the LESS hindered terminal carbon (giving the more stable 3° radical on the central carbon), and this radical then abstracts H from H−Br, placing Br on the terminal carbon instead — giving isobutyl bromide, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CH−CH<sub>2</sub>Br. Both mechanisms independently favour forming the more stable 3° intermediate (cation or radical), but since Br adds FIRST in the radical case (opposite order to H adding first in the ionic case), the final position of Br ends up reversed between the two conditions.
questions.hint: In each mechanism, ask which atom (H or Br) adds to the alkene FIRST, since that determines where the resulting stabilised intermediate (cation or radical) sits.
distractor_logic: This has the assignment backwards; tert-butyl bromide is the product WITHOUT peroxide (ionic, Markovnikov) and isobutyl bromide is the product WITH peroxide (radical, anti-Markovnikov), not the reverse.

Peroxide fundamentally changes which species (H<sup>+</sup> or Br•) adds first to the double bond, which reverses the final position of Br in the product; the two conditions do NOT give the same product for this substrate.

This IS a terminal alkene (2-methylpropene has a terminal =CH<sub>2</sub>), and the peroxide effect specifically requires and applies to terminal (or otherwise unsymmetrical) alkenes like this one to show a regiochemical difference.
mixed_topics: Alkenes: Markovnikov's Rule and Peroxide Effect

questions.topic: Alkenes: Markovnikov's Rule and Peroxide Effect
questions.question: Propyne is treated with HBr in the presence of peroxide (anti-Markovnikov conditions extend to alkynes too). Predict the major product, tracking the radical mechanism through the FIRST addition only.
options: Peroxide has no effect on alkyne + HBr addition, only on alkenes

1-Bromopropene (CH<sub>3</sub>−CH=CHBr, with Br on the terminal carbon C1): Br• adds to the terminal carbon (C1, less hindered), generating the more stable vinylic/allylic-adjacent radical at C2, which then abstracts H from HBr
2-Bromopropene forms, with Br on the internal carbon, matching standard Markovnikov addition regardless of peroxide
The triple bond is completely unreactive toward HBr under any conditions
questions.explanation: Just as with alkenes, peroxide generates Br• radicals that add to the LESS hindered (terminal) carbon of propyne's triple bond, HC≡C−CH<sub>3</sub>, placing the resulting vinyl radical on the more substituted internal carbon (C2, stabilised by the adjacent methyl); this radical then abstracts H from H−Br to complete the addition, giving 1-bromopropene with Br on the terminal carbon (C1) — the anti-Markovnikov regiochemistry, analogous to the alkene case.
questions.hint: Apply the same peroxide-effect logic used for alkenes (Br• adds to the less hindered carbon first) to this alkyne.
distractor_logic: 2-Bromopropene (Br on the internal carbon) would be the Markovnikov (non-peroxide) product; peroxide specifically reverses this regiochemistry, giving the anti-Markovnikov 1-bromopropene instead.
The peroxide (anti-Markovnikov) effect is documented for alkynes as well as alkenes in the NCERT syllabus, particularly for HBr addition; it is not restricted to alkenes only.

Alkynes readily undergo HBr addition (both with and without peroxide, following Markovnikov and anti-Markovnikov regiochemistry respectively); the triple bond is a reactive site for electrophilic/radical addition, not inert.
mixed_topics: Alkenes: Markovnikov's Rule and Peroxide Effect

questions.topic: Alkenes: Markovnikov's Rule and Peroxide Effect
questions.question: A chemist wants to synthesise 1-bromopentane specifically (a purely terminal, 1° bromide) starting from pent-1-ene. Which single reagent condition achieves this cleanly, and why would the OTHER standard condition fail to give this specific product?
options: Neither condition can give a terminal bromide from a terminal alkene under any circumstances
HBr without peroxide gives 1-bromopentane directly, since Markovnikov's rule always favours the terminal carbon
Peroxide has no bearing on which carbon receives the bromine atom in this reaction

HBr WITH peroxide (anti-Markovnikov): Br• adds to the terminal, less hindered C1, generating the more stable 2° radical at C2, giving 1-bromopentane; HBr WITHOUT peroxide (Markovnikov) would instead give 2-bromopentane (Br on the internal, more substituted carbon, via the more stable 2° carbocation), which is the WRONG regiochemistry for this specific target
questions.explanation: Pent-1-ene, CH<sub>2</sub>=CH−CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, under standard Markovnikov (no peroxide) HBr addition, gives 2-bromopentane (Br on the internal C2, via the more stable 2° carbocation). To specifically obtain the terminal 1-bromopentane, the anti-Markovnikov (peroxide) pathway must be used: Br• adds to the terminal C1 (less hindered, and placing the resulting radical on the more stable, more substituted C2), and that C2 radical then abstracts H from HBr, giving Br specifically at C1.
questions.hint: First work out what the NON-peroxide (Markovnikov) product would be, then determine which condition is needed to get the OPPOSITE regiochemistry.
distractor_logic: A terminal bromide CAN be obtained from a terminal alkene, specifically via the anti-Markovnikov (peroxide-catalysed) pathway; this is a standard, well-established synthetic strategy.
Peroxide fundamentally changes the regiochemical outcome of HBr addition (by switching the mechanism from ionic to radical), directly determining which carbon receives the bromine.

This has Markovnikov's rule backwards for this purpose; without peroxide, Markovnikov addition places Br on the MORE substituted (internal, C2) carbon, giving 2-bromopentane, not the terminal 1-bromopentane.
