questions.topic: Alkenes: Markovnikov's Rule and Peroxide Effect
questions.question: Explain, at the level of peroxide DECOMPOSITION chemistry, how a small amount of peroxide (R−O−O−R) is able to initiate a radical CHAIN reaction that consumes a much larger amount of alkene and HBr, rather than being consumed stoichiometrically itself.
options: Radical chain reactions require continuous re-addition of fresh peroxide throughout the reaction to sustain each propagation step

Peroxide's weak O−O bond homolyses (with heat or light) to give two RO• radicals, each of which abstracts H from HBr to generate Br•; this Br• then enters a self-sustaining PROPAGATION cycle (Br• + alkene → C-radical; C-radical + HBr → product + new Br•) that regenerates Br• at the end of every cycle, so one initiation event can drive many propagation cycles before termination
Peroxide is consumed in a 1:1 stoichiometric ratio with the alkene, just like any other reagent, and does not act catalytically
The peroxide directly adds across the double bond as a whole molecule, without ever breaking into radical fragments
questions.explanation: Peroxide's relatively weak O−O bond (BDE around 150 kJ/mol, much weaker than typical C−C or C−H bonds) homolyses readily upon mild heating or light to give two alkoxy radicals (RO•); each RO• abstracts a hydrogen from HBr (forming ROH and generating Br•). This Br• then enters the PROPAGATION cycle: it adds to the alkene (forming a stabilised carbon radical), which then abstracts H from another HBr molecule (forming the product and regenerating Br•) — this cycle repeats itself many times ('chain' reaction) from just the initial Br• generated, consuming alkene and HBr while requiring only a small, catalytic amount of the original peroxide to get started.
questions.hint: Distinguish the INITIATION step (which consumes peroxide, just once) from the PROPAGATION cycle (which repeats many times and regenerates the chain-carrying radical each time).
distractor_logic: Peroxide acts catalytically (in small, sub-stoichiometric amounts) precisely because it only INITIATES the chain; the bulk of alkene and HBr consumption happens in the self-sustaining propagation cycle, not via direct 1:1 reaction with peroxide.
Peroxide's O−O bond specifically homolyses into two radical fragments (RO•) as the initiation step; it does not add intact as a whole molecule across the double bond.

The defining feature of a chain reaction is that propagation steps repeat many times from a SINGLE initiation event, regenerating the chain-carrying radical (Br•) at the end of each cycle, without needing continuous fresh peroxide input.

questions.topic: Alkenes: Markovnikov's Rule and Peroxide Effect
questions.question: Both the peroxide effect (HBr + alkene, radical, anti-Markovnikov) and standard aromatic bromination (Br<sub>2</sub>/FeBr<sub>3</sub>, ionic, electrophilic substitution) involve bromine ending up on a carbon skeleton, but via fundamentally different initiating species. Contrast HOW bromine is delivered as the active species in each case.
options: In the peroxide effect, the active species is a Br RADICAL (Br•, generated via peroxide-mediated homolysis of H−Br), which adds to a π bond via a radical mechanism; in aromatic bromination, the active species is a Br CATION-like electrophile (Br<sup>+</sup> equivalent, generated by FeBr<sub>3</sub> polarising Br<sub>2</sub>), which attacks the ring via an ionic (electrophilic aromatic substitution) mechanism
Aromatic bromination uses a radical Br• species, while the peroxide effect uses an ionic Br<sup>+</sup> species (the reverse of the correct pairing)
Neither reaction actually involves elemental or radical bromine at any stage; both proceed via a completely different halogen source
Both reactions use exactly the same active bromine species (Br<sub>2</sub> itself, unmodified) and the same mechanism
questions.explanation: The peroxide effect on alkenes proceeds via a RADICAL chain: peroxide homolysis ultimately generates Br•, a neutral radical, which adds to the alkene's π bond. Aromatic bromination instead requires a Lewis acid catalyst (FeBr<sub>3</sub>) to polarise Br<sub>2</sub>, generating an electrophilic, partially cationic bromine species (effectively Br<sup>+</sup>, or a Br<sub>2</sub>·FeBr<sub>3</sub> polarised complex) that is attacked by the ring's π electron cloud in an ionic electrophilic aromatic substitution mechanism. Same halogen (Br), but two entirely different 'flavours' of reactive bromine species (neutral radical vs. electrophilic/cationic), reflecting the different mechanisms each substrate favours.
questions.hint: Ask what CHARGE (if any) and what TYPE of species (radical vs. ion) the reactive bromine intermediate carries in each named reaction.
distractor_logic: This reverses the correct pairing; the peroxide effect involves a RADICAL Br• species (from HBr), while aromatic bromination involves an ionic, electrophilic Br species (from Br<sub>2</sub>/FeBr<sub>3</sub>), not the other way around.

Both reactions genuinely do involve a bromine-based reactive species at their core (Br• in one case, an electrophilic brominating species derived from Br<sub>2</sub> in the other); the claim that neither involves bromine is incorrect.

The two reactions use different bromine sources under different conditions (HBr + peroxide-generated radical vs. Br<sub>2</sub> + Lewis-acid-generated electrophile) and proceed via different mechanisms; they are not identical.

questions.topic: Alkenes: Markovnikov's Rule and Peroxide Effect
questions.question: 2-Methylbut-2-ene, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C=CH−CH<sub>3</sub>, is treated with HCl (no peroxide effect applies to HCl, so only the standard ionic mechanism is relevant here). Between the two possible carbocation intermediates (3° at the more substituted carbon vs. 2° at the less substituted carbon), which forms preferentially, and what is the resulting major product?
options: The 2° carbocation forms preferentially since it has fewer steric clashes, giving 3-chloro-2-methylbutane as major product
Both carbocations are equally stable, so a 1:1 mixture of products forms
This alkene cannot react with HCl at all since HCl doesn't show the peroxide effect

The 3° carbocation (at the carbon bearing two methyl groups) forms preferentially, since it is more stabilised by hyperconjugation/induction from three attached alkyl groups (two methyls + the chain) than the alternative 2° cation; Cl<sup>−</sup> then captures this 3° cation, giving 2-chloro-2-methylbutane as the major product
questions.explanation: Protonation of 2-methylbut-2-ene at the terminal =CH<sub>2</sub>-equivalent (the CH<sub>3</sub>-bearing carbon, C3) would give a less stable 2° cation at C2; protonation at C2 instead would place H there and generate a 3° cation at C3 (bearing two methyl substituents). Since the 3° cation is significantly more stable (three alkyl groups providing hyperconjugative/inductive stabilisation, versus two for the 2° alternative), Markovnikov's rule (H adds to give the more stable cation) directs H to add such that the 3° cation forms; Cl<sup>−</sup> then captures it, giving 2-chloro-2-methylbutane as the major product. HCl does NOT show a peroxide effect (that anomaly is specific to HBr), so this straightforward ionic Markovnikov analysis applies regardless of any peroxide present.
questions.hint: Work out which protonation site leads to a 3° cation and which leads to a 2° cation, then apply the more-substituted-cation-is-more-stable rule.
distractor_logic: This gets the stability comparison backwards; the 3° cation (more alkyl substitution) is MORE stable than the 2° cation, not less, and 'fewer steric clashes' is not the deciding factor for carbocation stability — electronic stabilisation (hyperconjugation/induction) is.

Carbocation stability differs meaningfully between 2° and 3° cations (3° is substantially more stable), so the reaction is NOT expected to give a roughly equal mixture; one pathway strongly dominates.

HCl reacts perfectly normally with alkenes via the standard ionic Markovnikov mechanism; the ABSENCE of a peroxide effect for HCl doesn't mean HCl fails to react — it just means the reaction proceeds via the usual ionic (not radical) pathway regardless of whether peroxide is present.

questions.topic: Alkenes: Markovnikov's Rule and Peroxide Effect
questions.question: But-1-yne is treated with 1 equivalent of HBr in the presence of peroxide, giving an intermediate bromoalkene. This bromoalkene is then treated with NaNH<sub>2</sub> (a strong base capable of eliminating HBr, E2-type, to regenerate an alkyne). What is the final product, and does it match the STARTING alkyne?
options: The first step gives 2-bromobut-1-ene, and elimination gives but-2-yne, a different alkyne from the start

First step (peroxide, anti-Markovnikov): 1-bromobut-1-ene (Br on the terminal carbon, from Br• adding to the less hindered terminal position); second step (E2 elimination of HBr by strong base): regenerates but-1-yne, the SAME starting alkyne, since elimination removes H and Br from the same two carbons where they were added
NaNH<sub>2</sub> cannot perform any elimination reaction on a vinyl halide
Peroxide has no effect on alkynes, so the first step simply fails to react
questions.explanation: Peroxide-catalysed (anti-Markovnikov) HBr addition to but-1-yne, HC≡C−CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, places Br on the terminal carbon (C1) via the same less-hindered-carbon-first radical logic used for alkenes, giving 1-bromobut-1-ene, BrCH=CH−CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>. Treating this vinyl bromide with a strong base like NaNH<sub>2</sub> promotes E2-type elimination of H (from the adjacent carbon) and Br, reforming the triple bond at the SAME position — regenerating but-1-yne, the original starting material, illustrating that this particular addition/elimination sequence is 'reversible' in net effect (though not literally the same mechanistic steps in reverse).
questions.hint: Track exactly which carbon receives Br in the peroxide-catalysed addition, then ask what happens when H and Br are eliminated from adjacent carbons.
distractor_logic: This misassigns the regiochemistry of the peroxide-catalysed addition; anti-Markovnikov addition places Br on the terminal (less hindered) carbon, giving 1-bromobut-1-ene, not 2-bromobut-1-ene, so the elimination product traces back to but-1-yne, not but-2-yne.

NaNH<sub>2</sub> is a strong, sterically small base well-suited to promoting E2 elimination even on vinyl halides (forming an alkyne by removing H and X from adjacent sp<sup>2</sup> carbons); this is a standard method for alkyne synthesis from vicinal or vinyl dihalides.
The peroxide (anti-Markovnikov) effect is documented to extend to alkyne + HBr addition in the NCERT syllabus; the first step does proceed and does give a bromoalkene product.

questions.question: Isobutylbenzene's side chain, −CH<sub>2</sub>−CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>, attached to a benzene ring, is subjected to radical bromination (Br<sub>2</sub>, hν, high selectivity). Considering that BENZYLIC C−H bonds (adjacent to an aromatic ring) have unusually LOW bond dissociation energy (the resulting benzylic radical is resonance-stabilised by the ring, similar to how an allylic radical is stabilised by an adjacent double bond), which hydrogen is abstracted preferentially?
options: Radical bromination cannot occur on any carbon adjacent to a benzene ring due to the ring's electron-withdrawing effect

The benzylic CH<sub>2</sub> hydrogens (directly attached to the ring) are abstracted preferentially, since the resulting radical is stabilised by resonance delocalisation into the aromatic ring, giving a lower-BDE, more easily formed, and more stable radical than at any other position in the side chain
All hydrogens in the side chain are equally reactive since BDE is not affected by proximity to an aromatic ring
The 3° hydrogen on the isopropyl-like CH is always preferred, regardless of the ring's presence, since 3° radicals are inherently the most stable in ALL molecules
questions.explanation: Benzylic C−H bonds are especially weak (low BDE) because the resulting benzylic radical's unpaired electron can delocalise into the aromatic ring's π system via resonance (analogous to allylic stabilisation next to a C=C), making it even more stable than an ordinary 3° alkyl radical in many cases. In isobutylbenzene, Ph−CH<sub>2</sub>−CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>, this means the benzylic CH<sub>2</sub> (directly bonded to the ring, though only 2° by simple substitution count) is actually MORE reactive toward radical bromination than the isopropyl-like 3° C−H further down the chain, because resonance stabilisation (benzylic) typically outweighs simple hyperconjugative stabilisation (ordinary 3°).
questions.hint: Compare stabilisation by simple hyperconjugation (ordinary 3° radical) against stabilisation by RESONANCE into an aromatic ring (benzylic radical) — which is generally the stronger effect?
distractor_logic: Benzene rings do not universally deactivate adjacent aliphatic C−H bonds toward radical reactions; in fact, the ring specifically STABILISES an adjacent (benzylic) radical via resonance, making that position especially reactive, not unreactive.

This ignores benzylic stabilisation entirely; being 3° by substitution count is not the only factor, and a benzylic (resonance-stabilised) position, even if only 2°, is typically MORE reactive than an ordinary 3° position without ring stabilisation.

BDE at the benzylic position is measurably LOWER than at ordinary 2°/3° alkyl positions specifically because of the adjacent aromatic ring's resonance stabilisation of the resulting radical; proximity to the ring is chemically significant, not irrelevant.

questions.question: 2-Methylbut-2-ene is subjected to ALLYLIC bromination using N-bromosuccinimide (NBS, which maintains a very low, steady-state Br<sub>2</sub> concentration, favouring radical substitution at allylic C−H over ionic addition across the double bond). Identify the allylic position(s) and explain why NBS conditions favour SUBSTITUTION here rather than the ADDITION that plain Br<sub>2</sub> would favour.
options: NBS reacts only at the double bond itself via simple addition, identical to plain Br<sub>2</sub>, with no allylic selectivity
Allylic bromination with NBS always gives a completely different, non-selective mixture of every possible C−H position in the molecule
There are no allylic hydrogens in this molecule since it has no sp<sup>3</sup> carbons directly bonded to the alkene

The allylic positions are the two methyls on the trisubstituted alkene carbon AND the CH<sub>3</sub> on the other alkene carbon (all three are allylic, i.e., attached directly to an sp<sup>2</sub> alkene carbon); NBS's low, steady Br<sub>2</sub> concentration disfavours the bimolecular ADDITION pathway (which needs a higher effective Br<sub>2</sub> concentration to compete kinetically) while still supplying enough Br• via a radical chain to abstract the weak allylic C−H and favour SUBSTITUTION
questions.explanation: In 2-methylbut-2-ene, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C=CH−CH<sub>3</sub>, all three methyl groups attached directly to the two sp<sup>2</sup> alkene carbons are allylic positions (their C−H bonds are weakened by resonance stabilisation of the resulting allylic radical, which delocalises the unpaired electron onto the adjacent alkene carbon). NBS is specifically used to keep the effective Br<sub>2</sub> concentration very low (Br<sub>2</sub> is generated slowly in situ, reacting with the HBr byproduct as it forms), which favours the radical SUBSTITUTION pathway (which only needs a trace of Br• to sustain a chain) over the competing ionic ADDITION pathway (which requires a meaningfully higher Br<sub>2</sub> concentration to proceed at a useful rate) — this is the classic NCERT-adjacent rationale for NBS's role in selective allylic bromination.
questions.hint: Identify every C−H bond directly attached to one of the two double-bond carbons, then think about why a LOW steady-state halogen concentration favours the radical chain (substitution) pathway over ionic addition.
distractor_logic: This molecule does have allylic hydrogens; all three methyl groups (two on the trisubstituted carbon, one on the disubstituted carbon) are directly bonded to an alkene sp<sup>2</sup> carbon and are therefore allylic.

NBS-mediated allylic bromination is selective (favouring the weakest, most resonance-stabilised allylic C−H bonds specifically), not a non-selective free-for-all across every C−H bond in the molecule.

NBS is specifically chosen BECAUSE it does NOT simply mimic plain Br<sub>2</sub>'s addition chemistry; its low steady-state Br<sub>2</sub> concentration is exactly what shifts the reaction toward allylic substitution instead.

questions.question: 2,3-Dimethylbutane is monochlorinated (Cl<sub>2</sub>, hν) and, separately, monobrominated (Br<sub>2</sub>, hν). This symmetric molecule has only TWO types of hydrogen: 12 equivalent 1° H's (on the four methyls) and 2 equivalent 3° H's (on the two central CH carbons). Using approximate relative reactivities per H (Cl: 1°:3° ≈ 1:5; Br: 1°:3° ≈ 1:1600), calculate the approximate PERCENTAGE of tertiary product in each halogenation.
options: Chlorination gives 99.6% tertiary product and bromination gives 45%, the reverse of the correct calculation

Chlorination: %3° = (2×5)/(12×1 + 2×5) = 10/22 ≈ 45%; Bromination: %3° = (2×1600)/(12×1 + 2×1600) = 3200/3212 ≈ 99.6% — illustrating that bromination is dramatically more selective for the tertiary product despite the SAME 12:2 statistical ratio of hydrogens in both cases
Since there are more 1° hydrogens, the majority product must always be the primary chloride/bromide in both cases
Both reactions give exactly the same percentage of tertiary product, 2/14 ≈ 14%, since both start from the same statistical hydrogen ratio
questions.explanation: Using count × relative rate for each type: Chlorination: 1° contribution = 12×1 = 12; 3° contribution = 2×5 = 10; %3° = 10/(12+10) = 10/22 ≈ 45.5%. Bromination: 1° contribution = 12×1 = 12; 3° contribution = 2×1600 = 3200; %3° = 3200/(12+3200) = 3200/3212 ≈ 99.6%. This dramatically illustrates chlorination's low selectivity (both products form in substantial amounts, roughly 45:55) versus bromination's extremely high selectivity (the tertiary product utterly dominates, >99%), even though the STARTING statistical ratio of hydrogens (12 1° : 2 3°) is identical in both cases — the difference comes entirely from the much larger 1°:3° relative RATE ratio for Br<sub>2</sub> compared to Cl<sub>2</sub>.
questions.hint: Use the formula %(type) = (count × relative rate for that type) / (sum of count×rate over all types), plugging in the given relative rate ratios for each halogen separately.
distractor_logic: Using only the raw statistical hydrogen ratio (ignoring the very different relative RATES for Cl<sub>2</sub> vs. Br<sub>2</sub>) misses the entire point of selectivity differences; the two halogens give very different percentages despite starting from the same H-count ratio.

Even though there are more 1° hydrogens by raw count (12 vs. 2), the much higher per-hydrogen REACTIVITY of the 3° positions (especially pronounced for bromination) can make the tertiary product the majority (or even near-exclusive) product despite being outnumbered statistically.

This swaps the two calculated percentages; bromination (with its much higher 1°:3° rate ratio of 1:1600) is the MORE selective halogen, giving ∼99.6% tertiary product, while chlorination (1:5 ratio) is much LESS selective, giving only ∼45%.

questions.question: Ethylbenzene, Ph−CH<sub>2</sub>−CH<sub>3</sub>, undergoes radical bromination with NBS (allylic/benzylic-selective conditions). It is separately treated with Br<sub>2</sub>/FeBr<sub>3</sub> (ionic, ring-directed electrophilic substitution). Contrast the POSITION where bromination occurs in each case and the underlying reason.
options: Both conditions give bromination at exactly the same position, the ring carbon para to the ethyl group
Ethylbenzene has no reactive site for bromination under either condition since the ring and side chain are both unreactive

NBS (radical, benzylic-selective): Br substitutes at the benzylic CH<sub>2</sub> (side chain, adjacent to the ring), since that C−H bond is the weakest (most resonance-stabilised radical) in the molecule; Br<sub>2</sub>/FeBr<sub>3</sub> (ionic, EAS): Br substitutes on the RING itself (ortho/para to the ethyl group, since −C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub> is an activating, o/p-directing alkyl substituent), a completely different site governed by a completely different mechanism
NBS brominates the ring while Br<sub>2</sub>/FeBr<sub>3</sub> brominates the side chain, the reverse of the correct pairing
questions.explanation: These are two mechanistically and positionally distinct reactions on the same substrate: NBS-mediated radical bromination targets the weakest C−H bond available for H-abstraction, which is the benzylic CH<sub>2</sub> of the ethyl side chain (its radical is resonance-stabilised by the adjacent aromatic ring), giving 1-bromo-1-phenylethane (a side-chain product). Br<sub>2</sub>/FeBr<sub>3</sub>, by contrast, is an ionic electrophilic aromatic substitution that targets the electron-rich RING (activated and directed ortho/para by the ethyl group's inductive/hyperconjugative electron donation), giving ortho- or para-bromoethylbenzene (a ring-substituted product). Same starting material, same halogen, but entirely different reaction site depending on the mechanism/reagent chosen.
questions.hint: Ask which part of the molecule each set of conditions is designed to attack: the weak C−H bond in the side chain (radical logic), or the electron-rich aromatic π system (ionic EAS logic).
distractor_logic: This reverses the correct pairing; NBS (radical, weak-C−H-seeking) attacks the benzylic SIDE CHAIN, while Br<sub>2</sub>/FeBr<sub>3</sub> (ionic, electron-rich-arene-seeking) attacks the RING, not the other way around.

Ethylbenzene has reactive sites for BOTH types of bromination: a weak benzylic C−H bond for radical substitution, and an activated, electron-rich aromatic ring for electrophilic substitution; it is not unreactive toward either.
The two conditions target genuinely different sites (side chain for radical/NBS, ring for ionic/FeBr<sub>3</sub>) due to their different mechanisms; they do not converge on the same position.

questions.question: Pent-2-ene is subjected to ALLYLIC chlorination (using conditions that favour substitution over addition, analogous to NBS for bromination). This alkene has allylic positions on BOTH sides of the double bond (C1 methyl-type H's and C4 CH<sub>2</sub> H's, both adjacent to the C2=C3 double bond). Which side is expected to be MORE reactive, and why?
options: Neither position undergoes allylic substitution since pent-2-ene has no terminal double bond
The C1 (1° allylic, terminal methyl) position is more reactive because primary radicals are always preferred over secondary ones

The C4 side (a CH<sub>2</sub>, i.e. a 2° allylic position) is more reactive than the C1 side (a CH<sub>3</sub>, i.e. a 1° allylic position), since the resulting allylic radical at C4 benefits from BOTH allylic resonance delocalisation AND additional hyperconjugative stabilisation from being a more-substituted (secondary-type) radical carbon, compounding the two stabilising effects
Both allylic positions are exactly equally reactive since allylic resonance stabilisation is the only factor and substitution level doesn't matter once a position is allylic
questions.explanation: Pent-2-ene, CH<sub>3</sub>−CH=CH−CH<sub>2</sub>−CH<sub>3</sub>, has allylic C−H's at both C1 (the CH<sub>3</sub> attached to C2) and C4 (the CH<sub>2</sub> attached to C3). Both resulting radicals are allylic (resonance-delocalised over the adjacent former double bond), but the C4-derived radical is ADDITIONALLY a more-substituted (secondary-type) radical carbon (flanked by the C5 methyl), giving it extra hyperconjugative stabilisation on top of the allylic resonance that both positions share — so the two stabilising effects (allylic resonance + degree of substitution) compound, making the C4 (2° allylic) position more reactive than the C1 (1° allylic) position, paralleling ordinary 1°/2°/3° selectivity trends layered on top of the allylic effect.
questions.hint: Allylic resonance stabilisation is common to both positions here; look for an ADDITIONAL factor (substitution level of the resulting radical carbon) that distinguishes C1 from C4.
distractor_logic: This reverses the usual radical stability trend (more substituted radicals are generally MORE, not less, stable, whether allylic or not); the 1° allylic position is not preferred over the 2° allylic position.

Pent-2-ene's internal double bond (between C2 and C3) still creates allylic positions on BOTH adjacent carbons (C1 and C4), even though the double bond itself is not terminal; allylic substitution is not restricted to terminal alkenes.

Allylic resonance is a necessary but not sole factor; the DEGREE of substitution at the radical-bearing carbon (1° vs. 2°-type, beyond just being allylic) provides an additional, compounding stabilisation that differentiates the two allylic positions here.

questions.question: A synthesis target requires selectively brominating ONLY the ring position of p-cymene (4-isopropyltoluene, a benzene ring bearing both −CH<sub>3</sub> and −CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> at para positions), leaving the isopropyl group's own weak tertiary benzylic C−H completely untouched. Which reagent/condition choice correctly achieves this selectively?
options: Both Br<sub>2</sub>/FeBr<sub>3</sub> and NBS give identical product distributions, so the choice of reagent doesn't matter for this selectivity problem
No reagent can distinguish between ring and side-chain bromination in this molecule

Br<sub>2</sub>/FeBr<sub>3</sub> (ionic electrophilic aromatic substitution) selectively targets the electron-rich RING (activated by both alkyl substituents, directed to the positions ortho to each group), since this ionic mechanism has no pathway for radical benzylic C−H abstraction at all; using NBS or Br<sub>2</sub>/hν instead would risk competing benzylic substitution at the reactive tertiary isopropyl C−H
NBS is the correct choice for ring-selective bromination, since NBS never reacts at benzylic positions
questions.explanation: Br<sub>2</sub>/FeBr<sub>3</sub> operates via a purely IONIC electrophilic aromatic substitution mechanism (Lewis acid activates Br<sub>2</sub> into an electrophile, attacked by the ring's π electrons) — this pathway has no mechanistic route to abstract a benzylic C−H, so it cleanly and selectively substitutes on the ring. By contrast, NBS/radical conditions are specifically designed to generate a LOW, steady Br<sub>2</sub> concentration that favours radical benzylic/allylic C−H abstraction (and here, the tertiary benzylic C−H of the isopropyl group would be a prime, highly reactive target) OVER ring substitution — so NBS would be the WRONG choice if ring selectivity, not side-chain selectivity, is the actual synthetic goal.
questions.hint: Match the reagent to the mechanism it operates by: does ionic EAS have any pathway to abstract a C−H bond at all?
distractor_logic: Reagent/mechanism choice is precisely how such selectivity problems are solved in practice; an ionic electrophile (Br<sub>2</sub>/FeBr<sub>3</sub>) simply has no mechanistic pathway available to abstract a benzylic hydrogen, making it inherently ring-selective here.

The two reagents operate via fundamentally different mechanisms (ionic EAS vs. radical chain), targeting different sites (ring vs. benzylic C−H respectively), and do NOT give the same product distribution.
This has the reagent choice backwards for this specific goal; NBS is specifically designed to favour radical BENZYLIC/side-chain substitution, which is exactly what the synthesis needs to AVOID here.

questions.question: 3-Methylpent-2-ene is subjected to allylic bromination with NBS. Identify ALL distinct allylic C−H environments available (there is more than one), and predict which gives the major product based on the resulting radical's stability.
options: Two distinct allylic environments exist: the C1 methyl (attached to C2, a 1° allylic position) and the C4−H<sub>2</sub> (attached to C3, also giving an allylic radical, but one that is additionally stabilised since C3 already bears an ethyl-chain substituent); the C4 position gives the more stabilised (allylic + more substituted) radical and is the major site of substitution
There is only one allylic position in this molecule, so no comparison is needed
Allylic bromination is not possible on trisubstituted alkenes like this one
The C5 methyl (at the far end of the ethyl-like chain, two carbons removed from the double bond) is the most reactive site, since it is the most remote from steric hindrance
questions.explanation: 3-Methylpent-2-ene, CH<sub>3</sub>−CH=C(CH<sub>3</sub>)−CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, has its double bond between C2 and C3. Allylic positions are C1 (the CH<sub>3</sub> on C2) and C4 (the CH<sub>2</sub> on C3, part of the ethyl group) — both directly attached to an alkene carbon. (The methyl branch on C3 itself is technically also allylic but chemically equivalent in outcome-type to analysing C4 vs C1 for this comparison; the clearest major/minor contrast is between C1, giving a 1°-type allylic radical, and C4, giving a radical that is allylic AND flanked by an additional alkyl group (C5 methyl) for extra hyperconjugative stabilisation) — so C4 gives the more stabilised radical and is expected to dominate as the major substitution site.
questions.hint: Locate the double bond first (between which two carbons), then identify every C−H directly attached to either of those two carbons as a candidate allylic position.
distractor_logic: This molecule has multiple allylic C−H environments (at minimum C1 and C4, both directly attached to a double-bond carbon), not just one; a comparison between them is both possible and necessary to predict the major product.

The C5 position is NOT allylic (it is one carbon further removed from the double bond than C4, i.e., homoallylic), so its C−H bonds are not specially weakened by allylic resonance and would not be the preferred site of radical substitution.

Allylic bromination works perfectly well on trisubstituted (or any substitution pattern of) alkenes; the degree of substitution AT the double bond doesn't prevent radical abstraction from an adjacent (allylic) carbon.

questions.question: Toluene is subjected to (a) radical chlorination (Cl<sub>2</sub>, hν, high temperature or UV, favouring the weak benzylic C−H) to give benzyl chloride, and separately (b) ionic chlorination (Cl<sub>2</sub>/FeCl<sub>3</sub>, dark, room temperature, favouring ring EAS) to give a mixture of ortho- and para-chlorotoluene. What experimental condition differences (beyond just the catalyst) typically distinguish these two pathways, and why?
options: Temperature, light, and catalyst have no bearing on which pathway (benzylic vs. ring) dominates; the product ratio is fixed regardless of conditions

Radical (benzylic) chlorination is favoured by conditions that generate Cl• radicals — UV light or high heat, and the ABSENCE of a Lewis acid catalyst (which would instead promote the competing ionic ring pathway); ionic (ring) chlorination is favoured by a Lewis acid catalyst (FeCl<sub>3</sub>) in the dark/at room temperature, where no radical initiation occurs, so the ionic EAS pathway dominates instead
Radical chlorination requires FeCl<sub>3</sub>, while ionic chlorination requires UV light, the reverse of the correct pairing
Both reactions require identical conditions (UV light plus FeCl<sub>3</sub>) and the product distribution is purely random
questions.explanation: These two reaction pathways are controlled by choosing conditions that favour one mechanism's initiation over the other's: radical chlorination needs a way to generate Cl• (UV light or heat promoting Cl<sub>2</sub> homolysis) and is typically run WITHOUT a Lewis acid (which would otherwise activate Cl<sub>2</sub> for the competing ionic pathway instead), giving benzylic substitution via the resonance-stabilised benzylic radical. Ionic (ring) chlorination instead requires a Lewis acid catalyst (FeCl<sub>3</sub>) to polarise Cl<sub>2</sub> into an electrophile, and is typically run in the dark/at moderate temperature (where radical initiation is minimal), directing substitution onto the ring (ortho/para, since −CH<sub>3</sub> is o/p-directing and activating). This is a classic illustration of how reaction CONDITIONS (not just the identity of the reagent, Cl<sub>2</sub>, which is the same in both cases) determine which of two competing mechanisms dominates.
questions.hint: Ask what specifically INITIATES each mechanism (Cl• generation for radical vs. Lewis acid activation for ionic), and what conditions promote or suppress each initiation pathway.
distractor_logic: This reverses the correct pairing; radical (benzylic) chlorination is favoured by UV light/heat WITHOUT a Lewis acid, while ionic (ring) chlorination is favoured by a Lewis acid catalyst (FeCl<sub>3</sub>) typically without light, not the other way around.

The two pathways are deliberately run under DIFFERENT, mechanism-specific conditions (light/heat without Lewis acid for radical; Lewis acid without light for ionic) precisely to control which product dominates; the outcome is not random.

Reaction conditions (light, heat, presence/absence of Lewis acid catalyst) are precisely what allow a chemist to steer this same Cl<sub>2</sub>/toluene system toward either the benzylic or the ring product selectively; they are not irrelevant to the outcome.

questions.question: <svg viewBox="0 0 300 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:100%;height:auto"><line x1="150.0" y1="45.0" x2="193.3" y2="70.0" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="152.6" y1="54.6" x2="183.7" y2="72.6" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="193.3" y1="70.0" x2="193.3" y2="120.0" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="193.3" y1="120.0" x2="150.0" y2="145.0" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="183.7" y1="117.4" x2="152.6" y2="135.4" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="150.0" y1="145.0" x2="106.7" y2="120.0" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="106.7" y1="120.0" x2="106.7" y2="70.0" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="113.7" y1="113.0" x2="113.7" y2="77.0" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="106.7" y1="70.0" x2="150.0" y2="45.0" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="150.0" y1="45.0" x2="150.0" y2="17.0" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><text x="150.0" y="5.0" font-size="15" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle">OCH₃</text></svg> Anisole (methoxybenzene, shown above) is nitrated. −OCH<sub>3</sub> is a POWERFUL activator and o,p-director, even more strongly activating than a simple alkyl group. Explain this using BOTH resonance and inductive reasoning, and state which effect dominates.
options: Oxygen's lone pair is donated into the ring by RESONANCE at the ortho/para positions, strongly stabilising the arenium intermediate there (o,p-directing, strongly activating overall); oxygen's electronegativity DOES withdraw electron density inductively, but this inductive withdrawal is comparatively weak (through only one intervening bond to the ring) and is heavily outweighed by the strong resonance donation, so the NET effect is strong activation
−OCH<sub>3</sub> only withdraws electron density (both by induction and resonance), making it a deactivating, meta-directing group, similar to −NO<sub>2</sub>
Alkyl groups are always more strongly activating than −OCH<sub>3</sub>, since oxygen is electronegative and must dominate
−OCH<sub>3</sub> has no measurable resonance effect at all; its o,p-directing behaviour is purely inductive
questions.explanation: Oxygen in −OCH<sub>3</sub> has lone pairs that can be donated into the ring's π system by resonance (drawing additional resonance structures placing negative charge specifically at the ortho and para positions when the ring is attacked there), which is a strong, ring-activating, o,p-directing effect. Simultaneously, oxygen's electronegativity does pull σ-electron density away from the ring inductively (a mild deactivating tendency), but because this inductive effect operates over just one bond and is much weaker in magnitude than the resonance donation from the readily available lone pairs, the NET effect for −OCH<sub>3</sub> is strongly activating (much more so than a simple alkyl group like −CH<sub>3</sub>, which only has weaker hyperconjugative/inductive donation and no lone-pair resonance donation at all).
questions.hint: Identify which effect (resonance or induction) −OCH<sub>3</sub> can exert MORE strongly, given that oxygen has lone pairs available for donation into the ring.
distractor_logic: This is the behaviour of a group like −NO<sub>2</sub> (which withdraws by BOTH resonance and induction), not −OCH<sub>3</sub>; oxygen's lone pair donation by resonance is a strong ACTIVATING, not deactivating, effect.

−OCH<sub>3</sub>'s resonance donation (via oxygen's lone pairs into the ring) is in fact its DOMINANT electronic effect, responsible for its strong activation and o,p-directing behaviour; it is not purely inductive.

Because −OCH<sub>3</sub> can additionally donate by resonance (which simple alkyl groups cannot, having no lone pair to donate), it is typically MORE strongly activating than a simple alkyl group like −CH<sub>3</sub>, not less.

questions.question: <svg viewBox="0 0 300 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:100%;height:auto"><line x1="150.0" y1="45.0" x2="193.3" y2="70.0" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="152.6" y1="54.6" x2="183.7" y2="72.6" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="193.3" y1="70.0" x2="193.3" y2="120.0" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="193.3" y1="120.0" x2="150.0" y2="145.0" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="183.7" y1="117.4" x2="152.6" y2="135.4" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="150.0" y1="145.0" x2="106.7" y2="120.0" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="106.7" y1="120.0" x2="106.7" y2="70.0" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="113.7" y1="113.0" x2="113.7" y2="77.0" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="106.7" y1="70.0" x2="150.0" y2="45.0" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="150.0" y1="45.0" x2="150.0" y2="17.0" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><text x="150.0" y="5.0" font-size="15" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle">CHO</text></svg> Benzaldehyde (shown above, −CHO group) is nitrated. The carbonyl carbon is directly attached to the ring. Explain why −CHO is BOTH deactivating AND meta-directing, using resonance structures of the arenium intermediate for ortho/para vs. meta attack.
options: The carbonyl's oxygen is more electronegative than carbon, pulling electron density away from the carbonyl carbon (and, by extension, the ring) inductively; more importantly, if the electrophile attacks ORTHO or PARA, one resonance structure of the resulting arenium ion places the positive charge directly ON the carbon bearing the electron-poor −CHO group, which is highly destabilising (positive charge next to positive/electron-poor centre); attack at META avoids ever placing the positive charge on that carbon, making meta attack comparatively less destabilised, hence meta-directing overall (though still deactivating relative to benzene itself, since even the meta pathway is slowed by −CHO's inductive withdrawal)
Meta-directing groups are always MORE activating than ortho/para-directing groups, which is why −CHO speeds up the reaction relative to benzene
The carbonyl group donates electron density into the ring by resonance, exactly like −OCH<sub>3</sub>, making it activating and o,p-directing
−CHO has no electronic effect on the ring at all, and its directing behaviour is purely a steric phenomenon
questions.explanation: −CHO is an electron-withdrawing group (the carbonyl oxygen pulls electron density via both induction and resonance, since the carbon can also accept ring electron density into the C=O π* system). When the electrophile attacks ORTHO or PARA to −CHO, one of the resonance contributors to the arenium ion places the positive charge directly on the ring carbon bearing the −CHO group itself — an especially unfavourable arrangement (positive charge adjacent to/on an already electron-poor, carbonyl-bearing carbon). Attack at META avoids this particular destabilised resonance structure entirely, making meta-substitution the relatively favoured (least-bad) pathway, hence −CHO is meta-directing; but because ALL pathways (ortho, meta, AND para) are slowed relative to unsubstituted benzene by −CHO's overall electron-withdrawing character, the group is also deactivating (net rate decrease compared to benzene, even via the 'preferred' meta pathway).
questions.hint: Draw the resonance structures of the arenium ion intermediate for both ortho/para attack and meta attack, and check which set of structures places positive charge in a particularly unfavourable location.
distractor_logic: −CHO withdraws electron density (both inductively via the electronegative oxygen and by accepting ring electrons into the carbonyl's own π system), unlike −OCH<sub>3</sub> which has a lone pair to donate; −CHO is deactivating and meta-directing, the opposite electronic behaviour to −OCH<sub>3</sub>.

−CHO's directing behaviour is fundamentally ELECTRONIC (based on resonance stabilisation/destabilisation of the arenium intermediate at different attack positions), not primarily a steric effect from the group's size.

This is backwards; meta-directing groups (like −CHO, −NO<sub>2</sub>, −COOH) are typically deactivating overall (slower reaction than benzene at ALL positions, including the 'favoured' meta position), not more activating than o,p-directors.

questions.topic: Aromatic Hydrocarbons: Directive Influence of Substituents
questions.question: A disubstituted benzene ring bears both −NH<sub>2</sub> (strongly activating, o,p-directing, at C1) and −NO<sub>2</sub> (strongly deactivating, meta-directing, at C4, i.e. para to −NH<sub>2</sub>). A third electrophilic substitution is to be performed. Since the two existing groups' directing preferences might conflict, which group's influence typically DOMINATES in determining where the new substituent goes, and why?
options: Both groups contribute exactly equally, making the product an exact 50:50 mixture with no preference at all
The deactivating group (−NO<sub>2</sub>) always dominates regardless of what other group is present, since deactivation is described as a 'stronger' effect by definition
Directing effects only apply to monosubstituted rings; disubstituted rings show no positional preference at all for further substitution

The stronger ACTIVATING group (−NH<sub>2</sub>) typically dominates the regiochemistry, since activating groups accelerate attack at their own favoured positions much more strongly than a deactivating group merely disfavours its own meta positions; in general, when one substituent is activating and the other deactivating, the activating group's directing preference (here, ortho to −NH<sub>2</sub>, i.e. C2/C6) controls where reaction preferentially occurs
questions.explanation: When a ring carries both an activating and a deactivating substituent, the general rule (well beyond NCERT-basic level but a natural extension of resonance/inductive reasoning) is that the MORE STRONGLY activating group tends to dominate the directing outcome, because activating groups work by substantially accelerating attack at specific (their own o/p) positions, while deactivating groups work more by slowing down attack everywhere including their own favoured (meta) positions less selectively; here, −NH<sub>2</sub> (very strongly activating via its nitrogen lone pair) would direct new substitution mainly to positions ortho to itself (C2/C6), and this reinforces (or at least is not strongly opposed by) −NO<sub>2</sub>'s own meta-directing preference, since −NO<sub>2</sub> at C4 also directs meta to itself, which happens to include C2/C6 as well in this specific 1,4-relationship — both groups' preferences actually agree here on C2/C6 being favoured.
questions.hint: Compare the relative STRENGTH of activation vs. deactivation, and check whether the two groups' individually preferred positions happen to reinforce or conflict with each other in this specific substitution pattern.
distractor_logic: This is backwards; a strongly activating group like −NH<sub>2</sub> generally has a more decisive directing influence than a deactivating group, since it substantially speeds up reaction at specific positions rather than the deactivating group's more general rate-slowing effect.

Directing-group reasoning extends naturally to disubstituted (and more highly substituted) rings, by considering the combined/reinforcing or competing influence of each substituent present, not just single-substituent cases.

The two groups do not necessarily contribute equally; their relative strengths (here, −NH<sub>2</sub> being a very powerful activator) mean one group's directing preference typically dominates the observed regiochemistry.

(Br<sub>2</sub>/FeBr<sub>3</sub>). Three possible dibromobenzene products are shown above (ortho, meta, para, in that order). Given that −Br is (like −Cl) o,p-directing but net deactivating, which is the LEAST likely major product, and separately, why is the OVERALL reaction rate slower than for benzene itself despite −Br still being o,p-directing?
options: Para-dibromobenzene is the least likely product, since −Br is meta-directing, not o,p-directing
The overall rate is FASTER than benzene, since halogens are always net activating toward electrophilic substitution
All three isomers form in exactly equal amounts, since −Br has no directing preference at all

Meta-dibromobenzene (the middle structure shown) is the least likely major product, since −Br directs new substitution to ortho/para, not meta, positions relative to itself; the overall rate is slower than benzene because −Br's inductive electron withdrawal (from its high electronegativity) dominates over its comparatively weak resonance donation (poor 4p−2p orbital overlap with the ring), making it net deactivating even though it still directs to o/p when reaction does occur
questions.explanation: Like −Cl, the halogen −Br is o,p-directing (via weak resonance lone-pair donation stabilising the arenium ion at ortho/para attack) but net deactivating overall (via stronger inductive electron withdrawal from its high electronegativity, which slows the reaction at ALL positions compared to benzene) — this combination of directing preference and rate effect is the classic 'halogen anomaly' among EAS-directing groups. Since −Br directs to ortho/para, NOT meta, the meta-dibromobenzene isomer is the least favoured of the three shown, while ortho- and para-dibromobenzene are the expected major products (in some experimentally determined ratio, further influenced by sterics favouring para over ortho, similar to the toluene nitration case).
questions.hint: Recall that halogens are the specific, named exception among o,p-directors: they direct to o/p positions but still slow the reaction down overall relative to benzene.
distractor_logic: This misassigns halogens' directing behaviour; −Br (like −Cl) is o,p-directing, not meta-directing, so PARA-dibromobenzene is actually one of the two favoured (not disfavoured) products, and meta is the least likely.
The three isomers do NOT form in equal amounts; −Br has a clear electronic directing preference (o,p over meta), giving ortho and para products predominantly over meta, not an even statistical split.

Halogens are a well-known EXCEPTION to the general 'activating groups are o,p-directors, deactivating groups are meta-directors' pattern; despite being o,p-directors, they are net deactivating (slower than benzene), not activating (faster than benzene).

questions.topic: Aromatic Hydrocarbons: Directive Influence of Substituents
questions.question: Consider −CF<sub>3</sub> (trifluoromethyl) as a ring substituent, versus −CH<sub>3</sub>. Both attach to the ring via an sp<sup>3</sup> carbon with no lone pair on that carbon to donate by resonance, so NEITHER group can donate into the ring by resonance. Yet −CH<sub>3</sub> is activating/o,p-directing while −CF<sub>3</sub> is DEACTIVATING/meta-directing. Explain this contrast using purely inductive reasoning (since resonance donation is unavailable to both).
options: −CF<sub>3</sub> is actually activating and o,p-directing, just like −CH<sub>3</sub>, contrary to established experimental data
Fluorine atoms have no effect on electron density at all since they are too small to matter inductively
Both groups behave identically since neither can donate by resonance, so the deactivating behaviour of −CF<sub>3</sub> must be a resonance effect after all, contradicting the question's premise

−CH<sub>3</sub>'s C−H bonds hyperconjugatively/inductively DONATE electron density toward the ring (alkyl groups are weakly electron-releasing relative to H); −CF<sub>3</sub>'s three highly electronegative fluorines instead inductively WITHDRAW electron density strongly through the attached carbon, making −CF<sub>3</sub> net electron-withdrawing (deactivating) despite having the same basic sp<sup>3</sup>-carbon-attached structural motif as −CH<sub>3</sub>
questions.explanation: Neither −CH<sub>3</sub> nor −CF<sub>3</sub> has a lone pair on the ring-attached carbon to donate by resonance (both are simply sp<sup>3</sup> carbons), so the entire difference in their electronic effect on the ring comes down to INDUCTION. −CH<sub>3</sub>'s C−H bonds are weakly electron-donating relative to a C−H on the ring itself (via hyperconjugation, effectively a mild inductive push of electron density toward the ring), making it activating. −CF<sub>3</sub>, by contrast, has three highly electronegative fluorine atoms pulling electron density strongly AWAY from its carbon (and, through that carbon's bond to the ring, away from the ring itself) — a strong inductive WITHDRAWAL, making −CF<sub>3</sub> deactivating and (like other purely-inductive-withdrawing meta-directors) meta-directing, since ortho/para attack would place positive charge nearer this electron-poor group in the arenium intermediate.
questions.hint: Since resonance donation is ruled out for both groups by the question's own premise, the entire explanation must rest on comparing their inductive (electron-pulling vs. electron-pushing) character.
distractor_logic: Fluorine, despite its small size, is the most electronegative element and exerts a very strong inductive (through-bond) electron-withdrawing effect; this is a well-established and significant electronic influence, not a negligible one.

The question's premise (that neither group can donate by resonance) is correct, and the explanation does NOT require invoking resonance; the deactivating behaviour of −CF<sub>3</sub> is fully explained by strong inductive electron withdrawal from its three fluorines, with no contradiction.

Experimental data consistently shows −CF<sub>3</sub> is deactivating and meta-directing (unlike −CH<sub>3</sub>), precisely because of its strong inductive electron-withdrawing character from the three highly electronegative fluorines.

questions.topic: Aromatic Hydrocarbons: Directive Influence of Substituents
questions.question: Benzoic acid (−COOH substituent) is nitrated. Predict the major product's substitution pattern, and separately explain why Friedel-Crafts alkylation/acylation CANNOT be performed directly on benzoic acid itself (i.e., why this deactivated ring poses an additional practical problem beyond just slow reaction rate).
options: Friedel-Crafts reactions work perfectly well on benzoic acid with no special limitation
−COOH is activating and ortho/para-directing, giving predominantly ortho- and para-nitrobenzoic acid
−COOH has no directing influence at all since it is too far from the ring to have any electronic effect

−COOH is a deactivating, meta-directing group (similar reasoning to −CHO: the carbonyl oxygen withdraws by both induction and resonance, and ortho/para attack would place positive charge on the already electron-poor ring carbon bearing −COOH), so meta-nitrobenzoic acid is the major product; separately, Friedel-Crafts reactions fundamentally fail on any strongly deactivated ring (including benzoic acid) because the Lewis acid catalyst (AlCl<sub>3</sub>) cannot generate a strong enough electrophile-ring interaction on such an electron-poor arene, a general limitation of Friedel-Crafts chemistry on deactivated substrates
questions.explanation: −COOH, like −CHO, is a carbonyl-containing deactivating group: it withdraws electron density from the ring both inductively (electronegative oxygens) and by accepting ring electron density into its own carbonyl π system by resonance, making ortho/para attack (which would place positive charge on the ring carbon nearest this electron-poor group in the arenium intermediate) especially unfavourable — hence meta-directing, giving predominantly meta-nitrobenzoic acid. Separately, it is a well-known general limitation of Friedel-Crafts chemistry (both alkylation and acylation) that it does NOT proceed on rings that are already significantly deactivated (by strong electron-withdrawing groups like −COOH, −NO<sub>2</sub>, −CN, etc.), since the electrophile generated by the Lewis acid catalyst cannot productively react with such an electron-poor aromatic system — this is a standard textbook limitation of the Friedel-Crafts reaction, independent of and in addition to any ordinary rate-slowing consideration.
questions.hint: Compare −COOH's electronic character to the other carbonyl-containing group already analysed (−CHO) for the directing prediction, then recall the standard list of substrates on which Friedel-Crafts reactions are known to fail.
distractor_logic: −COOH is deactivating and meta-directing (analogous to −CHO), not activating; ortho/para-nitrobenzoic acid is the minor, not major, product.
−COOH, being directly attached to the ring, exerts both inductive and resonance electronic effects on it, exactly as −CHO does; it is not too remote to have a directing influence.
Friedel-Crafts reactions specifically FAIL on strongly deactivated rings like benzoic acid; this is a well-documented limitation of the reaction, not a case where it 'works perfectly well'.
mixed_topics: Aromatic Hydrocarbons: Directive Influence of Substituents

questions.topic: Aromatic Hydrocarbons: Directive Influence of Substituents
questions.question: m-Xylene (1,3-dimethylbenzene, two −CH<sub>3</sub> groups meta to each other) is nitrated. Since BOTH methyl groups are o,p-directors (relative to themselves), predict which ring position is most favoured, reconciling both groups' directing preferences simultaneously.
options: The position that is simultaneously ortho/para to BOTH methyl groups (specifically, C4/C6, which sit ortho to one methyl AND para to the other, given the 1,3-relationship of the two methyls) is most strongly favoured, since electrophilic attack there is reinforced (doubly activated) by both substituents' directing preferences pointing to the same position
Since the two methyls are meta to each other, their directing effects necessarily cancel out completely, giving no net preference anywhere on the ring
Nitration cannot occur on m-xylene at all since it already has two substituents
Only C2 (directly between the two methyl groups) can be favoured, since it is ortho to both, ignoring any steric hindrance from being flanked by two substituents
questions.explanation: In m-xylene (methyls at C1 and C3), position C4 is ortho to the C3 methyl and para to the C1 methyl; by symmetry, C6 is ortho to C1 and para to C3 — both C4 and C6 are simultaneously favoured (doubly activated/reinforced) by BOTH methyl groups' o,p-directing preference pointing to the same positions, making them the most favoured sites for further electrophilic substitution. Position C2 (between the two methyls, ortho to both) is also technically doubly-activated electronically but is disfavoured practically due to steric hindrance from being flanked on both sides; C5 (meta to both methyls) receives no directing reinforcement from either group and is the least favoured position overall.
questions.hint: Draw the ring with methyls at C1 and C3, then check each remaining position (C2, C4, C5, C6) for whether it is ortho, meta, or para to EACH of the two existing substituents.
distractor_logic: Further electrophilic substitution on an already-disubstituted ring is a completely normal, well-precedented reaction (as with any disubstituted arene); m-xylene readily undergoes nitration to give a trisubstituted product.

While C2 is indeed ortho to both methyls electronically, it suffers significant steric hindrance from being flanked by two substituents simultaneously, making C4/C6 (each favoured by one ortho + one para relationship, without this steric penalty) the more realistic major site(s).

The two groups' directing effects do not simply cancel from being meta to each other; each methyl group still independently directs to its OWN ortho/para positions, and these preferences can reinforce (add constructively) at certain ring positions like C4 and C6.

questions.question: <svg viewBox="0 0 300 160" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:100%;height:auto"><line x1="100" y1="80" x2="200" y2="80" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="100" y1="74" x2="200" y2="74" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="100" y1="80" x2="40" y2="35" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><text x="34" y="31" font-size="15" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="end" dominant-baseline="middle">CH₃</text><line x1="100" y1="80" x2="40" y2="125" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><text x="34" y="137" font-size="15" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="end" dominant-baseline="middle">CH₃</text><line x1="200" y1="80" x2="260" y2="35" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><text x="266" y="31" font-size="15" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="start" dominant-baseline="middle">CH₃</text><line x1="200" y1="80" x2="260" y2="125" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><text x="266" y="137" font-size="15" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="start" dominant-baseline="middle">CH₃</text></svg> An unknown alkene (shown above, a tetrasubstituted alkene with two methyls on each double-bond carbon) undergoes ozonolysis (O<sub>3</sub>, then Zn/H<sub>2</sub>O). Predict the product(s) and explain why this particular alkene gives an especially SIMPLE ozonolysis outcome.
options: The reductive workup (Zn/H<sub>2</sub>O) converts this alkene directly into an alcohol, not a carbonyl compound

This is 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C=C(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>; ozonolysis cleaves the C=C to give TWO IDENTICAL fragments, each (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C=O (acetone) — because the alkene is symmetric about its double bond (same two substituents, CH<sub>3</sub> and CH<sub>3</sub>, on each carbon), cleavage gives only a single distinct carbonyl product (2 equivalents of acetone) rather than two different fragments
Ozonolysis gives one molecule of acetone and one molecule of formaldehyde as two different fragments
This alkene cannot undergo ozonolysis since it is too heavily substituted
questions.explanation: The shown alkene, 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene, has each double-bond carbon bearing two identical CH<sub>3</sub> groups (perfectly symmetric substitution pattern). Ozonolysis cleaves the C=C bond and converts each carbon into a carbonyl carbon reflecting its own two substituents — here, since both carbons carry the identical (CH<sub>3</sub>, CH<sub>3</sub>) substitution pattern, BOTH resulting carbonyl fragments are identical: (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C=O, i.e., acetone. So the ozonolysis of this single alkene gives 2 equivalents of just ONE product (acetone), rather than a mixture of two structurally different fragments, precisely because of the molecule's symmetry.
questions.hint: Look at the substituents on EACH double-bond carbon individually before deciding whether the two resulting fragments will be identical or different.
distractor_logic: Ozonolysis works on alkenes of any substitution pattern, including fully tetrasubstituted ones like this; substitution level does not block the reaction (though it may affect reaction rate somewhat).

Zn/H<sub>2</sub>O is specifically the REDUCTIVE workup for ozonolysis, converting the ozonide intermediate into CARBONYL compounds (aldehydes/ketones), not alcohols; an oxidative workup (like H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>) would instead push aldehyde products further to carboxylic acids, but neither workup gives alcohols directly.

Both fragments here are identical (acetone from each carbon, since both carbons carry the same CH<sub>3</sub>/CH<sub>3</sub> substitution), not two DIFFERENT fragments like acetone and formaldehyde, which would require an unsymmetrical substitution pattern.

questions.question: <svg viewBox="0 0 300 160" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:100%;height:auto"><line x1="100" y1="80" x2="200" y2="80" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="100" y1="74" x2="200" y2="74" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="100" y1="80" x2="40" y2="35" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><text x="34" y="31" font-size="15" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="end" dominant-baseline="middle">CH₃</text><line x1="100" y1="80" x2="40" y2="125" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><text x="34" y="137" font-size="15" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="end" dominant-baseline="middle">CH₃</text><line x1="200" y1="80" x2="260" y2="35" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><text x="266" y="31" font-size="15" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="start" dominant-baseline="middle">H</text><line x1="200" y1="80" x2="260" y2="125" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><text x="266" y="137" font-size="15" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="start" dominant-baseline="middle">C₂H₅</text></svg> An unknown alkene (shown above) undergoes ozonolysis to give two DIFFERENT carbonyl fragments: acetone, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C=O, and propanal, CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHO. Working BACKWARD from these fragments (structure elucidation), reconstruct the original alkene's identity and confirm it matches the structure shown.
options: The two fragments imply the original compound was an alkyne, not an alkene, since two different fragments formed
The original alkene cannot be determined from ozonolysis fragments alone; the information is fundamentally insufficient

2-Methylpent-2-ene, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C=CH−CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>: removing the '=O' from each fragment and reconnecting the two carbonyl carbons with a double bond gives (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C=CH−CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, matching the shown structure exactly (one carbon bearing two methyls, the other bearing H and an ethyl group)
The original alkene must have been but-2-ene, since both fragments together have 4 total carbons visible in their names
questions.explanation: To reverse-engineer the alkene from ozonolysis fragments, replace each fragment's C=O with a C=C bond joining the two former carbonyl carbons directly, keeping all other substituents attached exactly as they were on each fragment: acetone's carbonyl carbon carries two CH<sub>3</sub> groups, and propanal's carbonyl carbon carries one H and one CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> (ethyl) group; joining these two carbons with a double bond gives (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C=CH−CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, i.e., 2-methylpent-2-ene — exactly matching the structure shown, confirming the reconstruction is correct and self-consistent.
questions.hint: Replace each fragment's C=O double bond with a C−C(=) connection to the OTHER fragment's carbonyl carbon, keeping every other substituent exactly where it was.
distractor_logic: Simply summing carbon counts from fragment NAMES is not the correct reconstruction method; you must track which specific substituents were on each carbonyl carbon and reconnect them properly via a double bond, which gives a 6-carbon alkene (2-methylpent-2-ene), not but-2-ene.

Two different ozonolysis fragments simply reflect an UNSYMMETRICAL alkene (different substituents on the two double-bond carbons), not an alkyne; alkynes undergo a different oxidative cleavage (typically all the way to carboxylic acids under vigorous conditions), not a two-fragment carbonyl-pair outcome via standard ozonolysis.

Ozonolysis fragment identification is in fact a standard, reliable structure-elucidation technique precisely because the fragments directly encode the original double bond's substitution pattern on each side; the information IS sufficient to reconstruct the alkene.

questions.question: <svg viewBox="0 0 300 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:100%;height:auto"><line x1="150.0" y1="45.0" x2="197.6" y2="79.5" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="152.5" y1="55.5" x2="186.8" y2="80.4" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="197.6" y1="79.5" x2="179.4" y2="135.5" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="179.4" y1="135.5" x2="120.6" y2="135.5" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="120.6" y1="135.5" x2="102.4" y2="79.5" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="102.4" y1="79.5" x2="150.0" y2="45.0" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/></svg> Cyclopentene (shown above) undergoes ozonolysis (O<sub>3</sub>, then Zn/H<sub>2</sub>O). Unlike an open-chain alkene (which gives two SEPARATE carbonyl fragments), explain why this RING alkene gives just ONE product, and identify it.
options: Ring alkenes cannot undergo ozonolysis at all, since the ring geometry prevents ozone from approaching the double bond
The ring stays completely intact and unreactive; only the ring's saturated C−H bonds are oxidised instead
Cyclopentene gives the same two separate fragments as any open-chain alkene would, formaldehyde and butanal

Since the double bond is part of a ring, cleaving it does NOT separate the molecule into two pieces (both 'ends' of the broken double bond remain connected via the rest of the ring); the single product is pentanedial (glutaraldehyde), OHC−CH<sub>2</sub>−CH<sub>2</sub>−CH<sub>2</sub>−CHO, a single open-chain DIALDEHYDE where both former ring-double-bond carbons are now converted to separate carbonyl ends of one continuous chain
questions.explanation: Ozonolysis cleaves the C=C bond, converting each of the two former double-bond carbons into a carbonyl. In an OPEN-CHAIN alkene, this cleavage separates the molecule into two distinct, physically separate fragment molecules. In a RING alkene like cyclopentene, however, the two double-bond carbons are ALSO connected to each other via the REST of the ring (the other 3 carbons) — so cleaving the double bond doesn't disconnect the molecule into two pieces; instead it 'opens' the ring into a single, longer open-chain molecule with a carbonyl group at EACH end: pentanedial (glutaraldehyde), OHC−(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>3</sub>−CHO, is the single dialdehyde product, reflecting the ring's original 5 carbons now laid out as a chain.
questions.hint: Trace the ring's connectivity carefully: after breaking just the C=C bond, are the two former double-bond carbons still connected to each other through the rest of the ring, or not?
distractor_logic: Ring alkenes undergo ozonolysis perfectly normally; the C=C double bond, whether in a ring or an open chain, is equally reactive toward ozone.

This is the outcome for an OPEN-CHAIN alkene, not a ring alkene; because cyclopentene's ring keeps both former double-bond carbons connected via the remaining ring carbons, cleavage gives ONE product (a dialdehyde), not two separate fragment molecules.
Ozonolysis specifically targets the C=C double bond (via initial ozonide formation across the π bond), not the ring's saturated C−H or C−C single bonds, which remain untouched by this reaction.

questions.question: <svg viewBox="0 0 300 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:100%;height:auto"><line x1="150.0" y1="45.0" x2="193.3" y2="70.0" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="152.6" y1="54.6" x2="183.7" y2="72.6" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="193.3" y1="70.0" x2="193.3" y2="120.0" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="193.3" y1="120.0" x2="150.0" y2="145.0" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="150.0" y1="145.0" x2="106.7" y2="120.0" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="106.7" y1="120.0" x2="106.7" y2="70.0" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="106.7" y1="70.0" x2="150.0" y2="45.0" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="150.0" y1="45.0" x2="150.0" y2="17.0" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><text x="150.0" y="5.0" font-size="15" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="middle" dominant-baseline="middle">CH₃</text><line x1="193.3" y1="70.0" x2="217.5" y2="56.0" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><text x="227.9" y="50.0" font-size="15" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="start" dominant-baseline="middle">CH₃</text></svg> 1,2-Dimethylcyclohexene (shown above) undergoes ozonolysis. Predict the single ring-opened product, applying the same ring-opening logic as for cyclopentene but now accounting for the two methyl substituents on the former double-bond carbons.
options: Ozonolysis gives two separate fragments, exactly as it would for an open-chain alkene, ignoring the ring
The methyl substituents are cleaved off entirely during ozonolysis, leaving an unsubstituted ring-opened dialdehyde

Heptane-2,6-dione, CH<sub>3</sub>CO−(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>3</sub>−COCH<sub>3</sub>: the ring opens to a single chain (since both former double-bond carbons remain connected via the other 4 ring CH<sub>2</sub> carbons), and each former double-bond carbon becomes a KETONE carbon (not aldehyde), since each already carried a methyl substituent (not H) in addition to the ring connections
The product is pentanedial, identical to unsubstituted cyclopentene's ozonolysis product, since the methyls don't affect the outcome
questions.explanation: 1,2-Dimethylcyclohexene's double bond sits between two ring carbons, EACH of which bears a methyl substituent (in addition to their two ring-carbon connections). Applying the same ring-opening logic as cyclopentene (the ring stays connected as one chain after C=C cleavage, since both former double-bond carbons remain linked via the other 4 CH<sub>2</sub> ring carbons), each former double-bond carbon becomes a carbonyl carbon — but since each carries a CH<sub>3</sub> substituent rather than an H, each becomes a KETONE carbon, not an aldehyde. The resulting single product is heptane-2,6-dione, CH<sub>3</sub>−CO−CH<sub>2</sub>−CH<sub>2</sub>−CH<sub>2</sub>−CO−CH<sub>3</sub> (a 7-carbon chain: 2 methyls + 4 ring CH<sub>2</sub>'s + accounting for the two carbonyl carbons themselves within that count), reflecting both the ring-opening (one product, not two) and the substitution pattern (ketone, not aldehyde, ends).
questions.hint: Apply the SAME ring-opening logic as the unsubstituted cyclopentene case, but now check what's attached to each former double-bond carbon (H, giving an aldehyde end; or CH<sub>3</sub>, giving a ketone end).
distractor_logic: The methyl substituents on the former double-bond carbons directly change the product's structure (ketone ends instead of aldehyde ends, and two extra carbons overall) compared to unsubstituted cyclopentene; they cannot simply be ignored.
Like cyclopentene, this ring alkene also gives a SINGLE ring-opened product (not two separate fragments), since the ring keeps both former double-bond carbons connected via the rest of the ring.

Ozonolysis does not cleave off substituents like methyl groups; it specifically cleaves the C=C double bond itself, converting each double-bond carbon (along with whatever substituents it already carried) into a carbonyl carbon.
