questions.question: <svg viewBox="0 0 300 160" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:100%;height:auto"><line x1="100" y1="80" x2="200" y2="80" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="100" y1="74" x2="200" y2="74" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="100" y1="80" x2="40" y2="35" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><text x="34" y="31" font-size="15" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="end" dominant-baseline="middle">CH₃</text><line x1="100" y1="80" x2="40" y2="125" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><text x="34" y="137" font-size="15" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="end" dominant-baseline="middle">H</text><line x1="200" y1="80" x2="260" y2="35" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><text x="266" y="31" font-size="15" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="start" dominant-baseline="middle">H</text><line x1="200" y1="80" x2="260" y2="125" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><text x="266" y="137" font-size="15" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="start" dominant-baseline="middle">CH₃</text></svg> Both cis-but-2-ene and trans-but-2-ene (the trans isomer shown above) are subjected to ozonolysis (O<sub>3</sub>, then Zn/H<sub>2</sub>O) separately. Compare their ozonolysis PRODUCTS, and explain what this reveals about ozonolysis as a technique for distinguishing cis/trans isomers.
options: Cis-but-2-ene gives acetaldehyde while trans-but-2-ene gives a completely different product, propanal, allowing easy distinction between the two
Ozonolysis cannot be performed on either cis- or trans-alkenes; only terminal alkenes react
The cis isomer gives twice as much product as the trans isomer under identical conditions

Both cis- and trans-but-2-ene give IDENTICAL ozonolysis products (2 equivalents of acetaldehyde, CH<sub>3</sub>CHO in each case), since ozonolysis breaks the C=C bond entirely and destroys any cis/trans spatial information in the process; ozonolysis is therefore USELESS for distinguishing geometric isomers, even though it IS useful for distinguishing constitutional isomers (different substitution patterns)
questions.explanation: Both cis- and trans-but-2-ene have the SAME constitutional structure (CH<sub>3</sub>−CH=CH−CH<sub>3</sub>) and thus the same substituents on each double-bond carbon (CH<sub>3</sub> and H); ozonolysis of either isomer cleaves the C=C bond and gives 2 equivalents of acetaldehyde, CH<sub>3</sub>CHO, REGARDLESS of whether the starting material was cis or trans, because the cleavage process itself destroys the spatial (cis/trans) relationship entirely — once the double bond is broken, there is no longer any restricted rotation to preserve that geometric information. This demonstrates an important limitation: ozonolysis is a powerful tool for determining CONSTITUTIONAL structure (which substituents were on the double bond) but provides NO information about the original alkene's geometric (cis/trans) configuration.
questions.hint: Ask whether the fragments resulting from ozonolysis retain any 'memory' of which side of the (now-broken) double bond each substituent was originally on.
distractor_logic: Cis and trans isomers share the same CONSTITUTIONAL structure (same atoms bonded to each other in the same pattern, differing only in spatial arrangement); ozonolysis, which only reveals constitutional information, cannot distinguish them and gives the same fragment (acetaldehyde) from both.
Both cis- and trans-alkenes (not just terminal alkenes) undergo ozonolysis readily; the reaction targets any C=C double bond, regardless of its substitution pattern or geometry.

Under identical stoichiometric conditions, both isomers give the same molar yield of the same product (acetaldehyde); there is no inherent quantitative difference in product amount between the cis and trans starting materials.

questions.question: <svg viewBox="0 0 300 160" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" style="max-width:100%;height:auto"><line x1="100" y1="80" x2="200" y2="80" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="100" y1="74" x2="200" y2="74" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="100" y1="80" x2="40" y2="35" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><text x="34" y="31" font-size="15" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="end" dominant-baseline="middle">CH₃</text><line x1="100" y1="80" x2="40" y2="125" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><text x="34" y="137" font-size="15" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="end" dominant-baseline="middle">C₂H₅</text><line x1="200" y1="80" x2="260" y2="35" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><text x="266" y="31" font-size="15" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="start" dominant-baseline="middle">CH₃</text><line x1="200" y1="80" x2="260" y2="125" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2"/><text x="266" y="137" font-size="15" fill="currentColor" text-anchor="start" dominant-baseline="middle">H</text></svg> An unknown trisubstituted alkene (shown above) is ozonolysed to give two fragments: butan-2-one, CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, and acetaldehyde, CH<sub>3</sub>CHO. Reconstruct the original alkene and verify it matches the structure shown.
options: 3-Methylpent-2-ene, CH<sub>3</sub>−CH=C(CH<sub>3</sub>)−CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>: butan-2-one's carbonyl carbon carries CH<sub>3</sub> and CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> (ethyl), and acetaldehyde's carbonyl carbon carries CH<sub>3</sub> and H; joining these two carbons with a double bond, keeping all substituents attached exactly as they were, reconstructs CH<sub>3</sub>−CH=C(CH<sub>3</sub>)−CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, matching the trisubstituted alkene shown
Reconstruction is impossible since one fragment is a ketone and the other is an aldehyde, an inconsistent combination
The original alkene must have had FOUR substituents (fully tetrasubstituted) on its double bond, since two different fragments formed
The original alkene was but-2-ene, since acetaldehyde alone suggests a 4-carbon symmetric alkene
questions.explanation: Butan-2-one's carbonyl carbon (originally a double-bond carbon) carries a CH<sub>3</sub> group on one side and a CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> (ethyl) group on the other — a disubstituted (no H) carbon. Acetaldehyde's carbonyl carbon carries a CH<sub>3</sub> group and an H — a monosubstituted carbon. Reconnecting these two carbonyl carbons with a double bond (replacing both C=O's with one C=C, keeping every substituent exactly as found) gives CH<sub>3</sub>−CH=C(CH<sub>3</sub>)−CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, i.e., 3-methylpent-2-ene — a TRIsubstituted alkene (three alkyl groups plus one H around the double bond), exactly matching the structure shown, confirming the reconstruction.
questions.hint: Note which fragment is a ketone (no H on that carbonyl carbon, meaning that double-bond carbon had two alkyl substituents) versus an aldehyde (one H, meaning that carbon had only one substituent besides H) before reconnecting.
distractor_logic: A ketone-plus-aldehyde fragment pair is a completely normal, expected outcome for an UNSYMMETRICAL, trisubstituted alkene (one double-bond carbon bearing two alkyl groups, the other bearing one alkyl group and one H); this combination is not inconsistent.

A ketone fragment (from a disubstituted double-bond carbon) plus an aldehyde fragment (from a monosubstituted double-bond carbon) together indicate a TRIsubstituted alkene overall (2+1 substituents on the double bond, plus 1 H), not a fully tetrasubstituted one, which would require BOTH fragments to be ketones.

Considering only one fragment (acetaldehyde) in isolation ignores the other fragment (butan-2-one) entirely; the full reconstruction requires combining information from BOTH fragments, which together indicate a 6-carbon, trisubstituted alkene, not but-2-ene.

questions.question: An unknown alkene, subjected to OXIDATIVE ozonolysis workup (O<sub>3</sub>, then H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>, rather than the reductive Zn/H<sub>2</sub>O), gives one equivalent of acetone and one equivalent of acetic acid (CH<sub>3</sub>COOH) as the two fragments. Explain how the oxidative workup changes fragment identity compared to reductive workup, and reconstruct the original alkene.
options: H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> workup converts KETONE fragments into carboxylic acids, while leaving aldehyde fragments unchanged, the reverse of the correct behaviour
Oxidative and reductive workups always give identical fragment sets for any alkene, so the workup choice is irrelevant to fragment identity

Oxidative workup (H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>) further oxidises any ALDEHYDE fragment all the way to a CARBOXYLIC ACID (while a KETONE fragment, having no H on the carbonyl carbon to begin with, is unaffected and remains a ketone under either workup); so acetic acid here actually originated as acetaldehyde (CH<sub>3</sub>CHO) under reductive conditions, meaning the original alkene was 2-methylbut-2-ene, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C=CH−CH<sub>3</sub>, which under Zn/H<sub>2</sub>O would have given acetone + acetaldehyde, but under H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> gives acetone + acetic acid instead
The presence of a carboxylic acid fragment means the ORIGINAL molecule must have been a carboxylic acid to begin with, not an alkene
questions.explanation: The key distinction between reductive (Zn/H<sub>2</sub>O, or Zn/AcOH) and oxidative (H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>) ozonolysis workup is specifically how ALDEHYDE-generating positions are handled: reductive workup stops at the aldehyde, while oxidative workup further oxidises that aldehyde to a carboxylic acid; ketone-generating positions (from disubstituted double-bond carbons, with no H to further oxidise on that carbon) are unaffected by either workup and give the same ketone regardless. So observing acetone (ketone, from a disubstituted carbon) + acetic acid (carboxylic acid, meaning oxidative workup pushed an aldehyde further) together tells you the original alkene had one disubstituted double-bond carbon (bearing 2 CH<sub>3</sub> groups, giving acetone) and one monosubstituted double-bond carbon (bearing 1 CH<sub>3</sub> and 1 H, which would have given acetaldehyde under reductive conditions, but is over-oxidised to acetic acid here) — reconstructing to 2-methylbut-2-ene, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>C=CH−CH<sub>3</sub>.
questions.hint: Ask which TYPE of carbonyl fragment (aldehyde, with an H, or ketone, with no H) is capable of being further oxidised, and work out what that fragment would have looked like under the milder, reductive workup instead.
distractor_logic: This reverses the correct behaviour; it is ALDEHYDE fragments (with an available H on the carbonyl carbon) that get further oxidised to carboxylic acids under H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> workup, while ketone fragments (no H available) are unaffected, not the other way around.

The carboxylic acid observed here is a WORKUP ARTIFACT (an aldehyde fragment that was further oxidised during the oxidative workup step), not evidence that the original starting material itself was a carboxylic acid; the original compound was an alkene, as stated.

The two workups genuinely give different fragment identities specifically at positions that would otherwise be aldehydes; oxidative workup pushes those all the way to carboxylic acids, so the fragment sets are NOT identical between the two workup choices.
